patterns.name: Australian IPND Customer Record (Integrated Public Number Database)
patterns.description: Integrated Public Number Database (IPND) data exchanged between carriage service providers, Data Providers, Data Users and the IPND Manager (Telstra): fixed-width upload and download files (HDR header record with an IPND file type, 905-character customer records, TRL trailer record), IPND file names (IPNDUP upload, IPNDES/LA/DI/LD/RS/EW download) and IPND extracts or reject reports listing public numbers with their List Code. List Code UL (Unlisted Number) and SA (Suppressed Address) records are protected by Telecommunications Act 1997 Part 13 (s 276 disclosure offence; s 285 permitted IPND uses exclude unlisted numbers). "Silent number" is an informal synonym for an unlisted number, not IPND terminology, and is used only as weak corroboration.
patterns.operation: Primary (65, discovery only): "Integrated Public Number Database", the token IPND, or an IPND HDR header record (HDRIPND + file type UP/PE/DI/ES/LA/LD/RS/PR/QU/QR/QP). 75: primary plus one IPND record structure: a fixed-width customer record laid out per the Telstra technical requirements (public number padded to 20 characters, Service Status C/D at position 21, List Code LE/UL/SA at 740-741 followed by a Usage Code R/B/G/C/N, and a 14-digit YYYYMMDDHHMMSS Transaction Date at 857-870), or a populated "List Code: UL/SA/LE" or "Public Number: <Australian number>" field. 85: primary plus two distinct record-structure hits (min_count 2, unique) plus either an IPND file artefact (IPNDUP upload file name, IPND download file name, or a TRL trailer record with sequence number, creation time and record count) or an independent IPND/Part 13 keyword (unlisted number, suppressed address, Data Provider, IPND Manager). Every tier ANDs NOT template/noise exclusion and NOT the IPND specification itself ("Technical Requirements for IPND", "Field Name Format From To Mandatory", "IPND User Guidelines for Data Files"). Proximity is 3000 characters because IPND records are 905 characters wide, so the header and the first two customer records sit about 2,700 characters apart.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium. The fixed-width customer record regex is tied to verified field positions (Telstra Data Users and Data Providers Technical Requirements for IPND, section 6) and is very specific. The labelled "List Code:" / "Public Number:" path is looser and can appear in CSP internal tooling or correspondence. The IPND specification and user guidelines contain the same header, file-type and list-code vocabulary, so they are explicitly excluded. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test records are synthetic, use ACMA-reserved fictional number ranges (07 5550 xxxx, 02 5550 xxxx, 0491 570 156) and were generated at the published field offsets.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier identifies IPND customer data: fixed-width IPND upload/download records and IPND extracts that link a public number to a customer name, service address and List Code. Records coded UL (Unlisted Number) or SA (Suppressed Address) exist because the customer asked for the number or address to be kept out of directories; disclosure is an offence under Telecommunications Act 1997 s 276 and can expose people who are hiding from a violent partner or stalker to physical harm. A bulk IPND file holds up to 10,000 such records per upload. Specification text, guidance, blank forms and training material are excluded from enforce tiers. Risk 9 supports PROTECTED Personal-Privacy because IPND data moves in bulk files that can expose many unlisted and suppressed-address customers at once.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED Personal-Privacy (PROT_Pvc) and the High tier because IPND records link a number to a name, service address and List Code, including UL and SA entries protected under Telecommunications Act s 276, and IPND data moves in bulk files of up to 10,000 records. Bulk suppressed-address data can expose people hiding from a violent partner or stalker, the same harm as silent elector records (PROTECTED, risk 10) and DFV-affected telco customer records (PROTECTED, risk 10).

generic.rationale: High Personal-Privacy handling applies because an IPND file can reveal the addresses of many customers who asked for them to be suppressed. Access should be limited to the staff who exchange data with the IPND Manager.

patterns.name: Telecommunications Act s 306 Law Enforcement Disclosure Record
patterns.description: Records that carriers and carriage service providers must make of disclosures of protected information (Telecommunications Act 1997 (Cth) Part 13, s 276 primary offence) to law enforcement and enforcement agencies: the s 306 record (made within 5 days of the disclosure and kept for 3 years) and the s 306A record for prospective authorisations. A populated record gives the name of the person who disclosed the information, the date of disclosure, the grounds (for example s 280 authorised by law, s 313 assistance), warrant or authorisation details including authorisations under ss 178, 179 or 180 of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979, the authorising officer and date, the requesting agency and request date, the service disclosed and the s 187AA data-set items. The same fields appear in agency authorisation / request notices received by the provider. OAIC guidance, the Acts, ACMA and TIA Act annual report statistics and blank templates are decoys. Overlaps with lawful-interception-warrant, which covers interception and stored communications warrants (TIA Act secrecy) rather than Part 13 disclosure records; a record that cites the TIA Act next to a service number may also fire that classifier.
patterns.operation: Primary: "section 306/306A record/register/disclosure", "record of (the) disclosure", "disclosure record/register", "Part 13 disclosure/record", a s 276/280/313 Telecommunications Act reference, "Telecommunications Act 1997", "prospective authorisation", or an authorisation under TIA Act s 178/179/180 (incl. 180A/180B). 65 is discovery-only (primary alone) and surfaces OAIC guidance, legislation and annual reports. 75 requires one populated field within 300 characters: name of the person who disclosed / authorising officer / requesting (enforcement) agency, a dated disclosure / authorisation / request / first-last disclosure field, grounds for the disclosure (a section reference or populated statement), an agency / authorisation / warrant reference containing a digit, a service number / carriage service / account number value, or a populated information-disclosed / s 187AA item field. Blank lines, bracket placeholders and n/a/tbc are rejected. 85 requires two distinct populated fields plus an independent corroborative term (enforcement agency, criminal law-enforcement agency, police, AFP, QPS, ASIO, TIA Act, 187AA, subscriber details, call charge records and similar). Every tier excludes template/fixture text; enforce tiers also exclude guidance/legislation and annual report signals.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: the s 306/306A record fields and TIA Act authorisation sections are specific, but OAIC guidance, carrier compliance manuals and legislation repeat them, and "record of disclosure" is also used for Privacy Act APP 6 notes. Enforce tiers require populated disclosure fields. Agency request and authorisation reference formats vary by agency and are matched only as labelled values containing a digit. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic (service numbers from the ACMA fictitious 0491 570 range).

customisation.note: Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's law enforcement request / authorisation reference format (see docs/identifiers.md#lea-request-reference). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

patterns.name: Completed TFN Declaration or Superannuation Standard Choice Form
patterns.description: Completed ATO Tax file number declaration (NAT 3092) and Superannuation standard choice form (NAT 13080) held by an employer: the form title or number together with populated fields such as a checksum-valid TFN, the payee's name or date of birth, the employee identification number, ticked residency or tax-free threshold answers, and the chosen fund's ABN, unique superannuation identifier (USI) or member number.
patterns.operation: Primary: the form title or number (tax file number declaration, TFN declaration, NAT 3092, superannuation standard choice form, standard choice form, NAT 13080). 65 is discovery-only (title alone) and surfaces ATO guidance, onboarding checklists and blank forms. 75 requires the title plus one populated field: a 9-digit TFN that passes the ATO mod-11 checksum, a populated person field (surname / given name / payee or employee name, employee identification number, date of birth with a date), a ticked residency or tax-free-threshold answer ([X], ☒, ☑, ✓), or a populated fund field (fund ABN, USI, member number, value containing a digit). 85 has two routes. For a TFN declaration it needs the title, the TFN, a person field, and a ticked answer or a fund field. For a choice form it needs the title, a person field, and two distinct fund fields. All tiers exclude template/fixture text.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium-high in practice: the titles and NAT numbers are specific, and the TFN evidence carries the ATO mod-11 checksum validator in the exported SIT (the local test harness does not evaluate checksums, so tests use checksum-valid values). The 75 route with only a person or fund field can fire on onboarding trackers that list a new starter's forms with dates of birth. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; tests are synthetic.

customisation.note: Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's superannuation member number format (see docs/identifiers.md#super-member-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

That set is enough to impersonate the person to the ATO or a super fund, lodge false returns or redirect super, and TFN handling is specifically regulated. Each form is one person's record; bulk payroll files with many TFNs are covered at higher risk by payroll-master-file-with-tax-file-numbers. Risk 7 supports OFFICIAL: Sensitive / SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy and Medium because a completed NAT 3092 or NAT 13080 combines a TFN with name, date of birth, residency and super fund membership, enough to impersonate the person to the ATO or a fund. PROTECTED is not met because each form is one person's record; bulk payroll files are rated separately.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling applies to a regulated tax identifier combined with identity and fund details. A single form is not High; bulk TFN files carry the stronger treatment.

patterns.name: Titled Person Reference
patterns.description: Identifies personal names preceded by salutations (Mr, Mrs, Ms, Dr, Prof, etc.) in Australian documents. Uses structural regex for honorific + capitalised name components with corroborative evidence from the consolidated Australian forename and surname dictionaries.
patterns.operation: Primary: honorific (Mr, Mrs, Miss, Ms, Dr, Prof, Rev, Hon, Sir, Dame, Lord, Lady) followed by two or three capitalised name tokens (case-sensitive). 65 (discovery only): titled name alone. 75: titled name plus at least one Australian forename or surname registry hit plus a populated contact/identity field (phone, mobile, email, address, DOB, customer/client/member/employee/patient/account/reference number). 85: titled name plus both forename and surname registry hits plus two distinct populated contact/identity fields. Business-name and street-address collisions and template framing are excluded from 75/85.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: a titled name alone is common in correspondence and public text, so enforce tiers now need an independent populated contact or identity field next to the name; the registry dictionaries confirm the tokens are plausible names but are not counted as independent evidence.

patterns.risk_description: A Titled Person Reference match combines an honorific with two or three capitalised name tokens and, to enforce, name-registry evidence plus a populated contact or identity field (phone, email, address, DOB or customer/member number); a titled name alone stays at 65 discovery. It can expose an identifiable person's name and role cue, which may aid correlation, unwanted contact, or a tailored professional pretext. Names and titles are often public, and the match contains no account, case, contact route, or credential. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL recognise a likely populated identity reference while reserving SENSITIVE for a name linked to substantive private or operational information.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to OFFICIAL and Low tiers because the detector can return a real titled name but ordinarily exposes only public-facing identity information. SENSITIVE is not met without confidential role context, contact details, a protected person, or a consequential personal record.

generic.rationale: A title plus personal name is generically Low with Low DLM because the combination is commonly observable and has bounded standalone confidentiality impact.

patterns.risk_description: The Legal full name pattern detects labels such as legal name, full name, given name, or surname, rather than resolving the text entered into that field. A standalone match usually communicates that a form or record expects identity information and can appear in blank templates, policies, or HR instructions. A completed name combined with account, employment, or case data would add correlation and targeting risk, but that content is not guaranteed by this detector. Risk 3 and OFFICIAL follow the phrase-level unit and avoid treating a field heading as a populated personal record.

patterns.risk_description: The detector recognises SCADA network diagram terminology with seven nearby critical-infrastructure terms and can match topology text containing HMI, RTU, PLC, protocols, VLANs, and addresses. A genuine diagram can reveal trust boundaries, device relationships, remote links, and management paths, reducing an attacker's discovery effort and supporting disruption. Training diagrams, standards, and generic architecture guidance remain plausible collisions because the medium-confidence regex does not verify a live operational network. For the Australian catalogue pattern, the confirmed substantive record is the consequence unit. A real topology exposes HMI/RTU/PLC relationships, trust zones, remote links, protocols and management paths. It materially lowers attack cost against an operational control environment and can support significant outage or safety damage. Risk 9 and PROTECTED InfoTech therefore apply to the confirmed record itself. Require asset relationships, addresses/VLANs/protocols and site/system identifiers; training diagrams and standards stay audit-only. This is confidence and exception handling, not a reason to reduce the consequence of a true positive.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 is warranted because a real topology exposes HMI/RTU/PLC relationships, trust zones, remote links, protocols and management paths. PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED InfoTech, PROT_IT, High and High InfoTech align with that credible significant-damage case. The Australian jurisdiction expression must be assessed on the genuine record rather than on its policy or training collisions. Require asset relationships, addresses/VLANs/protocols and site/system identifiers; training diagrams and standards stay audit-only. Those controls govern match disposition while the confirmed record remains PROTECTED.

generic.rationale: High InfoTech handling is appropriate because a real topology exposes HMI/RTU/PLC relationships, trust zones, remote links, protocols and management paths. Access should be restricted to operators and engineers responsible for the affected control environment or essential service. Lower-confidence Australian topic hits that lack the substantive record structure remain matching exceptions.

patterns.description: Content of an aviation industry participant's Transport Security Program (TSP, Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 s 16; disclosing TSP content without the participant's consent is an offence under Aviation Transport Security Regulations 2005 reg 2.06) and of maritime security plans, ship security plans and offshore security plans (Maritime Transport and Offshore Facilities Security Regulations 2003 regs 3.12, 4.115 and 5A.105 require them to be protected against unauthorised access, amendment and disclosure). Enforcement needs populated plan structure: named port / company / ship / offshore security officers (PSO, CSO, SSO), 24-hour security contact numbers, restricted and cleared zone or screening point tables, and executed Declarations of Security. Australian law has no "Security Sensitive Information" marking; US TSA Sensitive Security Information (49 CFR 1520) material is an explicit exclusion.
patterns.operation: Primary: "Transport Security Program(me)", "Maritime Security Plan", "Ship Security Plan", "Offshore (Facility) Security Plan" or "International Ship Security Certificate". 65 is discovery-only (primary alone) and will surface Home Affairs guidance, airport and port web pages and articles. 75 requires one populated plan structure within 300 characters: a security officer or security manager label (PSO/CSO/SSO or port/company/ship/offshore/airport/aviation security officer, manager or contact) followed by a person's name, a 24-hour / after-hours security contact with an Australian phone number, a land-side / water-side / air-side restricted zone, cleared zone, restricted zone or screening point row with a non-placeholder identifier, or a Declaration of Security with a reference number or a signed/agreed date. 85 requires two distinct structure hits plus an independent corroborative term (unlawful interference, approved by the Secretary, maritime security level, the Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 or Maritime Transport and Offshore Facilities Security Act 2003, TSP, ISSC). Every tier excludes template/fixture text; enforce tiers also exclude US SSI (49 CFR, 33 CFR, Transportation Security Administration, "Sensitive Security Information"), homeaffairs.gov.au / legislation.gov.au guidance and training-course wording.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: the plan names are statutory, but no marking is mandated and there is no public plan identifier, so enforcement relies on populated plan content (officer names, contact numbers, zone and screening-point tables, Declarations of Security). "Ship Security Plan" is also an international ISPS term, so non-Australian ship plans with the same structure will enforce. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier identifies populated content of an aviation Transport Security Program or a maritime, ship or offshore security plan: named security officers and their 24-hour numbers, restricted and cleared zone layouts, screening points and Declarations of Security. This is the operational blueprint an attacker would need to defeat preventive security at an airport, port, ship or offshore facility. Disclosing TSP content without consent is an offence (ATSR reg 2.06) and plans must be protected against unauthorised access and disclosure (MTOFSR regs 3.12, 4.115, 5A.105). Guidance, templates, US SSI material and training are excluded from enforce tiers. Risk 9 supports PROTECTED Government because one plan is a blueprint for defeating preventive security at the facility it covers.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED Government (PROT_Gov) and the High tier because a populated TSP or maritime, ship or offshore security plan gives named officers, 24-hour contacts, restricted zone layouts and screening points: an operational blueprint for defeating preventive security at an airport, port, ship or offshore facility. The label follows that harm. No Australian marking is mandated for these plans; ATSR reg 2.06 and the MTOFSR add disclosure restrictions on top.

generic.rationale: High Government handling applies, with statutory disclosure restrictions on top, because one participant's plan shows how its screening and restricted zones work. Access should be limited to the participant's security staff and the regulator.

patterns.name: Unique Student Identifier
patterns.description: Detects Unique Student Identifier (USI) patterns. A 10-character alphanumeric code (uppercase letters and digits) mandatory since January 2023 for higher education in Australia. The Purview design inventories the broad bare shape at 65, enforces a labelled value in education context at 75, and reserves 85 for labelled values with authoritative USI/VET record context.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern using universal engine. The top-level regex \b[A-Z0-9]{10}\b matches exactly 10 uppercase alphanumeric characters. The Purview engine uses two regexes: Pattern_usi_labeled (labeled format with USI/Unique Student Identifier/student identifier prefix + 10 alphanumeric chars) and Pattern_au_usi (bare 10-char format). The 65 tier is discovery-only; 75 requires the embedded USI label plus education context; 85 additionally requires USI Registry, Student Identifiers Act, RTO, AVETMISS, or equivalent authoritative record context. Template/sample text and repeated/sentinel digit values are excluded.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence: a 10-character uppercase alphanumeric pattern is extremely broad and will match tracking numbers, serial codes, product IDs, and many other identifiers. Corroborative evidence keywords such as USI, student identifier, or TAFE are essential for reliable detection.
regulations: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)

patterns.risk_description: This identifier detector matches a ten-character uppercase alphanumeric value and raises confidence when USI labels and education terms appear within the configured window. A genuine Unique Student Identifier persistently links one learner across Australian training providers, so disclosure can support record correlation, targeted impersonation, or unauthorised education enquiries. The broad bare format can collide with product codes and telephone-shaped strings, and the pattern's overall confidence is low, limiting certainty from an isolated token. Risk 6 and SENSITIVE Government fit a contextualised persistent learner identifier; PROTECTED requires linked identity evidence, bulk learner records, or significant damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 6 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, Government DLM, SENS_Gov, and Medium tier for a persistent education identifier. The next PROTECTED level is not met because a USI alone is not an authentication secret and the detector does not establish linked records, bulk exposure, or significant damage.

generic.rationale: Generic Medium Government now matches the accepted SENSITIVE crosswalk for one contextualised USI, without treating the identifier alone as a protected credential.

patterns.name: WHS Health Monitoring, Audiometric or Fitness-for-Work Medical Record
patterns.description: Statutory worker health monitoring records under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) and the model WHS Regulations: health monitoring reports for hazardous chemicals listed in Schedule 14 (including crystalline silica, isocyanates, cadmium and arsenic; ss 368, 374-378), lead (ss 406-418, blood lead levels) and asbestos (ss 435-444), audiometric testing for noise (s 58), plus pre-employment medicals and fitness-for-work / periodic medical assessments. The Regulation requires these reports to name the worker and date of birth, the registered medical practitioner and registration number, test results, disease advice, remedial recommendations and counselling needs, and to be kept as confidential records (30 years for hazardous chemicals and lead, 40 years for asbestos) not disclosed without the worker's written consent. Workplace drug and alcohol testing is out of scope (see au-drug-alcohol-test-result).
patterns.operation: Primary: health monitoring report / record / results / program / assessment, audiometric test / testing / assessment / report, audiogram, pre-employment medical or health assessment, fitness for work / duty medical / assessment / examination, biological monitoring, blood lead level / test / monitoring, respiratory (health) surveillance, silica health assessment / monitoring, periodic medical / health assessment. 65 is discovery-only (primary alone) and will surface WorkSafe / Safe Work Australia guidance, codes of practice, blank forms and policies. 75 requires a populated worker field (worker / employee / name, date of birth, employer / PCBU, occupation or position, with a non-placeholder value) AND a test-result structure within 300 characters: spirometry values (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC with L or %), blood lead in umol/L or ug/dL, urinary arsenic / cadmium / mercury / MOCA values, audiogram threshold values (Hz with dB, or dB HL), percentage loss of hearing, a chest X-ray finding, or a labelled fitness / result outcome (fit, unfit, fit with restrictions, normal, abnormal). 85 additionally requires a practitioner / recommendation / exposure structure (registered or examining medical practitioner by name, medical or AHPRA registration number, recommendation or remedial measures with a value, medical counselling required yes / no, hazardous chemical / substance / exposure with a value) plus an independent health-monitoring context term (Schedule 14, WHS Regulation, crystalline silica, asbestos, isocyanates, exposure standard, hearing threshold, spirometry, occupational history, remedial measures). Every tier excludes template/fixture text; enforce tiers also exclude legislation text, codes of practice, fact sheets / guides and course material.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: the report types are distinctive and test-result shapes (spirometry, blood lead, audiogram thresholds) are strong, but the same terms fill WHS guidance, codes of practice and occupational health brochures. patterns.name: Worker Screening or Background Check Outcome (AusCheck CIBCO, NDIS, Criminal History, Security Clearance)
patterns.description: Outcome records of worker screening and background checks about an identified person: the AusCheck Critical Infrastructure Background Check Outcome (CIBCO) used for SOCI critical workers under the CIRMP Rules (LIN 23/006 s 9; enhanced requirements LIN 26/075 s 9A), with findings such as Unfavourable Criminal History, CIRMP security-relevant offence, meets / does not meet statutory criteria, Adverse or Qualified Security Assessment; NDIS / Queensland disability worker screening clearance, exclusion, interim bar or negative notice (Disability Services Act 2006 (Qld)); national police check / criminal history check results; and security clearance outcomes at the PSPF Policy 12 levels (Baseline, NV1, NV2, PV). Screening reference, clearance and application numbers have no public format and are matched only by label. Bare reference numbers are covered by au-police-check-reference; clearance mentions without an outcome record by global-security-clearance-reference.
patterns.operation: Primary: Critical Infrastructure Background Check (Outcome), CIBCO, AusCheck background check / outcome / result / advice, critical worker suitability / background check / assessment, Adverse / Qualified Security Assessment, Unfavourable Criminal History, (NDIS / disability) worker screening check / clearance / exclusion / outcome / decision, police check / criminal history check result or outcome, security clearance outcome / decision / status, background check outcome. 65 is discovery-only (primary alone) and will surface AusCheck / NDIS Commission / CISC guidance, CIRMP Rules text, fact sheets and job ads. 75 requires a populated person field (applicant, worker, employee, candidate, full name, surname, given names, date of birth, position with a non-placeholder value) AND a labelled outcome (outcome / result / decision / finding / status / clearance level / criminal history / security assessment / suitability with a value such as meets or does not meet statutory criteria, unfavourable, no disclosable court outcomes, adverse, qualified, non-prejudicial, cleared, clearance granted, excluded, interim bar, negative notice, suitable / not suitable, granted / denied / revoked, Baseline, NV1, NV2, PV) within 300 characters. 85 additionally requires a check reference / authority / date field (application, reference, check, clearance, AusCheck, CIBCO or worker screening number by label; date of decision / outcome / check / application / expiry; issuing authority, screening unit or responsible entity code with a value) plus an independent screening context term (CIRMP, critical component, responsible entity, statutory criteria, ASIO, AGSVA, NDIS Commission, Disability Services Act 2006, identity verification, re-check). Every tier excludes template/fixture text; enforce tiers also exclude legislation text, fact sheets, guidance pages and job ads ("must be able to obtain", "apply now").
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: CIBCO, the AusCheck outcome terms and the worker screening outcome words are specific, but screening and clearance terms are heavily used in guidance, CIRMP policy documents and job ads, and no reference or clearance number has a public format. Enforce tiers therefore require a populated person plus a labelled outcome, and 85 a reference / authority / date. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic.
regulations: Security of Critical Infrastructure (Critical infrastructure risk management program) Rules (LIN 23/006) 2023 s 9, s 9A

patterns.name: Workforce Diversity or EEO Row-Level Extract
patterns.description: Row-level workforce diversity and equal employment opportunity (EEO) extracts: HRIS or payroll exports prepared for Workplace Gender Equality Agency (WGEA) reporting, Queensland public sector MOHRI workforce data and the workforce diversity census, equity and diversity audits under the Public Sector Act 2022 (Qld) ss 27-29, and internal diversity dashboards' source data. Each row ties an employee identifier to diversity attributes such as Aboriginal and / or Torres Strait Islander status, disability, culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) or non-English speaking background, language spoken at home, country of birth, gender and, where collected, sexuality. Aggregate reports, published workforce statistics and survey questionnaires are out of scope.
patterns.operation: Primary: a delimited header row (comma, pipe, tab or semicolon separated) that contains an employee identifier column (employee / staff / payroll / personnel ID, number or code, EmpID, AGS number) and at least two diversity attribute columns (ATSI / Indigenous / Aboriginal and / or Torres Strait Islander / First Nations status, disability, CALD, NESB, non-English speaking background, language spoken at home, main language, country of birth, ethnicity, cultural background, gender / gender identity, sex, sexuality / sexual orientation, LGBTIQ+), in any column order. 65 is discovery-only (header row alone) and surfaces data dictionaries, extract specifications and empty exports. 75 requires one populated data row within 300 characters: an ID-like value (0-3 letters then 3-10 digits) followed on the same line by two delimited diversity values (female, male, woman, man, non-binary, gender diverse, F, M, X, Y, N, yes, no, Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islander, both, neither, Indigenous, non-Indigenous, not stated, prefer not to say, declined, CALD, NESB, heterosexual, gay, lesbian, bisexual, queer, asexual and similar). 85 requires at least two distinct populated data rows. Every enforce tier excludes template/fixture text and data dictionary, valid values, policy, survey and guide wording. Space-aligned tables (for example PDF text without delimiters) and rows whose employee ID follows the diversity values are not matched.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: a delimited header row that joins an employee identifier to two or more diversity columns, followed by rows of ID-plus-attribute values, is distinctive of a row-level extract, and aggregate reports, questionnaires and policies do not carry it. Row values such as Y / N and F / M are generic, so a header-gated HR extract with unrelated yes / no columns can reach 75, and extracts with unusual column names or space-aligned layouts are missed. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic extracts laid out like WGEA and MOHRI source files.

customisation.note: Extend the populated-field evidence with the customer's employee ID / payroll number format (see docs/identifiers.md#employee-id). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier identifies row-level diversity and EEO extracts: an employee identifier joined to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status, disability, CALD / language, gender and sometimes sexuality, for each employee in the file. Those attributes are sensitive information under the Privacy Act 1988 (racial or ethnic origin, sexual orientation, health) and are collected by agencies on a voluntary, confidential basis for WGEA reporting, MOHRI and the Queensland workforce diversity census. Breach evidence shows HR extracts leaking from non-HR systems: the 2025 Western Sydney University incident exposed ethnicity, citizenship and disability data, and the 2026 PeopleSoft campaign exposed ethnicity and disability fields from student and HR records. A leaked extract exposes many people's identity attributes at once, invites discrimination and harassment, and undermines voluntary disclosure. Risk 8 aligns with the bulk sensitive-person-attribute classifiers (global-top500-015-sexual-orientation, global-top500-387-disability-assessment-records) one band above the single-attribute phrase classifiers (global-racial-ethnic-origin, risk 7), with the same SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy marking.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy and Medium because each row joins an employee identifier to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status, disability, CALD or sexuality data collected voluntarily for WGEA or MOHRI. PROTECTED is not met because the extract is workforce-scale HR data, not significant-damage material.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling applies to row-level special-category attributes across many employees. It is not High because the attributes, while sensitive, do not carry severe safety or systemic consequences.

patterns.name: Workplace Sexual Harassment, Bullying and Psychosocial Hazard Complaint
patterns.description: Complaints, reports and case records about sexual harassment, sex-based harassment, workplace bullying and psychosocial hazards that name the people involved: complainant and respondent details, incident date, location and alleged conduct, interim measures, investigation and outcome. Anchored on the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) s 47C positive duty, the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) psychosocial risk provisions (Part 3.2 Division 11) and the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 (Qld). Overlaps global-top500-064-employee-grievance-reports and global-top500-079-workplace-investigation-files (generic phrase classifiers); this one requires populated party and incident fields.
patterns.operation: Primary: a harassment/psychosocial phrase (sexual harassment, sex-based harassment, bullying or bullying and harassment complaint/report/allegation/incident/matter, harassment complaint/report/allegation/incident, psychosocial hazard/risk/injury/incident with optional report/notification/complaint/assessment, repeated unreasonable behaviour). 75 tier requires, within 300 characters, a populated party field (complainant, respondent, alleged harasser/perpetrator, person making the complaint, reported by, affected worker/employee, subject employee, witness, with a non-placeholder value) OR a populated incident field (date of incident/conduct with a date, or location / alleged conduct / description or details of the incident with at least three words). 85 tier requires the party field AND the incident field AND a process field (interim or protective measures, investigation or complaint outcome/status/finding, outcome, finding, action taken, support offered, referred to, investigator, with a value) AND an independent corroborative term (investigation, investigator, EAP, victimisation, confidential, support person, Sex Discrimination Act, WHS, code of conduct). All enforce tiers AND NOT the shared template-exclusion dictionary and a guidance/training exclusion (this code of practice, this policy/procedure applies, fact sheet, frequently asked questions, positive duty guidelines, case study, hypothetical, training module, catchwords). 65 is discovery-only and will surface policies, the Code, AHRC guidance and aggregate psychosocial risk registers.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: the primary phrases are the statutory and Code of Practice terms, but they saturate policies, training and AHRC/WorkSafe guidance, so enforce tiers need populated complainant/respondent or incident fields, and 85 needs parties, incident particulars and a process field together. Complaint and case numbers are organisation-defined and are not shape-checked. Aggregate psychosocial risk registers (hazard, likelihood, controls) stay at 65 by design. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic complaint records.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier identifies a sexual harassment, sex-based harassment, bullying or psychosocial hazard complaint or report that names the complainant, respondent or affected worker together with incident particulars. SENSITIVE rather than PROTECTED applies because one complaint file causes serious personal harm and victimisation risk without significant damage to government.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling with restricted access protects complainants from victimisation and respondents from unproven allegations. Generic High is not applied to a single case record.

patterns.name: Working With Children Check Number (NSW / VIC / WA)
patterns.description: Detects Working With Children Check (WWCC) clearance numbers across Australian states. Covers the NSW structural format (WWC + 7 digits + check letter, e.g. WWC1234567E) and the labelled VIC / WA / generic forms where a WWCC or working-with-children phrase precedes a card or clearance number. The Queensland Blue Card is handled by a separate classifier.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine). Pattern_au_wwcc_number matches either the NSW structural form (WWC + 7 digits + trailing letter) or a WWCC / working-with-children phrase followed within 50 characters by a 6-9 digit card/clearance number with an optional trailing letter. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires WWCC evidence (min 2) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires WWCC evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires WWCC evidence. Evidence uses one keyword group (13 child-screening terms) within 300-character proximity.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the NSW WWC#######E form is highly specific, but the labelled VIC / WA / generic forms match a broad 6-9 digit number near a working-with-children phrase, so corroborating child-screening keywords are required. WA assessment-notice numbering is not publicly standardised and is covered only by the labelled proximity branch.

should_match.value: NSW Working with Children Check number WWC1234567E is valid until 2029 for the applicant
Working with Children Check clearance 1088651V issued to the volunteer this month
VIC WWC Check card 0512345A-01 held by the classroom teacher on file
WA Working with Children Check registration 20481523 sighted by the coordinator

should_not_match.value: The child protection policy was updated by the school board last week
Working with children is rewarding work in early childhood education
Card number 4111 1111 1111 1111 was declined at the terminal
Working with children policy 20240815 was updated for all 12 campuses

false_positives.description: A working-with-children phrase near an unrelated 6-9 digit number could match without being a clearance number.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborating child-screening keywords within the proximity window.

false_positives.description: Sample clearance numbers in HR templates or training material may match the labelled form.
false_positives.mitigation: The high and medium tiers apply the template-exclusion NOT-group to suppress sample and training content.

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds the distinctive NSW WWC number form or a labelled six- to nine-digit Working With Children Check card, clearance, or registration number for NSW, Victoria, or Western Australia. A genuine number can identify a screening credential and support nuisance verification or impersonation, but it does not reveal disqualifying history, assessment evidence, or a clearance decision beyond what a separate verification service returns. The normal unit is one administrative screening identifier with bounded harm and requires the holder's identity plus outcome data for material privacy or child-safety impact. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are appropriate, while a complete screening file or adverse child-protection record would warrant SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 reconciles with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, and the OFFICIAL DLM because the detected WWCC number is a clearance reference rather than a criminal-history or child-protection record. SENSITIVE is not met without holder attribution and substantive screening or adverse-outcome information.

generic.rationale: Low generic classification and Low DLM fit a WWCC reference number whose consequential sensitivity lies in the associated screening record, not the number alone.

This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. patterns.operation: Matches Azure Storage account keys in assignment context (key=value or key:value format) with Base64-encoded values. This is a broader variant that catches keys in configuration files and code. Corroborative evidence: 8 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: matches storage key assignments but the Base64 pattern can overlap with other encoded data. Context keywords improve accuracy. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

Account key in YAML format
Storage account key with placeholder value

false_positives.mitigation: Check for common placeholder patterns and template indicators.

false_positives.description: Non-Azure storage service keys that use similar naming.
false_positives.mitigation: Require proximity to Azure-specific keywords for differentiation.

patterns.risk_description: The regex identifies a Base64-like Azure Storage account key assigned to a storage or account-key property, so the match is a credential value rather than a storage record. A valid key can be combined with the corresponding account name to read, alter, or delete data exposed through that account's permitted services. The immediate party at risk is the owner of one storage account and its users, while placeholders, non-Azure encoded values, and the missing account identifier limit what the match alone proves. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE are justified for a usable key because compromise can cause serious contained operational or data harm; evidence of a privileged production account holding protected or critical data would raise the consequence.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps consistently to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and the SENSITIVE InfoTech DLM because an active storage key can enable serious unauthorized operations once its account is known. PROTECTED is not met by the normal match because the regex does not establish the account identity, permissions, production status, data sensitivity, or tenant-wide reach.

generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls because a storage-key assignment is actionable secret material and warrants restricted sharing and prompt rotation when validated. High treatment is not automatic because Base64 overlap and placeholder configurations remain plausible and the match does not demonstrate broad privileged compromise.

A normal match therefore threatens one account and the people or services relying on it, while unrelated Base64 data and documented examples can produce non-credentials. patterns.risk_description: This SIT matches a signed Azure Storage URL containing service-version and signature parameters, so it finds a delegated access token tied to a storage endpoint rather than an account-wide master key. A live SAS can be replayed to perform whatever read or write operations its uninspected scope and expiry allow, exposing the resource owner and users of that container, file share, table, or blob. The ordinary match does not reveal permissions, expiry, validity, or data sensitivity, and catalogued examples or expired URLs can be benign. Risk 8 SENSITIVE captures serious but contained harm from a usable token; PROTECTED would require demonstrated destructive rights, broad scope, or significant protected-resource impact.

PROTECTED is not met by this generic SAS detector because it does not require write/delete permissions, broad resource scope, a live expiry, or evidence of significant damage.

generic.rationale: Generic treatment is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls because signed storage URLs are bearer credentials and should not be shared casually. High is not the default when the token may be read-only, expired, example data, or narrowly scoped to one object.

patterns.name: Canada Marking - Protected A/B/C + Classified
patterns.description: Detects Government of Canada protective markings under the Treasury Board Standard on Security Categorization (Appendix J of the Directive on Security Management): the Canada-distinctive "Protected" designations Protected A / Protected B / Protected C (information whose compromise could injure interests outside the national interest), and the classified levels Confidential / Secret / Top Secret (injury to the national interest). "Protected A/B/C" is unique to Canada and matched at high confidence in both title-case and ALL-CAPS renderings; the classified words are shared vocabulary with other nations and are matched only at lower, Canada-government-context-gated tiers. Rendering verified directly against the Treasury Board Standard on Security Categorization; matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the Canada-distinctive "Protected <A|B|C>" designation in either its policy title-case (Protected B) or ALL-CAPS banner (PROTECTED B) rendering, tolerant of hyphen or PDF-line-wrap whitespace before the level letter; carries only a template/noise NOT-exclusion. Tier 75 matches the bare TOP SECRET banner-words phrase, AND-gated by Canada-government corroborative context. Tier 65 matches the bare CONFIDENTIAL / SECRET words, AND-gated by Canada-government context plus a NOT-exclusion for common non-government SECRET collocations (TRADE SECRET, CLIENT SECRET, API SECRET, SECRET MANAGER, SECRET SANTA).
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the "Protected A/B/C" designation: the word Protected (leading capital) immediately followed by a single bare A, B or C is a structurally distinctive, Canada-unique marking with negligible natural-language collision, verified against the Treasury Board Standard on Security Categorization; matched case-sensitively so lowercase "protected b" cannot fire, and constrained by a trailing word boundary so "Protected Areas"/"Protected Building" cannot fire. The classified words CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET are shared Five-Eyes vocabulary and extremely collision-prone, so — following this SIT's Canada-specific role — they are placed at lower tiers gated by Canada-government corroborative evidence within 300 characters (TOP SECRET at 75 as a distinctive two-word phrase; bare CONFIDENTIAL/SECRET at 65) plus, for the bare words, a dedicated collocation NOT-group.

should_match.value: This record is designated Protected B under the Treasury Board Standard on Security Categorization.
should_match.description: Canada-distinctive Protected B designation in policy title-case

should_match.value: Cover sheet stamped PROTECTED C — extremely sensitive personal information, handle accordingly.
should_match.description: Protected C in ALL-CAPS banner rendering

should_match.value: The briefing note is classified TOP SECRET and was prepared for the Government of Canada Privy Council Office.
should_match.description: Gated bare TOP SECRET — Canada-government corroborative context (Government of Canada, Privy Council Office) present within 300 characters

should_match.value: This SECRET memorandum must be handled per the Government of Canada Directive on Security Management.
should_match.description: Gated bare SECRET — Canada-government corroborative context (Government of Canada, Directive on Security Management) present within 300 characters

should_match.value: Marking: Protected-A applied to the salary schedule in the personnel file.
should_match.description: Protected-A with a hyphen separator (the [\s-]+ separator tolerates a hyphen before the level letter)

should_not_match.value: please keep these files protected and do not disclose anything secret without approval
should_not_match.description: lowercase prose (case-sensitive exclusion — neither "protected" nor "secret" is capitalised as a marking)

should_not_match.value: PROTECTED AREAS OF THE NATIONAL PARK REQUIRE A PERMIT FROM PARKS CANADA
should_not_match.description: ALL-CAPS prose — "PROTECTED A" is followed by the rest of "AREAS" (no word boundary after the A), so it fails at the regex level

should_not_match.value: THE COMPANY'S TRADE SECRET FORMULA IS CONFIDENTIAL AND STORED UNDER AN NDA
should_not_match.description: ALL-CAPS non-government collocation — excluded from the top-level Protected pattern (no PROTECTED A/B/C) and from the gated bare tier by the TRADE SECRET NOT-group

false_positives.description: ALL-CAPS prose (headings, legal boilerplate, or fully-capitalised documents) defeats the case-sensitivity signal the bare TOP SECRET / SECRET / CONFIDENTIAL tiers rely on — any all-caps rendering with no marking intent can fire those gated tiers if Canada-government context also happens to be present.
false_positives.mitigation: Treat gated-tier (65/75) hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps. The Protected A/B/C tier (85) is structurally distinctive and does not depend on the context gate.

false_positives.description: The classified words CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET are shared Five-Eyes vocabulary already covered by the US/UK/NZ/AU marking families; a genuine Canadian classified document is expected to co-fire those SITs. This SIT deliberately gates its classified-word tiers on Canada-government context so its distinctive contribution is the Canada-unique Protected A/B/C designation rather than redundant broad firing on generic classification words.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy policies should treat cross-jurisdiction co-fire on the shared classified words as corroborating, not conflicting; do not remove the Canada-context gate, which is what keeps this SIT's classified tiers precise.

false_positives.description: The title-case "Protected A/B/C" form has a small residual: rare constructions such as "Protected A-list" or a standalone "Protected A" heading followed by a boundary can match without marking intent. "Protected Area(s)", "Protected Building", and similar are NOT affected — the trailing word boundary requires the A/B/C to stand alone.
false_positives.mitigation: Residual is rare and low-impact; the template/noise NOT-exclusion suppresses sample/training content, and the ALL-CAPS banner rendering (the dominant real-world marking form) is unambiguous.

false_positives.description: Coverage gap (false negative, not false positive): the bare classified tiers (CONFIDENTIAL / SECRET / TOP SECRET) match ALL-CAPS only. Treasury Board policy text and many banners also render these in Title Case (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential); Title-Case classified banners are therefore NOT detected. Deliberate precision tradeoff — a bare title-case "Secret"/"Confidential" is un-gateable everyday English. The Protected A/B/C tier (85) matches both title-case and ALL-CAPS, so only the shared classified words carry this recall gap.
false_positives.mitigation: Accepted recall tradeoff; ALL-CAPS banners are the dominant high-assurance rendering, and Canadian classified content is independently covered by the US/UK/NZ/AU marking SITs.

false_positives.description: French-language Government of Canada markings (Protégé A/B/C, Confidentiel, Secret, Très secret) are applied per-document-language, NOT co-rendered bilingually the way EUCI markings are. They are not implemented here: the Treasury Board Standard's English text defines the English terms, and verifying the exact French banner rendering from a French primary source was out of scope for this release.
false_positives.mitigation: Documented as a known coverage gap for French-language Canadian documents rather than authored from assumption; the English designations and classified words are the verified, shipped forms.

patterns.risk_description: The Canada marking detector is an umbrella for Protected A, Protected B, Protected C, CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET, and TOP SECRET, so its normal true-positive unit is a marking event whose exact branch determines the actual harm. Protected A can indicate limited injury outside the national interest, while Protected C and the upper classified branches can signal severe privacy, operational, or national-interest consequences. The current deployment does not expose a branch value that policy can reliably route, so flattening the detector to SENSITIVE would allow high-rung matches to inherit controls below their stated marking. Until branch-aware routing is implemented and tested, risk 9 and PROTECTED are the safe fixed outcome; the future event model must apply the exact Canadian level rather than one static class.

sensitivity_labels.ca_gov: Protected A / Protected B / Protected C / Confidential / Secret / Top Secret
sensitivity_labels.psr: IN CONFIDENCE / CONFIDENTIAL / SECRET / TOP SECRET

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, Marking Protected, and High because the detector includes Protected C, SECRET, and TOP SECRET branches associated with severe personal, operational, or national-interest harm. Protected A and Protected B branches can carry lower consequences, but a positive umbrella match does not identify the branch and can therefore represent the highest-consequence marked content covered by the detector. PROTECTED is the highest accepted classification tier; risk 10 is not required because the match does not establish catastrophic breadth, while branch-aware routing remains an owner-review requirement.

generic.rationale: The fixed generic outcome remains High Government because the unsplit detector can return Canadian markings whose mishandling requires PROTECTED controls, even though lower branches will eventually route separately.

patterns.name: Canadian Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects North American Numbering Plan (NANP) telephone numbers in Canadian contexts: the domestic NPA-NXX-XXXX form (bracketed, hyphenated, dotted, spaced, or bare, with an optional leading trunk "1") and the international +1 NPA-NXX-XXXX form. Area-code (NPA) and exchange-code (NXX) groups are constrained to a leading digit of 2-9 with the N11 service-code shape (211/311/411/511/611/711/811/911) excluded from both groups, per NANPA's published format rules. This pattern is structurally identical to us-phone-number because NANP area codes are drawn from a single pool shared by the US, Canada, and Caribbean member territories — the digit sequence itself cannot distinguish a Canadian number from a US one. This is the sibling of us-phone-number; the two are differentiated by jurisdiction/regulation metadata and country-specific corroborative evidence keywords only, not by regex — see us-phone-number's description for the documented family convention.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (NANP has no checksum; structural leading-digit and N11-exclusion constraints reduce but do not eliminate digit collision with other 10-digit identifiers). Reference: North American Numbering Plan Administration (NANPA), https://www.nanpa.com/; CNAC (the Canadian Numbering Administrator), https://cnac.ca/. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+1) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: NPA/NXX leading-digit constraints (2-9) and N11 exclusion narrow the format meaningfully, but NANP numbers carry no checksum and a 10-digit Canadian-shaped sequence still collides with invoice numbers, order numbers, and other structured identifiers. Per the phone-family convention set by au-fixed-line-telephone (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; high digit-collision formats never get a zero-evidence tier), both the domestic and +1 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +1 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

should_match.description: Domestic bracketed Toronto area code with fictional NANPA 555-01XX exchange
Domestic hyphenated Vancouver area code
International +1 form, Montreal area code, space-separated
Domestic bare digits with no separators, Calgary area code

should_not_match.description: Area code starts with 1 (NPA must start 2-9, not 0 or 1)
Exchange code is 911, an N11 service code, excluded from the NXX position
Only exchange + subscriber digits, no area code — not a full 10-digit number
Valid-shaped digit run embedded inside a longer reference number, rejected by digit boundaries

false_positives.description: A bare 10-digit sequence with NPA/NXX leading digits in the 2-9 range and no N11 shape can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, tracking numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +1 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: NANP area codes are shared across the US, Canada, and Caribbean NANP member territories, so this pattern's regex will also structurally match US- or Caribbean-issued numbers with no way to tell from the digits alone.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy alongside us-phone-number using each pattern's jurisdiction-specific evidence keywords (e.g. "Canadian phone number" vs "US phone number") to bias classification, and rely on surrounding document context (postal addresses, currency, entity names) for jurisdiction attribution rather than the number itself.

false_positives.description: The domestic sub-regex also fires inside the +1 international rendering (empirically verified: in "+1 514 555 0134" it matches the "1 514 555 0134" substring, because the optional trunk-1 branch starts right after the "+", which is not a digit), so an international value produces a domestic-tier match as well as an international-tier match.
false_positives.mitigation: Benign co-fire, left in place deliberately: both sub-regexes carry identical evidence gating and confidence levels, so the duplicate match cannot inflate confidence — it can only duplicate a finding at the same level, which reporting layers de-duplicate by offset. A structural fix would need variable-width negative lookbehind (to reject "+1 " at any separator width), which the universal engine target does not support.

patterns.risk_description: The identifier pattern finds Canadian-context NANP numbers in domestic or +1 form with constrained area and exchange digits, but the digits cannot distinguish Canada from US or Caribbean NANP jurisdictions. A real number enables calls, smishing, vishing, nuisance contact, and identity correlation, especially when an attacker already knows the subscriber's name or account relationship. One match normally affects one contact point, carries no authentication authority, and can also be an invoice or tracking number despite mandatory phone context. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect bounded standalone harm; SENSITIVE would require linkage to credentials, protected relationships, precise location, or a sensitive personal profile that makes targeting materially more consequential.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to OFFICIAL because a Canadian-format phone number enables contact and social engineering but does not independently authenticate or reveal a sensitive relationship. SENSITIVE is not met without linked credentials, location, identity, or protected-context information that creates credible direct harm.

generic.rationale: Generic Low handling fits one telephone contact point with bounded misuse value and uncertain Canadian attribution within the shared NANP numbering space.

Risk 3 OFFICIAL reflects limited standalone harm; SENSITIVE would require a protected or vulnerable occupant, confidential residence, active threat, movement aggregation, or an identified address directory.

patterns.description: Detects SIN patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Validation: Luhn algorithm. Reference: https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/sin.html Corroborative evidence: 3 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: pattern has structural constraints but corroborative keywords are recommended to reduce false positive rates.

Space-separated SIN (Luhn-valid)
Continuous SIN digits (Luhn-valid)

patterns.risk_description: The pattern validates a nine-digit Canadian Social Insurance Number with a Luhn check and nearby SIN or civic-credential language. Disclosure can help an impostor make employment, tax, credit, or benefits enquiries in the holder's name, but the number alone does not authenticate those services. One individual is exposed by a normal match, and successful misuse generally needs a name, date of birth, address, or access to an account or application process. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect that bounded correlation value; a populated tax, payroll, benefits, or identity dossier would raise the surrounding material toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and a Low tier because a validated SIN is an atomic reference identifier rather than a credential or composite record. SENSITIVE is not met without companion identity data or a transaction, benefits, payroll, or case context capable of causing moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM are appropriate for one Canadian SIN whose misuse depends on material corroborating data and access to a separate process. Baseline handling plus correlation controls addresses the limited standalone exposure without treating it as a complete identity file.

patterns.name: Central Bank Monetary Policy Pre-Decision
patterns.description: Detects draft monetary policy decisions and pre-announcement rate recommendations: a rate value (percentage, basis points or per cent) near a central bank / Reserve Bank reference and a recommendation line proposing a rate action. Published RBA statements, media commentary and forecasts are excluded.
patterns.operation: Pattern type: keyword proximity evaluated through purview tiers. Primary: a rate value (d.d%, N basis points/bps, d.dd per cent). Every enforce tier also requires a central bank reference (RBA, Reserve Bank, central bank, Monetary Policy Board). 65 (discovery only): rate value alone. 75: rate + institution + a recommendation/assessment/proposed-decision line that proposes a rate action (reduce, cut, raise, hold, tighten, ease...). 85: rate + institution + two distinct structures (recommendation line, pre-decision/embargo marker, or a labelled board meeting / decision date) + policy-content evidence (cash rate target, deliberation, policy options, inflation/CPI, trimmed mean, unemployment, tightening/easing). Media-release, forecast, published and guidance framing is excluded on every enforce tier.
patterns.confidence_justification: A labelled recommendation proposing a rate action beside an RBA reference and a rate value is characteristic of pre-decision papers; the previous 75 tier could fire on 'board paper' alone because a decision keyword group was also a primary. Published statements and economist forecasts are excluded by the filter group. Medium because internal economic commentary written as a recommendation can still match.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a pre-decision central-bank monetary policy paper by combining rate, tightening or easing, recommendation, basis-point, and embargo terms. Premature disclosure can enable market positioning across bonds, currencies, equities, and derivatives and can weaken the integrity of board or policy deliberations. A confirmed substantive record therefore has a credible significant-damage path and warrants risk 9 with PROTECTED Financial handling. Risk 9, rather than 10, recognises that the scale depends on the decision's imminence, policy materiality, and actual market exposure; forecasts, commentary, and public analysis remain outside that consequence assessment. Quality pass 2026-09-24: enforce tiers (75/85) now require populated record structure (labelled fields with real values, identifiers or data rows); phrase-only mentions in guidance, marketing, blank forms and news stay at 65 discovery.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 is proportionate for a confirmed pre-decision monetary-policy record because it can be traded before announcement and can materially impair a nationally important decision process. PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED Financial, PROT_Fin, High, and High Financial remain aligned. The detector still requires genuine recommendation, embargo, decision-state, or voting context so that predictions and public analysis are not treated as the protected record.

generic.rationale: Pre-decision monetary-policy material requires High Financial handling when it contains a genuine unreleased recommendation or decision position. Premature release can enable cross-market positioning and compromise policy execution, while commentary and speculative forecasts remain lower-consequence material.

patterns.name: Switzerland Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects Swiss passport numbers issued by fedpol (Federal Office of Police). Passports of the 2003, 2006 and 2010 series carry an eight-character number consisting of one uppercase letter followed by seven digits (e.g. E1234567); the 2010 series always begins with the letter X. The letters O and I are never used, to avoid confusion with the digits 0 and 1. The 2022 series (the only series issued since October 2022) has no published fixed structure — fedpol deliberately keeps the numbering rules non-public — so 2022-series numbers may not match this shape. Only the documented 2010-and-earlier format is covered.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine, case-sensitive). Pattern_ch_passport matches one uppercase letter (excluding O and I) followed by exactly seven digits. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires passport evidence (min 2 unique terms) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires passport evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires passport evidence. Evidence uses one keyword group (passport terms in the four Swiss national-language contexts plus English) within 300-character proximity. fedpol states the 2022-series numbering rules are deliberately not public, so only the documented 2003/2006/2010-series shape is targeted; 2022-series numbers may fall outside it and be missed.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: one letter plus seven digits is a distinctive but not unique shape (order numbers, invoice references and Swiss identity-card numbers share it), so corroborating passport keywords are required on every tier. Case-sensitivity and the O/I exclusion further narrow the match surface.

should_match.value: Passport no: X4720145 issued by fedpol, valid until 2032
should_match.description: 2010-series number (X prefix) with passport label context
Format example published by the Canton of Bern identification-document guidance
German-language passport label with letter-prefixed number

should_not_match.description: Letter O is never used in Swiss passport numbers
Letter I is never used in Swiss passport numbers
Only six digits after the letter — too short
Nine digits after the letter — too long
Lowercase letter — passport numbers are printed uppercase (pattern is case-sensitive)

false_positives.description: Swiss identity-card numbers share the letter-plus-digits shape (eight or nine characters).
false_positives.mitigation: Keyword evidence is passport-specific (Reisepass, passeport, passaporto); residual overlap is an acceptable same-sensitivity collision (both are Swiss identity documents).

false_positives.description: Product codes, order references and ticket numbers of the form letter-plus-seven-digits.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires passport keywords within the 300-character proximity window; high and medium tiers additionally apply the template-exclusion NOT-group.

false_positives.description: The 2022-series numbering rules are not published; 2022-series passports (issued since October 2022) may not follow the letter-plus-seven-digits shape and would then be missed (a coverage gap, not a false positive).
false_positives.mitigation: Documented limitation — no authoritative 2022-series structure exists to author against, so only the documented 2010-and-earlier shape is matched. No checksum is published; structure plus keyword evidence is the strongest available gate.

patterns.risk_description: The Swiss pattern detects documented 2003, 2006, and 2010 passport numbers consisting of one allowed uppercase letter and seven digits; it neither captures the passport data page nor reliably covers the unpublished 2022-series numbering scheme. A matched legacy number could assist form completion or identity correlation after the traveller's name and document details are obtained independently. One true positive exposes one holder's reference, while Swiss identity-card numbers, orders, invoices, and tickets can share the same compact shape. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are justified for this bounded and partially ambiguous unit; SENSITIVE would require verified document imagery, credentials, or a substantive identity and travel profile.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 and OFFICIAL better reflect the Swiss detector's atomic legacy passport number, its identity-card overlap, and its inability to establish identity or possession. SENSITIVE is not met without corroborated document content, authentication factors, or rich linked personal information that creates credible direct harm.

generic.rationale: The generic Low result treats the legacy Swiss passport string as a correlation identifier, with limited standalone authority and documented semantic ambiguity.

patterns.risk_description: This detector recognizes the Swiss AHV number's fixed 756 country prefix and dot-separated thirteen-digit presentation with social-security context. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL capture the limited standalone privacy impact, while a benefits file or identity package containing the holder's details would warrant SENSITIVE treatment.

classification.rationale: The fixed 756 structure supports risk 5, PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low because an AHV number is a reliable persistent reference but reveals no benefits or contribution history. SENSITIVE requires correlated identity, entitlement, employment, pension, or medical records, or an authentication path the number alone does not provide.

generic.rationale: Low classification and Low DLM fit a single Swiss administrative identifier with bounded correlation and impersonation value. The consequence becomes materially greater only when the number is attached to pension, payroll, health, or account records.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier targets a composite child-safety investigation file through harm notifications, substantiated-harm findings, protection orders, placements, or safety plans near child, privacy, department, or statutory evidence. Unauthorized disclosure could expose alleged abuse, a child's location or care arrangements, reporter information, and investigative outcomes, potentially retraumatising the child, compromising family proceedings, or creating a direct safety concern. The normal true positive is one case file and public annual reports, policy, and training are excluded, so serious legal and personal consequences are expected without assuming a whole child-protection system. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE Legal are appropriate; PROTECTED would require a specific life-safety threat, protected witness or operation, bulk case compromise, or comparable significant damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF and QGISCF PROTECTED and PROTECTED Legal (owner decision 2026-09-25) because a statutory child-safety file under the Child Protection Act 1999 (Qld) can expose alleged abuse, a child's location and care arrangements, and the notifier; disclosure creates a direct safety risk and can compromise proceedings.

generic.rationale: High Legal handling fits an individual child-safety investigation whose disclosure can reveal a child's whereabouts, abuse findings or the reporter, with direct safety and legal consequences.

patterns.risk_description: This pattern identifies privileged defence strategy for class, representative, or group proceedings when exposure, settlement authority, or legal-strategy indicators appear nearby. A genuine file can disclose class-definition challenges, common-question analysis, causation weaknesses, damages models, settlement ceilings, and tactical sequencing, giving claimants a direct litigation advantage and affecting many potential claims. A class action inherently aggregates claimants and material exposure. Strategy leakage can affect evidence, settlement leverage and liabilities across the class and defendant. The normal true-positive unit belongs at risk 9, PROTECTED Legal, while broad or contextual false positives remain a separate detection issue.

classification.rationale: The QLD custom classifier is assessed on its confirmed substantive record rather than an uncorroborated topic hit. A class action inherently aggregates claimants and material exposure. Strategy leakage can affect evidence, settlement leverage and liabilities across the class and defendant. Accordingly the workbook should record risk 9, PROTECTED in both frameworks, PROTECTED Legal, PROT_Leg and High rather than retain the Medium tier.

generic.rationale: Class-action defence strategy is High Legal information because the proceeding aggregates claimants and material exposure, making tactical leakage consequential across the whole class. The QLD custom classifier carries High Legal handling when its substantive match is confirmed.
