patterns.name: China Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects People's Republic of China passport numbers. The current ordinary (e-)passport uses an 'E' prefix followed by one letter (excluding I and O) and 7 digits, or 'E' plus 8 digits. Older series use a 'G' prefix plus 8 digits, and earlier passports used 'P', 'D' (diplomatic) or 'S' (service) prefixes plus 8 digits. The short, loosely structured format means corroborative keyword proximity is strongly recommended.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_passport Matches a passport prefix letter (E/G/D/S/P) followed by an optional second letter and 7-8 digits. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: although the prefix letters are constrained, the body is only 7-8 digits, so the pattern can collide with reference codes and serial numbers that happen to start with one of these letters. Corroborative passport keywords within 300 characters are essential for reliable detection.

should_match.description: Current ordinary e-passport, E + letter + 7 digits
Older G-series passport, G + 8 digits, labelled
E-series passport with E + 8 digits

should_not_match.description: Leading 'A' is not a valid PRC passport prefix letter
Second letter I is excluded from the e-passport alphabet

should_not_match.value: please attach a copy of your chinese passport before the visa appointment
should_not_match.description: Prose mention of a passport without an actual number

false_positives.description: Reference codes, invoice numbers or serial numbers that begin with E, G, D, S or P followed by 7-8 digits.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative passport keywords within 300 characters and validate document context.

patterns.risk_description: The China passport pattern identifies current E-series and older G, D, S, or P prefixed passport numbers with seven or eight trailing digits in passport context, not a document image or citizenship record. Disclosure may help populate a booking or visa pretext after the traveller's name, date of birth, and issue details have been sourced independently. One match affects one holder, while invoices and serial references beginning with the same limited prefix set can mimic the structure. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect that bounded correlation value; SENSITIVE would require a passport copy, credentials, or a combined identity and travel file.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF and QGISCF OFFICIAL because the PRC passport number is a standalone document reference with no independent power to authenticate or authorise travel. SENSITIVE is not met without the data page, authentication factors, or linked biographical and itinerary information enabling direct fraud.

generic.rationale: Generic Low treatment recognises the number's identity-correlation utility while reserving stronger classification for complete passport or traveller records.

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence detector finds an 18-character Mainland China Unified Social Credit Code with restricted alphabet and administrative-division structure near corporate-registry terminology. A USCC identifies a legal person or organisation in public registration, tax, licensing, and due-diligence processes; disclosure can aid company profiling or a more convincing supplier impersonation but does not expose the linked records themselves. The normal unit is a public organisational identifier with negligible standalone confidentiality harm and no authority to transact or access government systems. Risk 2 and OFFICIAL are appropriate, while SENSITIVE would require nonpublic tax, credit, licensing, ownership, or transaction information associated with the entity.

classification.rationale: Risk 2 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, and the OFFICIAL DLM because a USCC is a public corporate registry identifier rather than confidential government or financial data. patterns.name: Confidential Human Source Identity
patterns.description: Detects documents containing the identities of police informants (confidential human sources, confidential / registered informants, registered sources) embedded within criminal organisations. Informant identity is the single most sensitive category of law enforcement information globally. Disclosure has historically resulted in murders and creates immediate lethal risk. Absorbs the former confidential-informant-identities classifier.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary keywords (confidential human source, confidential / registered informant, registered source, source handler, source controller, CHIS, informant registration / file / handler / agreement / identity, source identity, covert source) within 300 characters. 65 = primary phrase only (discovery). 75 = primary plus one independent populated field: person record fields (name, DOB, informant, CNI ...), a labelled source identifier or handler field (CI number, informant number, registered source number, source code name, source reference, handler, controller), or a hand-authored source-management term (source reliability, source payment, informant management ...). Bare "CI" is never used on its own - only inside a labelled field such as "CI number:". 85 = two distinct populated structure hits (two person record fields, two source/handler fields, or one of each) plus independent source-management evidence or the COVERT marker. patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies records that connect a confidential human source or registered informant to personal details, handler information, source references, reliability ratings, access, payments, or operational reporting. Disclosure can expose the source inside a criminal organisation, trigger lethal retaliation, endanger handlers and family, and compromise current and future intelligence derived from the relationship. classification.rationale: Risk 10 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED Law-Enforcement, and High because source identification can cause lethal retaliation and collapse intelligence access. No higher QGISCF classification exists beyond this maximum accepted tier.

generic.rationale: High with High Law-Enforcement DLM is essential because source identity and handler linkage create immediate, potentially irreversible safety and operational consequences.

patterns.name: Coronial Finding Published
patterns.description: Detects published coronial findings and recommendations under the Coroners Act 2003 (Qld). Although coronial findings are public documents, they contain sensitive details about the circumstances and cause of death, manner of death, and identity of deceased persons. Government agencies handling these documents should classify them as SENSITIVE Legal due to the distressing nature of the content.
patterns.operation: Primary: coronial finding(s)/inquest/investigation/report, inquest into / findings of inquest / inquest findings or recommendations, coroner's finding/recommendation/report/court, non-inquest findings. 65 (discovery only): phrase alone - statistics, textbooks and news stay here. 75: phrase plus a populated findings-header field as used in published Queensland findings (citation, title of court, jurisdiction, file no(s), delivered on/at, hearing dates, findings of, catchwords, representation, counsel assisting, date/place of death, deceased). 85: two distinct populated header fields plus a named deceased ('Inquest into the death of <Name>' / 'death of <Name>') plus independent cause/manner evidence (cause of death, manner of death, autopsy, post-mortem, forensic pathologist, toxicology, Coroners Act 2003, recommendations). Template and guidance/training framing excluded from 75/85.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low-medium: coronial findings are published documents, so the classifier labels handling rather than secrecy. Enforce tiers need the published findings header structure; 85 also needs a named deceased and cause/manner evidence. Statistics, textbooks and news carry the phrases without the header fields and stay at 65.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies published coronial findings by combining coronial-finding language with the published findings header fields (citation, file number, delivered on, findings of, deceased), and at 85 a named deceased plus cause or manner of death. Although the subject matter may be distressing and personally sensitive, the normal true positive is an officially released public document whose lawful publication has already removed the core confidentiality interest. Misuse is mainly contextual republication or insensitive handling and generally causes limited incremental harm beyond the public finding itself. Risk 3 and OFFICIAL are proportionate; SENSITIVE would require an unpublished draft, suppressed detail, protected witness, or non-public evidence excluded from the released finding.

classification.rationale: Risk 3 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because the detector expressly targets a final public finding rather than confidential coronial evidence. SENSITIVE is not met without draft, suppressed, protected-witness, or otherwise non-public content.

generic.rationale: Low with Low DLM reflects the document's official public status while recognising that respectful handling remains appropriate for distressing death details.

patterns.risk_description: This pattern finds draft government submissions to coronial inquests when coronial terms occur near draft, approval, privilege, confidentiality, or not-for-publication indicators. A real draft can disclose sensitive death circumstances, unresolved causation positions, proposed admissions, systemic-failure analysis, and agency responses before filing, distressing families and prejudicing the inquest. The affected unit is one pre-filing submission, not published findings or general guidance about coronial procedure. Risk 8 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require protected witnesses, credible life-safety risk, Cabinet involvement, or severe system-wide consequences beyond the inquest.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to SENSITIVE and Medium tiers because a draft coronial submission exposes death-related facts, admissions, and legal positions before filing. PROTECTED is not met without life-safety, protected-witness, Cabinet, or severe systemic consequences.

generic.rationale: A draft coronial submission is generically Medium with Medium Legal DLM because it contains non-public death evidence and government positions awaiting formal filing.

patterns.name: Council Customer Reference Linked to a Named Customer (Assessment, Rate Account, Application, Animal Registration, Infringement)
patterns.description: A parameterised template for council customer references: rates assessment and property numbers, rate and water account numbers, development / building / plumbing application numbers, animal registration numbers and infringement notice numbers, when they appear in council correspondence, CRM exports and customer records alongside a named customer. Every council numbers these differently and none of the formats is published, so the public version anchors on the field labels (Assessment No, Property No, Rate Account, Application No, Animal Registration No, Infringement No and close variants) with a loose, placeholder-guarded, digit-bearing value. Each reference type is a separate regex so that a deployment can extend it with the council's real format through the existing identifier types council-property-number, utility-account-number, council-development-application-number, animal-registration-number and infringement-notice-number. The record-specific council classifiers (rates arrears, concessions, animal registration, infringement / SPER, water hardship) remain the higher-confidence detectors; this template catches the long tail of customer correspondence that carries a council reference. Published DA notices, council FAQ pages and blank forms are decoys.
patterns.operation: Primary (any one of five labelled reference regexes, each a separate slot): property / [rate[s]] assessment [no. / number / ID]; rate[s] / water [and sewerage] / council account [no. / number / ID] or customer no. / number / ID / reference; [development / building / plumbing / planning / operational works] application, DA, BA, approval or permit no. / number / ref[erence]; animal / dog / cat / pet registration no. / number, registration tag no. / number or tag no. / number; [penalty] infringement [notice] no. / number / ref[erence] or PIN no. / number. Each label must be followed on the same line by a value that starts with a digit or a short letter prefix and contains a digit, and that is not a placeholder (n/a, tbc, withheld, underscores, brackets, 0000, 123456). 75 requires, within 300 characters, a populated customer field (name, customer [name], ratepayer, [registered] owner['s name], applicant['s name], account holder, full name, postal / residential / mailing address, email, phone or mobile, followed by a name of two or more capitalised words, a street address, an email address or an Australian phone number, or a "Dear" salutation followed by a two-word name) AND a council context term (council, regional / city / shire council, local government, rates notice, ratepayer, animal management, local law, customer service centre). Both tiers AND NOT the shared template-exclusion dictionary; 75 also ANDs NOT a guidance / public-notice exclusion (frequently asked questions, fact sheet, how do I find, where to find, for example, public notice, public notification, properly made submission). There is no 85 tier: the value formats are customer-defined and a reference plus a name is not strong enough evidence on its own. 65 is discovery-only.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low. None of the council reference formats is published (the identifier registry lists all five types as customer-defined or unpublished), so the public version matches a labelled, digit-bearing loose value. Labels such as "Application No" and "Customer No" are generic, which is why 75 needs both a populated customer field and a council context term, and why there is no 85 tier. recommended_confidence is 75. Precision improves when a deployment supplies the council's real formats through the identifier slots. 75 is a heuristic evidence tier, not measured accuracy. Test values are synthetic.

customisation.note: Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's council property / rates assessment number format (see docs/identifiers.md#council-property-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's utility customer account number format (see docs/identifiers.md#utility-account-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's development application number format (see docs/identifiers.md#council-development-application-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's animal registration number format (see docs/identifiers.md#animal-registration-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

Extend the labelled-field evidence with the customer's infringement notice number format (see docs/identifiers.md#infringement-notice-number). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

patterns.risk_description: The classifier identifies council correspondence and customer records that tie a named person, address, phone or email to a council reference (rates assessment, rate or water account, application, animal registration or infringement number). generic.rationale: Low with Low handling fits one customer reference linked to a name; bulk CRM exports covering many ratepayers deserve a stronger aggregate assessment.

patterns.risk_description: This detector finds a counter-terrorism assessment containing threat analysis, radicalisation indicators, persons of interest, foreign-fighter links, or fixated-threat recommendations. A genuine file can reveal monitoring focus and analytic judgments, allowing a subject to alter behaviour, conceal associations, or avoid referral and surveillance. Disclosure can reveal subjects, sources, threat judgements, intelligence gaps and planned action, enabling evasion or an attack and endangering people. Significant national-interest and life-safety harm is inherent. Once corroborated as an actual Counter-Terrorism Assessment File record, risk 10 and PROTECTED Law-Enforcement are proportionate to the significant damage disclosure can cause.

classification.rationale: The QLD custom classifier is assessed on its confirmed substantive record rather than an uncorroborated topic hit. Disclosure can reveal subjects, sources, threat judgements, intelligence gaps and planned action, enabling evasion or an attack and endangering people. Significant national-interest and life-safety harm is inherent. The major consequence supports risk 10 and a consistent PROTECTED crosswalk using PROTECTED Law-Enforcement, PROT_Law and High handling.

generic.rationale: Counter-terrorism assessments are High Law-Enforcement information because subjects, sources, intelligence gaps and planned actions can affect national security and life safety. The QLD custom classifier carries High Law-Enforcement handling when its substantive match is confirmed.

patterns.risk_description: Despite its name, the detector targets an unpublished Queensland court filing with a proceeding number, registry, parties, claim or charge, and case-specific allegations rather than an isolated public reference number. Disclosure can expose child-protection, criminal, medical, family, or civil claims before adjudication, prejudice parties, and reveal addresses or evidence not yet in the public domain. Published judgments, court directories, legal commentary, and blank forms are excluded, so the normal unit is a substantive filing for one proceeding. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require a suppression order, protected witness, sealed evidence, or court-restricted material with significant safety or justice consequences.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium because an unpublished filing exposes attributed allegations and case details before public adjudication. PROTECTED is not met without sealing, suppression, protected persons, or significant court-restricted consequences.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium Legal DLM protect substantive unpublished filings while distinguishing them from public judgments, directories, and bare proceeding references.

Published annual reports, parliamentary reviews, and academic descriptions of mutual assistance are excluded, so the normal match is an operational exchange rather than a public cooperation reference. generic.rationale: High with High Law-Enforcement DLM is proportionate to cross-border operational compromise and the potentially irreversible loss of trusted intelligence access.

patterns.risk_description: This keyword-proximity detector targets an actual Crown Solicitor or Office of the Crown Solicitor opinion when privilege, advice, opinion, or LPP indicators occur nearby, not a public mention of the office. Disclosure can waive legal professional privilege and expose the State's candid liability analysis, vulnerabilities, recommended position, and instructions, allowing an opponent to reshape litigation or negotiations. The affected unit is one privileged government opinion with serious but contained legal and financial consequences. Risk 8 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require statewide systemic exposure, Cabinet-level consequences, a protected operation, or broad compromise of privileged holdings.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium tiers because disclosure can waive privilege and prejudice a significant matter. PROTECTED is not met for one opinion without broad privileged compromise, Cabinet, protected-operation, or significant statewide damage.

generic.rationale: A Crown Solicitor opinion is generically Medium with Medium Legal DLM because it contains privileged government advice whose disclosure prejudices a specific matter.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a cybercrime investigation evidence package containing digital-forensic findings, malware analysis, cryptocurrency tracing, dark-web activity, seized-device results, or covert online personas. Disclosure can show a suspect which infrastructure, wallets, tooling, and attribution evidence investigators have identified, enabling evidence destruction, asset movement, or technical countermeasures. Public threat reports, conference material, academic research, training, and ordinary corporate incident response are excluded, leaving a bounded law-enforcement package rather than an enterprise security platform. Risk 8 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require active covert identities, critical-system exploit access, or compromise spanning multiple major operations.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium because detailed technical evidence can seriously prejudice attribution, seizure, and prosecution in one case. PROTECTED is not met without covert-identity, critical-system, or broad multi-operation compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium with Medium Legal DLM protects case-specific malware, tracing, and forensic evidence without assuming system-wide defensive or investigative compromise.

patterns.name: German Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects German mobile telephone numbers per the Bundesnetzagentur's (BNetzA) Nummernplan für Mobile Dienste: the (0)15, (0)16, and (0)17 mobile sub-ranges, in both the domestic (leading trunk "0") and international (+49, leading 0 dropped) forms. BNetzA's own published length table shows the national significant number (the digits after the leading 0, including the "1" of "15/16/17") is 10 digits for most 016x/017x allocations and 11 digits for the 015x range and the 1609/176 exceptions — every quantifier below is bounded to this documented 10-11 digit span rather than left open-ended. The 10-11 bound is applied as a single envelope across all three ranges (the regex cannot pin 015x to exactly 11 and non-exception 016x/017x to exactly 10 without per-sub-range length alternation), so a 10-digit 015x or an 11-digit non-exception 016x/017x rendering is accepted — a deliberate, documented over-acceptance kept small by the envelope itself. Beyond the DIN 5008:2020 space-grouped form, two widespread legacy DIN 5008 renderings of the mobile prefix are covered: the slash form "0171/3920045" and the parenthesised form "(0171) 3920045" — both deprecated by the current DIN 5008 (which prescribes plain space grouping) but still common in signatures and letterheads — plus the "+49 (0)171 ..." letterhead form (nonstandard per ITU-T E.123, but ubiquitous). Geographic (Ortsnetz) landline numbers are intentionally out of scope (so the landline renderings "030/12345678" and "(030) 12345678" are likewise not matched): BNetzA states area codes run 2-5 digits and new allocations are capped at 11 significant digits (10 for the Berlin/Hamburg/Frankfurt/Munich two-digit-code exception), but does not publish a verified minimum length for the existing stock of legacy numbers, so a low-end bound would be invented rather than sourced — mirroring in-phone-number's decision to scope out India's similarly under-specified STD/landline numbers.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (German mobile numbers carry no checksum). Reference: Bundesnetzagentur, Nummernplan für Mobile Dienste, https://www.bundesnetzagentur.de/DE/Fachthemen/Telekommunikation/Nummerierung/MobileDienste/start.html; digit-length table at https://www.bundesnetzagentur.de/DE/Fachthemen/Telekommunikation/Nummerierung/MobileDienste/LaengeRNB/start.html. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+49) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the 01[5-7] mobile-family leading digits and the 10-11 digit length bound (drawn directly from BNetzA's published Rufnummernblock length table) narrow the format, but German mobile numbers carry no checksum and a 10-11 digit sequence with those leading digits is still a high digit-collision format. Per the phone-family convention (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; a +CC prefix alone is insufficient gating; there is no 65 rung), both the domestic and +49 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +49 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

0180 is a special-rate service prefix, not a 015/016/017 mobile range — third digit 8 is excluded
Only 4 digits after the 0152 mobile prefix, far short of the required 8-9

should_not_match.description: Date written with slashes — the slash branch requires a 4-digit 015/016/017 mobile prefix and 7-8 subscriber digits

false_positives.description: A 10-11 digit sequence with the 01[5-7] mobile leading-digit shape can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, order numbers, or other structured identifiers of similar length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +49 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: Geographic (Ortsnetz) landline numbers are not detected at all (a false negative, not a false positive, but noted for completeness): BNetzA documents a 2-5 digit area code and an 11-digit cap for new allocations (10 for the Berlin/Hamburg/Frankfurt/Munich exception), but publishes no verified minimum length across the existing stock, so bounding a landline regex would mean inventing a lower bound rather than sourcing it.
false_positives.mitigation: A future revision could add landline coverage if a genuinely verifiable minimum-length constraint is confirmed from a primary BNetzA source, following the same verification bar applied here.

patterns.risk_description: The German identifier detects BNetzA mobile ranges 015, 016, and 017 in domestic, +49, slash, parenthesised, and common letterhead forms; geographic landlines are intentionally outside scope. A true mobile number can support targeted calls, SMS phishing, harassment, or account-recovery pretexts when combined with the subscriber's identity and service context. The ordinary unit is one contact route, while ten- or eleven-digit orders and invoices can share the shape and the detector supplies no proof of ownership. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are proportionate; SENSITIVE would require a number tied to credentials, a protected service, intimate communications, or location and identity data enabling serious direct targeting.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with OFFICIAL because a German mobile number facilitates contact and pretexting but lacks authentication authority and sensitive context on its own. SENSITIVE is not met without linked credentials, protected relationships, communications, or location information that materially increases harm.

generic.rationale: The generic Low result treats a German mobile number as a bounded contact identifier rather than a credential or complete subscriber record.

patterns.risk_description: The regex recognises a Danish CPR candidate as six date-like digits plus four digits, with an optional hyphen and civic-label context. A genuine CPR number encodes date-of-birth information and persistently links a resident across health, tax, and public services, so it can aid targeted impersonation when paired with a name. Ten-digit phone numbers, dates, and administrative references can collide with the structure, and the match alone supplies neither service access nor a complete person record. Risk 5 OFFICIAL captures bounded encoded-attribute and correlation harm; SENSITIVE would require verified attribution or linked health, financial, or government-service information.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low because one CPR candidate reveals limited structure but does not authenticate the resident or expose a substantive service record. SENSITIVE is not met without person linkage and additional sensitive content.

generic.rationale: Low generic handling is appropriate for an isolated date-shaped CPR candidate with notable phone-number overlap. Medium controls should apply to validated resident records or datasets linking the number to names and service history.

All tiers exclude template/fixture text and DFV awareness, statistics, strategy and textbook material. 65 is discovery-only.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: enforce tiers require DVO terminology plus a populated aggrieved/respondent/named person field; 85 also requires a Queensland statutory, police or form anchor. patterns.name: Spanish Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects Spanish national telephone numbers per Spain's closed 9-digit numbering plan (Plan Nacional de Numeración Telefónica, administered under CNMC oversight): mobile numbers (segment N=6 in full, plus N=7 partially opened for mobile use in the 71/72/73/74 sub-ranges by the SETSI Resolución de 12 de marzo de 2010, BOE-A-2010-5251; the first 7-prefixed mobile numbers entered service from late 2010/2011 once the then-regulator CMT assigned the new ranges to operators) and geographic numbers (leading 8 or 9, with the second digit constrained to never be 0 — a constraint that incidentally excludes the 900/901/902/905 toll-free and premium-rate service ranges, whose second digit is 0). Spain has no domestic trunk prefix, so the +34 international form carries the same 9 significant digits as the domestic form, just with the +34 prefix in place of nothing.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (Spanish numbers have no checksum). Reference: CNMC, Registro de Numeración de Telecomunicaciones, https://www.cnmc.es/en/sectores-que-regulamos/telecomunicaciones/registros-de-numeracion (9-digit closed plan); Resolución de 12 de marzo de 2010, de la Secretaría de Estado de Telecomunicaciones y para la Sociedad de la Información (SETSI, not CMT — the ministry attributes numbering resources; the regulator then assigns them), BOE-A-2010-5251, https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-2010-5251, opening the 71/72/73/74 mobile sub-ranges, as reported in CNMC's 2012 sectoral report, https://www.cnmc.es/sites/default/files/1539217_7.pdf; leading-digit breakdown corroborated by the Spanish government's consumer information service, https://www.consumoresponde.es/. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+34) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the mobile (6, or 7 with second digit 1-4) and geographic (8/9 with non-zero second digit) leading-digit constraints narrow the format, but Spanish numbers carry no checksum and a 9-digit sequence with those leading digits is still a high digit-collision format. Per the phone-family convention (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; a +CC prefix alone is insufficient gating; there is no 65 rung), both the domestic and +34 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +34 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

should_match.description: Domestic mobile, N=6 segment, illustrative synthetic value (no official CNMC-reserved fictional range exists — verified absent during research)
Domestic mobile, N=7 segment (71-74 sub-range opened by the March 2010 SETSI resolution, in service since 2010/2011), illustrative synthetic value
Domestic geographic, leading 9 with non-zero second digit, illustrative synthetic value
International +34 form of the mobile number, same 9 significant digits (no trunk 0 to drop)
International form written with the 00 dialling prefix instead of +

should_not_match.description: Leading digit 5 is not a valid mobile (6, 7) or geographic (8, 9) leading digit
Leading 9 but second digit is 0 — a toll-free/premium-rate service number, excluded by the non-zero-second-digit geographic constraint
Only 8 digits — one short of the required 9
Valid-shaped digit run embedded inside a longer reference number, rejected by digit boundaries

Australian business number in a signature block next to a phone label. Its last nine digits (824 753 556) have a valid geographic shape; the digit-group lookbehind rejects them because they continue a longer grouped number.

false_positives.description: A 9-digit sequence with a valid mobile or geographic leading-digit shape can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, order numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +34 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: No official CNMC-reserved fictional or test number range exists for Spain (confirmed by web research, unlike NANP's 555-01XX or Ofcom's drama numbers), so illustrative synthetic values were used instead of an authoritative reserved range.
false_positives.mitigation: Test values use clearly non-representative sequential digit patterns; deployers should substitute their own tenant's synthetic test data for live validation rather than relying on a non-existent official reserved range.

false_positives.description: A valid-shaped nine-digit run can be the tail of a longer space-grouped number, such as the Australian business number "51 824 753 556" (its last nine digits read as a geographic 8xx number), which sits next to a phone label in most Australian signature blocks.
false_positives.mitigation: The domestic sub-regex has a fixed-width lookbehind (?<!\d[ .-]) that rejects a match preceded by a digit and a single separator, so it only starts at the beginning of a number. The same lookbehind stops it firing inside the spaced +34 rendering ("+34 612 345 678"), which the international sub-regex reports instead; that sub-regex also accepts the 00 dialling prefix ("0034 612 345 678"), a form the domestic sub-regex used to cover.

patterns.risk_description: The regex identifies Spanish nine-digit mobile or geographic phone shapes, with optional +34 and flexible separators, rather than confirming the subscriber or whether the number is active. A real number can enable nuisance contact, phishing, messaging-app discovery, or identity correlation when paired with a name or account. The normal unit is one person or organization contact, and practical harm usually needs that companion context; invoice and order numbers with valid leading digits can also collide. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect bounded standalone exposure, while a vulnerable person's confidential contact, a bulk directory, or a sensitive case link would reach SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because one Spanish phone number is a contact identifier that requires identity or service context for material misuse. SENSITIVE is not met without vulnerable-person context, sensitive account linkage, repeated harassment risk, or aggregation capable of moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low with Low DLM suits one Spanish contact number whose ordinary misuse is limited and reversible. Sensitive linkage or bulk contact data requires stronger handling.

references.title: CNMC: Registro de Numeración de Telecomunicaciones (9-digit closed numbering plan)
BOE-A-2010-5251: Resolución de 12 de marzo de 2010, de la SETSI — attribution of the 71/72/73/74 sub-ranges to mobile services (primary source)
CNMC: Informe Económico Sectorial 2012 — Numeración (reporting the March 2010 SETSI resolution and the subsequent CMT range assignments)
Consumo Responde (Spanish government consumer service): Tipología de los números de teléfono existentes en España

changelog.description: Digit-group boundary (2026-10-16 boilerplate run): the domestic sub-regex fired at 75 on the last nine digits of an Australian ABN ("ABN 51 824 753 556" next to a "Phone:" label). patterns.description: Detects Spain Physical Addresses patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type that uses machine learning and function-based detection for physical address identification. This keyword list provides address-related terms for supplementary matching.
patterns.operation: Function-based detection in Microsoft Purview. This pattern uses keyword matching for country-specific address terminology to identify physical address data.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence: broad keyword matching on address terms requires additional context and corroborative evidence for accurate physical address detection. Address keywords alone produce high false positive rates without structural validation.

should_match.description: Contains address keyword 'calle'
Contains address keyword 'avenida'

false_positives.mitigation: Require structural address patterns (number + street type + name) rather than isolated keyword matches.

false_positives.description: Navigation or mapping references that mention road types without containing actual addresses
false_positives.mitigation: Use proximity-based corroborative evidence to ensure keywords appear alongside numeric components.

patterns.risk_description: The custom Spanish pattern is a low-confidence keyword list using calle, avenida, and paseo, with wide scope and no validation of a complete postal address. A genuine residence can support targeted mail or unwanted contact when linked to an identified occupant, but the same phrases commonly describe hotels, businesses, monuments, and tourist routes. Navigation and destination text are documented false positives. Risk 3 OFFICIAL reflects low standalone harm; SENSITIVE would require a protected or vulnerable resident, concealed home, active threat, movement linkage, or an aggregated person-address dataset.

classification.rationale: Risk 3 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, the OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low tier for ordinary Spanish address terminology. The next SENSITIVE level is not met because no resident identity, protected property, current safety issue, movement trail, or consequential register is established.

generic.rationale: Generic Low and Low handling fit a Spanish physical address that needs trustworthy occupant attribution or heightened safety context for material misuse.

Spanish tax identification number
Spanish DNI/NIF format

patterns.risk_description: The Spanish tax-ID rule matches eight digits followed by a letter in NIF, DNI, or tax context. Depending on the holder, the value can identify an individual taxpayer or support business and administrative records, and reuse may assist false invoicing, identity correlation, or a tax-themed approach. It does not by itself expose a return, income, debt, payment method, or access credential, and the same broad shape can overlap other national identifiers. The next SENSITIVE level is not met because the match supplies neither confidential tax facts nor the additional identity and account access needed for moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM reflect limited correlation and impersonation value from the NIF-shaped identifier alone. A tax return, assessment, payment record, or authenticated government-service record would be classified on its richer content.

patterns.name: EU AI Act Declaration of Conformity (High-Risk AI System)
patterns.description: Detects EU declarations of conformity for high-risk AI systems under Article 47 and Annex V of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). By drawing up the declaration the provider assumes responsibility for compliance; pre-signature drafts and the surrounding conformity-assessment correspondence reveal the provider's compliance posture, notified-body findings, and certificate details before market placement.
patterns.operation: Concept (topic) classifier, not an identifier detector. Primary detection: 'EU declaration of conformity' coupled within a bounded 400-character window to AI-specific context (AI system, artificial intelligence, or the Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 citation) so generic CE product declarations do not reach any tier. Corroborated within 300 characters by Annex V content vocabulary (sole responsibility, harmonised standards, notified body, conformity assessment procedure, authorised representative). Noise exclusion for news, marketing, academic, and legal-alert contexts.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. 'EU declaration of conformity' is New Legislative Framework boilerplate shared with every CE-marked product class, so the primary regex requires AI context inside a bounded window and corroboration leans on the Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 citation and Annex V vocabulary. Residual collisions (multi-product declarations mentioning AI incidentally, compliance commentary) keep this below identifier-grade precision.

1. AI system: 'RoadSense Perception Module', type RS-PM-4, serial range 0001-0400.
2. Provider: Continova Mobility GmbH, Ingolstadt, Germany.
3. This declaration of conformity is issued under the sole responsibility of the provider.
7. Conformity assessment procedure performed by notified body NB 2797; certificate AI-2026-0114.
should_match.description: Annex V declaration of conformity for a high-risk AI system

should_match.value: The undersigned declares that the high-risk AI system identified above is in conformity with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and complies with Regulation (EU) 2016/679. References to the relevant harmonised standards used are listed in the schedule to this EU declaration of conformity, together with the identification of the notified body and the certificate issued.
should_match.description: Declaration body text with GDPR statement and harmonised standards schedule

should_match.value: Draft for legal sign-off, not yet released: attached is the electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for the AI system 'TriageAssist' pursuant to Article 47. Once the notified body confirms the certificate scope, we must keep the declaration at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years and lodge a copy with the technical documentation.
should_match.description: Pre-release email circulating the signed declaration for an AI system

Analysts expect notified-body capacity to be the main bottleneck, a industry newsletter reported.
should_not_match.description: News analysis of AI Act conformity obligations (plural phrasing, no declaration text)

We argue that the declaration's assumption-of-responsibility function is weakened by reliance on provider self-assessment.
should_not_match.description: Academic paper analysing the Article 47 declaration (filter-dependent negative)

should_not_match.value: Internal memo to product teams, reproduced in this month's compliance newsletter: Article 47(1) requires the provider to draw up 'a written machine readable, physical or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system' and to keep it at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after market placement.
should_not_match.description: Regulation text quoted verbatim in an internal memo (filter-dependent negative)

false_positives.description: Generic CE / New Legislative Framework declarations of conformity (machinery, EMC, RED, medical devices) — the document class shares its title and most boilerplate ('sole responsibility', 'harmonised standards', 'notified body') with every CE-marked product
false_positives.mitigation: Primary regex requires AI-specific context (AI system / artificial intelligence / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) within a bounded 400-character window of the declaration phrase, so purely non-AI declarations do not reach any tier; residual risk remains for multi-regulation declarations that mention AI incidentally

false_positives.description: Signed declarations are provided to authorities and may accompany the product publicly, so a copy is not always sensitive
false_positives.mitigation: Treat matches as candidates for classification review; sensitivity concentrates in pre-signature drafts and attached conformity-assessment correspondence

false_positives.description: Compliance-consultancy marketing and template libraries referencing the declaration for AI systems
false_positives.mitigation: Noise exclusion on 'book a demo', 'free trial', 'webinar', 'client alert'. The shared template-exclusion dictionary is deliberately NOT used — its 'documentation' term collides with 'technical documentation', which Article 47(1) requires the declaration to be lodged with, so genuine declarations would be suppressed

false_positives.description: News, legal analysis, academic commentary, and internal memos or newsletters quoting Article 47 obligations or the regulation's text verbatim
false_positives.mitigation: Noise exclusion on press/academic/newsletter terms; commentary typically uses plural or paraphrased forms rather than the declaration's own content vocabulary. A verbatim Article 47(1) quotation in a plain internal memo carrying no noise term will still satisfy the AI-coupled primary and reach the 75 tier — an accepted residual collision for a concept-class matcher, documented here because such memos discuss exactly this document class

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies an EU AI Act Article 47 declaration of conformity for a high-risk AI system, including provider, system, standards, notified-body, and conformity-assessment details. A final signed declaration may accompany the product or be provided to authorities and can be public, while pre-signature drafts may reveal limited compliance posture or unresolved certificate information. The detector also risks matching generic CE declarations unless AI-specific context and Annex V vocabulary corroborate the topic, so one match does not establish a confidential technical dossier. Risk 5 supports OFFICIAL; SENSITIVE would require attached non-public findings, material control failures, trade secrets, or pre-market correspondence whose disclosure causes direct regulatory or commercial harm.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because a declaration is often an externally supplied compliance statement with bounded confidential content. SENSITIVE is not met without non-public findings, failures, trade secrets, or consequential pre-market correspondence.

generic.rationale: Low with Low DLM reflects the declaration's frequently public compliance function while allowing attached confidential assessment material to be handled separately.

patterns.name: EU AI Act Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)
patterns.description: Detects deployer-side fundamental rights impact assessments (FRIA) under Article 27 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). A FRIA is performed before deploying certain high-risk AI systems by public bodies, private providers of public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and life/health-insurance pricing systems (Annex III points 5(b) and (c)). Completed FRIAs contain candid assessments of risks of harm to specific categories of natural persons and are sensitive before notification and remediation.
patterns.operation: Concept (topic) classifier, not an identifier detector. Primary detection: keyword proximity on the defined term 'fundamental rights impact assessment' corroborated within 300 characters by Article 27's required-content vocabulary (categories of natural persons, specific risks of harm, human oversight measures, internal governance, complaint mechanisms, market surveillance authority) and AI Act citations. The 85 tier additionally requires structural support from either the case-insensitive FRIA acronym regex or an Article 27 / Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 citation, so documents that use the full defined term plus such a citation reach the recommended confidence without the acronym (the FRIA keyword evidence term is case-sensitive; full-title documents lacking any citation stop at the 75 tier). Noise exclusion for news, marketing, academic, legal-alert, and template/sample contexts.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. 'Fundamental rights impact assessment' is the regulation's defined term and strongly indicates the document class, but the phrase also circulates in academic and policy literature (including pre-AI Act methodologies such as the Dutch FRAIA) and in consultancy marketing; corroborative Article 27 content vocabulary and noise exclusions reduce but cannot eliminate that collision. No identifier-grade precision is promised.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a completed or draft Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment for deployment of a high-risk AI system, including affected categories of people, specific risks of harm, oversight, governance, complaints, and mitigation measures. Premature disclosure can expose vulnerable-group analysis, acknowledged discrimination or service risks, unresolved safeguards, and the deployer's regulatory posture; working papers may also contain examples or personal data from the underlying process. Academic, policy, marketing, legal-alert, template, and ordinary GDPR DPIA content can resemble the topic, so FRIA and AI Act structure are important corroboration. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy; PROTECTED would require named vulnerable individuals, bulk sensitive evidence, or a critical deployment failure capable of significant harm.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy, and Medium because candid affected-group and harm analysis can create moderate rights, legal, and reputational consequences. PROTECTED is not met without identified vulnerable people, bulk sensitive evidence, or significant critical-service harm.

generic.rationale: Medium with Medium Personal-Privacy DLM protects non-public analysis of affected people and rights risks while distinguishing it from person-level dossiers or bulk sensitive evidence.

patterns.name: EU AI Act GPAI Model Documentation
patterns.description: Detects general-purpose AI (GPAI) model provider documentation under Article 53 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689): Annex XI technical documentation for the AI Office, Annex XII information packs for downstream providers, the Article 53(1)(d) public summary of training content, and Article 55 systemic-risk evaluation material (adversarial testing / red-teaming reports). Pre-publication drafts reveal model internals, training-data provenance, compute and energy figures, and systemic-risk findings.
patterns.operation: Concept (topic) classifier, not an identifier detector. Primary detection: keyword proximity on the regulation's defined vocabulary ('general-purpose AI model', 'public summary of training content', 'summary about the content used for training', 'technical documentation of the model') corroborated within 300 characters by Annex XI/XII item vocabulary (number of parameters, modality, computational resources, energy consumption, acceptable use policies, curation methodologies) and Article 53/55 terms (AI Office, downstream providers, systemic risk, adversarial testing). Noise exclusion for news, marketing, and academic contexts.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. 'General-purpose AI model' is the regulation's defined term and anchors the document class, but it also saturates news, marketing, and academic commentary on the AI Act; tiers therefore require Annex XI/XII item vocabulary and AI Office / systemic-risk corroboration, and the bare-primary tier is discovery-only. No identifier-grade precision is promised.

patterns.risk_description: This detector identifies Article 53 or 55 documentation for a general-purpose AI model, including model architecture, parameters, compute and energy use, training-data provenance, downstream-provider information, public training summaries, and adversarial-testing findings. Pre-publication material can expose trade secrets, copyright and privacy risk, evaluated weaknesses, and planned mitigations, helping competitors or attackers while weakening the provider's regulatory position. Public training-content summaries, open model cards, news, policy analysis, academic commentary, and compliance marketing can share the vocabulary, so the normal true positive must contain substantive Annex XI, Annex XII, or systemic-risk content. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy; PROTECTED would require exploitable systemic weaknesses, bulk personal training data, or compromise of a widely deployed model causing significant damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy, and Medium because training provenance and non-public risk findings can materially expose data practices and model weaknesses. PROTECTED is not met without bulk personal data, systemic exploitability, or significant cross-deployment harm.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium Personal-Privacy DLM protect non-public training provenance and risk analysis while distinguishing it from public summaries and open model documentation.

patterns.name: EU AI Act Technical Documentation (High-Risk AI System)
patterns.description: Detects Article 11 / Annex IV technical documentation for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). This documentation must demonstrate compliance of the high-risk AI system before placing on the market and contains commercially sensitive material — system architecture, design specifications, training-data datasheets, risk management findings, and known limitations — whose uncontrolled disclosure exposes trade secrets and the provider's compliance posture.
patterns.operation: Concept (topic) classifier, not an identifier detector. Primary detection: keyword proximity on Annex IV's distinctive section vocabulary ('general description of the AI system', 'post-market monitoring plan', 'technical documentation of a/the high-risk AI system', 'technical documentation referred to in Article 11') corroborated within 300 characters by the AI Act's own terms (intended purpose, risk management system, human oversight, harmonised standards, Annex IV, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Noise exclusion for news, marketing, academic, and legal-alert contexts.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. Annex IV's enumerated section headings are distinctive of the document class, but the same phrases appear verbatim in legal alerts, compliance guides, and training material discussing the AI Act; noise exclusions and corroborative evidence reduce but cannot eliminate that concept-class collision. No identifier-grade precision is promised.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies Article 11 and Annex IV technical documentation for a high-risk AI system, including architecture, intended purpose, training-data requirements, risk management, known limitations, human oversight, and post-market monitoring. Disclosure can expose trade secrets, unresolved compliance gaps, failure modes, and attack-relevant system detail, harming the provider and potentially weakening safeguards for people affected by the system. Other CE technical files, law-firm alerts, marketing, news, policy analysis, and academic discussion use similar language, so high-risk AI and Annex IV context must corroborate the document. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy; PROTECTED would require actionable compromise of a critical deployment, bulk sensitive training data, or systemic weaknesses capable of significant harm.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy, and Medium because design, data, limitation, and oversight details can materially expose both provider interests and affected people. PROTECTED is not met without critical-service exploitability, bulk sensitive data, or significant systemic harm.

generic.rationale: Medium with Medium Personal-Privacy DLM protects non-public system and data-risk documentation while reserving High handling for critical or system-scale compromise.

patterns.name: European Debit Card Number
patterns.description: Detects European debit and credit card numbers for Visa, Mastercard, and American Express networks. The pattern matches 13- to 16-digit card numbers based on the leading digits assigned to each network by the ISO/IEC 7812 standard. This is commonly used for PCI-DSS compliance scanning across EU-regulated financial data.
patterns.operation: Corroborative evidence: 6 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: financial-payment-card-terms, financial-cvv, financial-expiry.
patterns.confidence_justification: Card numbers have well-defined prefix ranges (4 for Visa, 51-55 for Mastercard, 34/37 for Amex) and fixed lengths, giving this pattern strong structural precision. Luhn validation as a post-match step further reduces false positives.

should_match.description: Valid Visa test card number (16 digits)
Valid Mastercard test card number
Valid American Express test card number (15 digits)

should_not_match.description: 16-digit number that does not match any known card prefix
Too few digits to be a valid Visa card number
Discover card prefix, not covered by this EU-focused pattern

false_positives.description: Random 16-digit numbers that happen to start with a valid card prefix (e.g. serial numbers, tracking codes)
false_positives.mitigation: Apply Luhn checksum validation on matched values. Require corroborative evidence keywords such as 'card number' or 'CVV' within proximity.

patterns.risk_description: This high-confidence identifier detector finds structurally valid Visa, Mastercard, or American Express payment-card numbers in European financial context. A card number is a payment credential component that can support card-not-present fraud, account targeting, or convincing phishing, especially when expiry or security-code context is nearby. The normal match exposes one cardholder to serious but usually contained loss and replacement burden, although further authentication data may still be required. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE are justified; a complete card database, issuer compromise, or broad reusable authentication package would raise the impact.

classification.rationale: A valid payment-card number supports risk 8, OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE Financial because it is materially more actionable than a receiving-account coordinate and can contribute directly to payment fraud. PROTECTED is not met by one card number without bulk compromise, full authentication data, or significant-damage scale.

generic.rationale: A debit-card number is Medium Financial information because it is a reusable payment credential component with serious cardholder impact, even when supplementary data is required.

patterns.description: Detects DORA Article 6 ICT risk management framework documentation and the digital operational resilience strategy of financial entities — board-approved framework documents, risk tolerance statements, and internal audit reviews of the framework. These documents describe the entity's defensive architecture, control gaps, and risk appetite; disclosure hands attackers a map of weaknesses.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary topic phrases (ICT risk management framework, digital operational resilience strategy) within 300 characters of Article 6 vocabulary (risk tolerance level, information security objectives, key performance indicators, digital operational resilience testing, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554). Negative keyword exclusion for regulator publications, consultancy explainers, and training material. Concept classifier: matches the topic, not identifier-grade evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. 'ICT risk management framework' and 'digital operational resilience strategy' are DORA Article 6 defined phrases, and the 85 tier additionally requires Article 6 vocabulary (risk tolerance level, information security objectives, key performance indicators, digital operational resilience testing). The phrases also appear across the DORA advisory ecosystem — consultancy and academic material is suppressed only by noise exclusions.

patterns.risk_description: The EU DORA concept detector recognises Article 6 ICT risk-framework material through risk tolerance, resilience strategy, security objectives, performance indicators, and internal-audit terms, with public-material exclusions. Published regulation, consultancy commentary, and templates can match, whereas an attributed internal framework may reveal control gaps and defensive priorities useful to an attacker. A topic-level hit lacks direct harm until current organisational ownership, residual risk, or implementation weakness is present. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL fit public or generic framework material; SENSITIVE requires a board-approved internal framework or gap assessment exposing current exploitable weaknesses.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low because the medium-confidence concept can identify published regulation, consultancy material, templates, or an unattributed framework without exposing a live control weakness. SENSITIVE requires a current organisation-specific framework, audit result, or gap assessment that identifies residual risk, defensive priorities, or exploitable ICT control deficiencies.

generic.rationale: Low generic handling reflects the accepted topic-level outcome, with stronger controls required when corroboration establishes a current internal defensive framework or audit finding.

patterns.name: EU DORA Major ICT-Related Incident Report
patterns.description: Detects DORA Article 19 major ICT-related incident reports — the initial notification, intermediate report, and final report submitted to the competent authority under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/302 — and voluntary notifications of significant cyber threats. These reports detail live vulnerabilities, affected services, and root causes; premature disclosure aids attackers and can move markets.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary topic phrases (major ICT-related incident, significant cyber threat) within 300 characters of Article 19 reporting vocabulary (initial notification, intermediate report, final report, root cause analysis, incident reference code, competent authority, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554). Negative keyword exclusion for press releases, consultancy webinars, and training material. Concept classifier: matches the topic, not identifier-grade evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher. 'Major ICT-related incident' and 'significant cyber threat' are DORA Article 19 terms of art rarely used outside the regulation's orbit, and the 85 tier additionally requires reporting-stage vocabulary (initial notification, intermediate report, final report, incident reference code, root cause analysis). News coverage and consultancy explainers about DORA incident reporting share this vocabulary and are suppressed only by noise exclusions.

patterns.risk_description: EU DORA Major ICT-Related Incident Report detects Article 19 initial, intermediate, final, or voluntary notifications containing affected services, impact, containment, root cause, and reporting status. Disclosure during an incident can expose live weaknesses, aid follow-on attacks, reveal customer disruption, and create regulatory or market harm for the financial entity. The normal report is operationally sensitive but usually bounded to one incident and organization. Risk 7 and SENSITIVE Financial are justified; PROTECTED would require critical-sector cascade, severe safety effects, or release likely to cause significant system-wide damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with OFFICIAL: Sensitive, SENSITIVE Financial, label SENS_Fin, and the Medium tier because a live incident filing exposes consequential operational and financial details. PROTECTED is not met without critical-service, safety, or systemic significant-damage consequences.

generic.rationale: Medium Financial handling protects regulated incident reports whose live impact, root-cause, and recovery details can aid attackers and harm the reporting entity.

patterns.name: EU DORA Register of Information
patterns.description: Detects extracts and working copies of the DORA Article 28(3) register of information on contractual arrangements with ICT third-party service providers, including the ESAs' Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 template content (contractual arrangement reference numbers, provider LEIs, ICT service supply chain, critical or important function flags). The register maps a financial entity's entire ICT outsourcing estate and its concentration risk; disclosure exposes supplier dependencies and attack surface.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary topic phrases (register of information, contractual arrangement reference number, ICT third-party service provider) within 300 characters of DORA register vocabulary (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, critical or important function, ICT service supply chain, LEI, type of ICT services). Structural corroboration: the 85 tier requires an Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 template code (B_01.01-B_07.01, B_99.01) in addition to — not instead of — the register vocabulary; extracts carrying vocabulary but no template code stop at the 75 tier. Negative keyword exclusion for press releases, consultancy explainers, and template/training material. Concept classifier: matches the topic, not identifier-grade evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: honest topic matcher, not an identifier detector. The Article 28(3) phrase 'register of information' and the ITS field name 'contractual arrangement reference number' are regulation-specific terms of art, and the 85 tier additionally requires both DORA register vocabulary (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, critical or important function, LEI, ICT service supply chain) and a B_xx.yy template code; vocabulary-only extracts (e.g. submission memos) reach the 75 tier. Compliance-consultancy and news content about DORA uses the same vocabulary and is suppressed only by noise exclusions.

patterns.risk_description: EU DORA Register of Information detects the structured outsourcing register of ICT contractual arrangements, provider identifiers, service supply chains, critical-function flags, substitutability, and exit planning. Disclosure can map supplier dependencies and concentration risk, helping an attacker target weak providers or disrupting procurement and supervisory activity. A normal register extract creates moderate operational and commercial harm, with impact scaling by breadth and detail. Risk 6 and SENSITIVE Financial are appropriate; PROTECTED would require a sector-critical dependency map or exploitable architecture whose release could cause significant systemic damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 6 maps to OFFICIAL: Sensitive, SENSITIVE Financial, label SENS_Fin, and the Medium tier because the register exposes non-public ICT supplier and dependency information. PROTECTED is not met by an ordinary extract without sector-scale criticality or significant strategic consequence.

generic.rationale: Medium Financial handling is appropriate for a regulated outsourcing register that exposes supplier concentration, service dependencies, and exit constraints.

patterns.name: EU Driver's License Number
patterns.description: Detects EU driver's license number patterns across all EU member states. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Broad keyword-based detection for EU driver's license references. Matches alphanumeric sequences of 5-20 characters at word boundaries combined with driver's license keywords. Corroborative evidence: 5 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: broad pattern covering multiple EU member state formats. Corroborative keywords are essential for reliable detection due to the wide range of formats matched. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

should_match.description: Common EU format with letter prefix and digits
Mixed alphanumeric EU driver's license format
Longer alphanumeric format used by some EU states

should_not_match.value: ABCD
should_not_match.description: Too few characters (4 instead of minimum 5)

should_not_match.value: A1B2C3D4E5F6G7H8I9J0K
should_not_match.description: Too many characters (21 instead of maximum 20)

should_not_match.value: demo mock test data id flag
should_not_match.description: Template/sample context negative — this pattern has no numeric structural component (broad 5-20 char alnum shape), so unlike the numeric identifier patterns the fix is word-length rather than digit-count: every token is under the 5-character minimum (demo/mock/test/data are 4 chars, id/flag are 2-4), so the universal-engine top-level regex correctly does not match anywhere in the value, while the tokens are still drawn from the template-exclusion dictionary (demo, mock) to preserve the template/placeholder framing for the Purview-tier NOT-group this test case also exercises

false_positives.description: Generic alphanumeric sequences matching the broad EU driver's license format appearing in unrelated contexts such as product codes, serial numbers, or reference identifiers.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords within the proximity window to confirm driver's license context.

patterns.risk_description: This EU-wide detector treats any five-to-twenty-character alphanumeric sequence as a licence candidate when multilingual driving-licence terminology is present. A genuine value may support identity correlation, rental impersonation, or targeted licensing scams, but the pattern does not establish the issuing member state or a specific national format. Product codes, serials, and reference identifiers share the broad shape, and a match provides no holder name, photograph, address, entitlement, or registry status. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit the uncertain atomic signal; a country-specific validated number, licence image, or populated driver record would raise the context toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low for a broad EU licence candidate. SENSITIVE is not met because country, holder, document validity, and substantive driver information are not established by the match.

generic.rationale: Low classification and Low DLM reflect a member-state-ambiguous licence candidate whose independent meaning and exploitability require substantial corroboration.

patterns.name: International Bank Account Number (IBAN)
patterns.description: Detects International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) used across European and global banking systems. IBANs consist of a two-letter country code, two check digits, and up to 30 alphanumeric characters representing the domestic bank account number. This pattern matches IBANs with or without space or hyphen delimiters between digit groups.
patterns.operation: Validation: Mod 97 (ISO 7064). Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bank_Account_Number Corroborative evidence: 10 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: financial-deposit-terms.
patterns.confidence_justification: The two-letter country code prefix followed by exactly two check digits provides a strong structural anchor. Combined with corroborative evidence keywords and the fixed digit-group format, false positive rates are low in most document contexts.

should_match.description: German IBAN with space-separated digit groups
UK IBAN with no delimiters
French IBAN with space-separated digit groups

should_not_match.description: Too short to be a valid IBAN (only 4 BBAN characters)
Digit-only string missing the country code prefix

should_not_match.value: INVALID123456789
should_not_match.description: Starts with more than two letters, not a valid IBAN structure

false_positives.description: Strings that begin with a two-letter country code followed by two digits but are not actual IBANs (e.g. product codes, reference numbers)
false_positives.mitigation: Validate the check digits using the MOD-97 algorithm defined in ISO 13616. Require corroborative evidence keywords within proximity.

patterns.risk_description: This high-confidence identifier detector finds a checksum-valid International Bank Account Number used to route payments to a bank account. IBANs are commonly placed on invoices and supplied to payers, and possession of one does not authenticate the account holder or authorise an outgoing transfer. Disclosure can still aid invoice redirection, phishing, or attempted direct-debit abuse against the account holder, but those paths require impersonation, a mandate, or another process failure. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit the standalone coordinate; a wire instruction, debit mandate, or banking credential paired with the IBAN would justify SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: A checksum-valid IBAN warrants risk 5, PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low because it reliably identifies a receiving account but does not authenticate the holder or authorise an outgoing transfer. SENSITIVE requires payment instructions, mandate evidence, authentication secrets, transaction history, or another composite financial record that gives the routing coordinate direct misuse value.

generic.rationale: An IBAN is Low as an atomic financial identifier because it is routinely shared for payment receipt and requires additional authority or deception to cause direct loss.

patterns.name: EU Marking - RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED (EUCI ladder)
patterns.description: Detects European Union Classified Information (EUCI) protective markings as defined in Article 2(2) of Council Decision 2013/488/EU: the four bilingual French/English classification levels rendered together as a single marking — RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED, CONFIDENTIEL UE/EU CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET UE/EU SECRET and TRÈS SECRET UE/EU TOP SECRET (the slash carries no surrounding spaces and TRÈS carries a grave accent, per the primary source). Named historically for RESTREINT but scopes the full EUCI ladder. The single-language French components (RESTREINT UE, CONFIDENTIEL UE, SECRET UE, TRÈS SECRET UE) are matched at a lower tier. Marking syntax verified directly against the Council Decision text; matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the canonical dual French/English EUCI marking (e.g. RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED) exactly as defined in Council Decision 2013/488/EU Article 2(2), tolerant of hyphen or PDF-line-wrap-inserted whitespace between the wrappable tokens. Tier 75 matches the single-language French components (RESTREINT UE / CONFIDENTIEL UE / SECRET UE / TRÈS SECRET UE) — these are the exact French halves of the verified dual markings, each carrying the distinctive "UE" (Union Européenne) marker. Both tiers carry only a template/noise NOT-exclusion — the case-sensitive structured marking token is the high-confidence evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the dual French/English forms: "RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED" and its ladder are structurally unmistakable — the bilingual "<FR-LEVEL> UE/EU <EN-LEVEL>" construction with the no-space slash appears nowhere in natural language and is verified verbatim against Council Decision 2013/488/EU. The single-language French components (75) carry the distinctive trailing "UE" EU marker and are the exact French halves of the verified markings, so they too have negligible natural-language collision. The English-only halves (EU RESTRICTED, EU CONFIDENTIAL, EU SECRET, EU TOP SECRET) are deliberately not matched as a standalone tier, to avoid the higher false-positive surface of an "EU " prefix on common English classification words — documented below.
