patterns.risk_description: The regex recognizes an HL7 version 2 message header beginning with the MSH segment and relies on nearby healthcare identifiers or codes to corroborate the low-confidence structure. A genuine message commonly carries patient identity, encounter, diagnosis, order, result, or routing data in later segments, so disclosure can expose linked clinical workflow even though the matched header itself is structural. Template exclusions and domain context reduce false positives, but one detected message does not imply a bulk feed or safety-critical interface compromise. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE remain proportionate; PROTECTED would require large message volumes, complete longitudinal records, or operational access that could materially disrupt care.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, the Personal-Privacy DLM, and Medium for a corroborated clinical message. PROTECTED is not met because one header match proves neither bulk patient content nor control of a safety-critical integration.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium Personal-Privacy DLM reflect the likely linked clinical content of a genuine HL7 message without assuming an entire interface feed or patient database.

patterns.name: Bulk Staff Personal Details Extract
patterns.description: Tabular HRIS, payroll or reporting exports of staff personal details that do not carry TFNs: a CSV, spreadsheet or pipe/tab-delimited header row of HR column labels (employee / staff ID, name, date of birth, home address, position / classification, commencement or termination date, employment status) followed by populated staff rows. Detected from the extract's own structure, so it fires wherever the file lands (code repositories, reporting databases, file shares, test data folders), not only in HR-branded systems.
patterns.operation: Primary: a header row with at least 4 HR column labels in a row, separated by commas, semicolons, pipes, tabs or runs of spaces (employee / staff / payroll ID, first / last / given / family name, surname, DOB / date of birth, home / residential / postal address, suburb, postcode, position title / number, job title, classification, level, commencement / start / termination / end date, employment status / type, cost centre, department, work unit, gender, phone, email). 65 is discovery-only (header alone) and will surface blank import templates and column lists. 75 requires, within 300 characters, an employee ID column label, a date of birth or home address column label, a position, classification, commencement/termination date or employment status column label, and at least one populated data row (an ID-like value followed on the same line by a date). 85 requires the same column labels plus 2 or more distinct populated rows whose date is a date-of-birth-like value (a day/month/year date with a year from 1940 to 2009). Every enforce tier excludes template/fixture text and data dictionary / file specification wording.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: a header of HR column labels followed by rows that pair an ID with a birth-year date is distinctive of a staff extract, and blank import templates, data dictionaries and org-chart role lists lack either the personal-detail column or populated rows. Some non-HR person extracts (member, student or volunteer lists that use "staff" or "employee" style ID columns) will also match, and extracts whose cells are split onto separate lines by the text extractor lose the header-row structure and fall below 65. The 85/75 tiers are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; tests are synthetic extracts.

customisation.note: Extend the populated-field evidence with the customer's employee ID / payroll number format (see docs/identifiers.md#employee-id). The public fallback is the documented label-anchored regex, so the classifier works without customisation at lower precision.

patterns.risk_description: A bulk staff extract ties hundreds or thousands of identified people to their date of birth, home address, job and employment dates in one file. That combination is enough for identity fraud, targeted phishing and locating a specific worker at home, including staff with protective orders. Recent breach notifications in the university and HR-SaaS sectors involved exactly this record class: staff and former-staff extracts held as test data in code repositories, in reporting databases and in bulk HCM exports rather than in the HR system itself. Payroll master files that add TFNs and bank details are covered at the same risk by payroll-master-file-with-tax-file-numbers. Risk 8 supports OFFICIAL: Sensitive / SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy and Medium because the extract ties hundreds or thousands of staff to date of birth, home address, position and employment dates. PROTECTED is not met because the file lacks TFNs, bank details or credentials, though it supports identity fraud and locating workers at home.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling applies to bulk identity and home-address data for staff, including those with protective orders. It is not High without financial or credential fields.

patterns.name: Http Authorization Header
patterns.description: Detects HTTP Authorization header patterns containing Bearer tokens, Basic credentials, and other authentication schemes. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Matches HTTP Authorization headers with Bearer, Basic, and other authentication scheme values. Bearer tokens are typically JWTs or opaque tokens; Basic auth contains Base64-encoded username:password pairs. Corroborative evidence: 8 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: Authorization header with Bearer or Basic scheme prefix followed by token value is a well-defined HTTP authentication pattern. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

should_match.description: Bearer token with JWT format
Basic auth with Base64 credentials
Bearer token with opaque token format

should_not_match.value: Authorization:
should_not_match.description: Empty authorization header

should_not_match.value: The Authorization header is required
should_not_match.description: Documentation reference without actual header

should_not_match.value: template example placeholder record identifier
should_not_match.description: Template/sample context should be excluded even when anchor words are present

false_positives.description: API documentation and HTTP specification references showing Authorization header examples.
false_positives.mitigation: Check for common placeholder tokens and documentation context.

false_positives.description: Log files containing Authorization headers with redacted or expired tokens.
false_positives.mitigation: Check for redaction markers like [REDACTED] or expired JWT timestamps.

patterns.risk_description: This SIT finds an HTTP Authorization header carrying a Bearer token or Base64 Basic credential of at least ten characters, so the match is a presented authentication value tied to a request. A live header can be replayed against its service to assume the represented session or decode and reuse the Basic username-password pair. One user, service account, or API client and its authorized resources are the normal scale, while redacted logs, expired tokens, and specification examples can be harmless. Risk 8 SENSITIVE reflects serious direct access potential; PROTECTED would require evidence that the header conveys broad administrative or critical-system authority.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps consistently to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because both supported header schemes can contain immediately reusable credentials. PROTECTED is not met without a confirmed live target, privilege set, broad scope, or significant critical-service impact.

generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls because Authorization values should be suppressed from logs and rotated or revoked after exposure. High is not assigned to every header when examples, redaction, expiry, and ordinary user scopes remain plausible.

patterns.name: International Bank Account Number (IBAN) - Global
patterns.description: Detects International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) across the full ISO 13616 / SWIFT IBAN Registry country set, extending coverage beyond the EU-focused eu-iban pattern to non-EU IBAN countries verified against the SWIFT IBAN registry — at minimum United Kingdom (GB, 22 chars), Switzerland (CH, 21), Norway (NO, 15), Saudi Arabia (SA, 24), United Arab Emirates (AE, 23), and Turkey (TR, 26). The structural regex widens eu-iban's BBAN length range (12-36 alphanumeric characters) down to 8-32 specifically to also catch shorter formats such as Norway's 15-character IBAN (11-character BBAN), which falls below eu-iban's minimum and would not match it. This pattern intentionally co-fires with eu-iban for EU country codes, since neither pattern restricts the 2-letter prefix to a specific country allow-list — see false_positives.
patterns.operation: Validation: Mod 97 (ISO 7064) via Func_iban. Reference: SWIFT IBAN Registry (ISO 13616 Registration Authority, https://www.swift.com/standards/data-standards/iban). Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: financial-deposit-terms.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the two-letter country code prefix followed by exactly two check digits, combined with the mod-97 checksum validator, produces low false positive rates. The widened length range trades a small amount of extra structural looseness (to reach Norway's shorter format) for broader global coverage; the checksum validator carries the precision that the regex alone cannot express without banned per-country length alternation.

should_match.description: Exact 65 discovery probe using the SWIFT/ISO 13616 published UK IBAN
Switzerland (CH) IBAN, 21 characters, space-separated groups
Norway (NO) IBAN, 15 characters — the global minimum length, shorter than eu-iban's regex can match
Saudi Arabia (SA) IBAN, 24 characters, no delimiters
United Arab Emirates (AE) IBAN, 23 characters, no delimiters
Turkey (TR) IBAN, 26 characters, no delimiters
Exact 75 probe with an explicit IBAN label

should_match.value: Beneficiary IBAN GB33BUKB20201555555555 for the transfer
should_match.description: Exact 85 probe with label and payment-instruction context

should_not_match.value: GB33BUKB
should_not_match.description: Only 8 characters — too short, missing the mandatory second BBAN group
Digit-only string missing the two-letter country code prefix

should_not_match.value: INVALID123456789
should_not_match.description: Starts with more than two letters before any digit, not a valid IBAN structure

should_not_match.value: Product serial AB12CD345678901
should_not_match.description: IBAN-shaped serial candidate lacks banking context and should not enforce

false_positives.description: Co-fires with eu-iban for EU country codes, since both patterns use the same generic 2-letter-country + 2-digit-checksum + alphanumeric BBAN structure and neither restricts the country code to an allow-list. This is expected and by design.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy either pattern alone, or both if RulePack budget allows and de-duplicate at the reporting layer. The mod-97 Func_iban checksum validator rejects the overwhelming majority of structurally- shaped non-IBAN strings regardless of which pattern fires.

false_positives.description: Product codes, serial numbers, or reference numbers beginning with two letters and two digits (e.g. invoice-prefix or license-plate-like strings) can coincidentally satisfy the structural pattern.
false_positives.mitigation: Validate the check digits using the MOD-97 algorithm (Func_iban). Require corroborative evidence keywords within the proximity window.

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence detector finds a structurally valid global IBAN and applies the ISO 7064 mod-97 check with nearby banking context. An IBAN identifies a payment destination and can aid invoice redirection, account correlation, or convincing bank-themed social engineering, but it does not authenticate the holder or authorise a debit or transfer. The normal unit is one account-routing identifier, often deliberately supplied on invoices, so direct harm remains low and requires identity, mandate, or transaction context. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL are appropriate, while an IBAN linked to a holder, balances, payment history, or usable banking credentials would justify SENSITIVE treatment.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, and the OFFICIAL DLM because a validated IBAN is an atomic payment-routing identifier rather than an authentication secret or financial record. SENSITIVE is not met without account-holder linkage, transaction data, or authority capable of direct financial misuse.

generic.rationale: Low generic classification and Low DLM fit a single IBAN whose standalone disclosure has limited consequence and becomes materially sensitive only through correlation with customer or transaction data.

patterns.name: IEC 61850 SCL Substation Configuration File
patterns.description: IEC 61850 System Configuration Language (SCL) files for a configured substation or IED: SCD, ICD, CID, SSD and IID exports from substation configurator tools. Detects the SCL XML namespace and the populated Communication section (ConnectedAP with IP addressing, GOOSE and Sampled Values multicast MAC addresses in the 01-0C-CD range, APPIDs) plus IED, logical device and control-block structure. A populated SCD/CID gives the station bus network plan, IED names and GOOSE trip-signal addressing for a live substation.
patterns.operation: Primaries: the SCL namespace (xmlns="http://www.iec.ch/61850/2003/SCL"), a populated ConnectedAP element (ConnectedAP iedName=...), or an "IEC 61850" phrase near SCL / .scd / .icd / .cid / .ssd / .iid. 65 is discovery-only (any primary). 75 requires the namespace plus an IED, LDevice, LLN0, ConnectedAP, SubNetwork or Substation element, or the namespace or ConnectedAP plus populated addressing (a dotted-quad P type="IP", a GOOSE/SV MAC P type="MAC-Address" 01-0C-CD-xx-xx-xx, or a P type="APPID"). 85 requires the namespace or ConnectedAP plus a populated P type="IP", a second distinct addressing structure (01-0C-CD MAC or APPID) and a control block (GSE/SMV cbName address block, GSEControl, ReportControl or SampledValueControl). Placeholder IP 0.0.0.0 is not counted. All enforce tiers exclude template/noise text, XML schema documentation (xs:element, xs:complexType), libiec61850 samples and the OpenSCD TrainingIEC61850 fixture, and the libiec61850 sample address 10.0.0.2. Proximity is 1000 characters because the header, Communication and IED sections of an SCL file sit close together but exceed 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High: the SCL namespace URI and the P type="IP" / P type="MAC-Address" / P type="APPID" address elements are machine-format structures that essentially only occur in IEC 61850 SCL files. Residual false positives are developer fixtures and schema documentation, which are excluded. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic SCL fragments shaped like the libiec61850 and OpenSCD sample files.

patterns.risk_description: A populated SCD/CID/ICD file maps a substation's IEC 61850 station and process bus: IED names, IP addresses, GOOSE and Sampled Values multicast addressing, APPIDs and the control blocks that carry protection trips and interlocks. Disclosure gives an attacker the target list and addressing needed to spoof GOOSE messages or reach protection relays, with consequences for supply and public safety. Configuration files for critical infrastructure assets can be SOCI protected information. Schema text, library fixtures and marketing are excluded from enforce tiers. Risk 9 supports PROTECTED InfoTech because one file is enough to target a live substation's protection scheme.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED InfoTech (PROT_IT) and the High tier because a populated SCD or CID maps a live substation's IED names, IP addresses and GOOSE trip-signal addressing, enough to spoof protection messages or reach protection relays. One substation's file enables an attack on a critical asset, the same harm as SCADA network diagrams (PROTECTED, risk 9) and substation protection relay settings (PROTECTED, risk 10). Schema text, library fixtures and marketing stay out of enforce tiers.

generic.rationale: High InfoTech handling applies because one substation's configuration supplies the addressing needed to interfere with protection and control. Access should be limited to the engineers responsible for that substation.

patterns.name: JWT
patterns.description: Detects JSON Web Token candidates with three Base64url segments. The 75 tier additionally requires the standard encoded "alg" header prefix and an explicit JWT field label. The 85 tier requires an encoded JSON payload too and binds that fuller token structure to an Authorization, Cookie, or Set-Cookie transport field. Enforcing tiers reject template and placeholder text.

patterns.risk_description: The regex recognizes a three-segment Base64url token beginning with an encoded JSON object, so it finds a JWT-shaped value but does not require a Bearer header or validate its signature. If the token is active and accepted by its issuer's service, disclosure can permit session replay; even an unusable token may reveal claims about its subject, issuer, roles, or tenancy. The likely scale is one identity or application session and its granted resources, with expired, unsigned, test, identity-only, and example tokens reducing direct harm. Risk 8 SENSITIVE is retained for a validated access token because compromise can be serious, while PROTECTED requires proven broad privilege or critical-service scope.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech for a normal usable JWT that can replay one session or expose sensitive claims. PROTECTED is not met by token shape because signature validity, expiry, token purpose, audience, privileges, and organisational consequence are not verified.

generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls because JWTs in documents and logs should be validated, expired or revoked, and removed where possible. High classification depends on a confirmed privileged access token rather than any syntactically valid JWT, many of which are test or identity artefacts.

patterns.name: Kraken API Key
patterns.description: Detects Kraken REST API credentials: the public API key (56 base64 characters) and the private key / API secret (86-88 base64 characters, base64 of 64 bytes). Because base64 strings have no distinctive prefix, this pattern is context-gated: it requires a nearby Kraken label and an assignment (= or :) before the value. A leaked private key allows signing authenticated requests to the account.
patterns.operation: A Kraken label followed within a short gap by an assignment (= or :) and a base64 value of either 56 characters (public key) or 86-88 characters (private key / secret, base64 of 64 bytes with optional = padding). base64 class is [A-Za-z0-9/+] with = padding; / and + are literal. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: Kraken keys are base64 strings with no self-identifying prefix, so a bare value is indistinguishable from any other base64 blob; detection relies on an adjacent Kraken label plus an assignment. The two fixed lengths (56 and 86-88) narrow the value shape but are not distinctive enough on their own to alert without context.

should_match.description: Kraken public key (56 base64 chars), zero-entropy filler in an assignment
Kraken private key (86 base64 chars + == padding = 88), zero-entropy filler
Kraken public key with repeated-block 56-char base64 filler

should_match.value:
kraken private key: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==
kraken private key: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAADAFAEADAFAEAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==
should_match.description: Two distinct Kraken API Key values in one file; the 85 tier needs two distinct tokens (one token, or the same token repeated, stays below 85)

should_not_match.value: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
should_not_match.description: Bare 56-char base64 value with no Kraken context (could be any base64 blob)

should_not_match.value: KRAKEN_API_KEY=AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
should_not_match.description: Wrong length (40 base64 chars, neither 56 nor 86-88)

should_not_match.value: store your kraken api key and private key securely offline
should_not_match.description: Prose mention with no assignment and no base64 value

false_positives.description: A 56 or 86-88 character base64 blob (hash, signature, other vendor secret) appearing near the word kraken in prose.
false_positives.mitigation: The pattern already requires an assignment (=/:) between the Kraken label and the value; require corroborative Kraken keywords and treat obvious placeholders (alphabet runs, all zeros) as non-sensitive.

false_positives.description: Documentation or examples showing placeholder base64 strings near Kraken text.
false_positives.mitigation: Check for placeholder markers (example, AAAA, xxxx) and require Kraken context.

patterns.risk_description: The medium-confidence pattern detects a Kraken-labelled base64 API credential in either the 56-character public-key form or the longer private signing-secret form. A matched private key can sign authenticated requests, while a public key can identify the account credential and becomes dangerous when paired with its secret. The affected scale is one Kraken account, with key permissions, balance, IP restrictions, signing requirements, and revocation limiting financial harm. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE reflect the detector's ability to find the complete private secret, while a public-key-only match is lower and unrestricted high-value withdrawal authority would raise the impact.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because the detector includes the Kraken private key that can authenticate material account activity. PROTECTED is not met because some matches are public keys and the pattern does not establish unrestricted permissions, high account value, or severe irreversible loss.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium InfoTech handling fit mixed Kraken API credentials because a private match is directly usable while public-key matches and account restrictions reduce the normal maximum harm.

patterns.name: Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) - Global
patterns.description: Detects ISO 17442 Legal Entity Identifiers (LEIs) — the 20-character uppercase alphanumeric codes issued under the Global LEI System (GLEIF) that uniquely identify legal entities in financial transactions. Structure: characters 1-4 are the LEI-issuer (LOU) prefix, characters 5-6 are reserved and set to "00", characters 7-18 are the entity-specific part, and characters 19-20 are numeric check digits (ISO 7064 MOD 97-10). Requiring the literal "00" at positions 5-6 and two digits at positions 19-20 makes the format far more distinctive than a generic 20-character alphanumeric run. Known recall cost: pre-2013 CICI-era legacy LEIs — interim identifiers issued before the "00" reservation, grandfathered into the GLEIF system and still live and checksum-valid — do not carry "00" at positions 5-6 and are NOT matched. This class includes major counterparties such as Microsoft (INR2EJN1ERAN0W5ZP974), Deutsche Bank (7LTWFZYICNSX8D621K86) and Apple (HWUPKR0MPOU8FGXBT394), so documents dealing with such entities' LEIs will be missed. This is a deliberate precision-over-recall trade-off: dropping the "00" anchor would widen the pattern to any 20-character uppercase alphanumeric run ending in two digits.
patterns.operation: Validation: the ISO 7064 MOD 97-10 check over base-36 character expansion is not expressible as a regex and no Purview validator function exists for LEI, so the check digits are enforced only as structural \d{2}. Reference: ISO 17442 via GLEIF "ISO 17442: The LEI Code Structure". AllDigitsSameFilter guards against repeated-digit sentinels (an all-zeros string satisfies both the structure and the mod-97 arithmetic). Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the fixed 20-character length, uppercase-only charset, reserved "00" at positions 5-6 and numeric check-digit pair at positions 19-20 make coincidental collisions rare; the evidence-gated 85 tier is the recommended workhorse. The 65 tier is discovery-only because the MOD 97-10 checksum cannot be enforced in the exported SIT, so a bare structural match is not confirmed to be an issued LEI. Recall is knowingly reduced by the "00" requirement: live, checksum-valid pre-2013 CICI-era legacy LEIs without "00" at positions 5-6 — including major counterparties such as Microsoft, Deutsche Bank and Apple — are structurally excluded, a deliberate precision choice documented in the description.

false_positives.description: A 20-character uppercase serial/reference number that happens to carry "00" at positions 5-6 and two trailing digits can satisfy the structure; the MOD 97-10 checksum that would reject most such strings is not expressible as a regex and has no Purview validator function.
false_positives.mitigation: Require LEI/GLEIF keywords within the proximity window for the reporting tier; keep the bare structural tier discovery-only. Downstream consumers can verify candidates against the GLEIF API for authoritative validation. The "00" positions 5-6 anchor is what keeps this collision surface small; its cost is the known false-negative class of pre-2013 non-"00" legacy LEIs (CICI-era registrations, including major counterparties such as Microsoft, Deutsche Bank and Apple) described in the pattern description.

false_positives.description: Repeated-digit sentinels such as an all-zeros 20-character string satisfy the structure, and all-same-digit values pass any weighted-mod checksum (0 mod N = 0).
false_positives.mitigation: AllDigitsSameFilter drops repeated-digit values before they can match.

patterns.risk_description: The LEI detector matches a twenty-character ISO 17442-style legal-entity code with the reserved 00 positions and trailing check digits, supported by LEI or GLEIF language. An LEI is a public counterparty identifier used in financial reporting and registry data, not an account number, trade credential, or secret about a natural person. Its presence can help link documents to an entity or make a fabricated counterparty record look plausible, but exploitation requires transaction, relationship, or payment information that the code does not contain. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL fit the low business impact; non-public trade positions, settlement instructions, or a counterparty dossier would raise the surrounding context toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 consistently maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low because an LEI is an intentionally public entity reference. SENSITIVE is not met without confidential counterparty, transaction, exposure, or settlement data.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM accurately represent the negligible-to-limited confidentiality of one LEI. The financial document carrying it may be sensitive, but that record-level harm must not be imputed to the public code.

patterns.name: Litecoin Address
patterns.description: Detects Litecoin addresses in two forms. Native SegWit bech32 addresses use the human-readable part "ltc1" (distinctive, 85-gated). Legacy base58 addresses are P2PKH with version byte 0x30 (leading "L") and P2SH with version byte 0x32 (leading "M"), 26-35 characters (most 34) — a single-letter prefix that is weaker (75-gated). Prefixes/version bytes/lengths verified against the Litecoin address-prefix docs and documented example addresses.
patterns.operation: Two tiers. Tier 85 matches the distinctive "ltc1" bech32 form (HRP + bech32 body). Tier 75 matches the legacy L/M base58 form (weaker single-letter prefix). BOTH tiers are AND-gated by cryptocurrency/wallet domain context (crypto-wallet-context dict) within proximity plus a template/sample noise NOT-group — no bare high tier. Case-sensitive (base58 and bech32 are case-sensitive; the legacy "3" P2SH form is intentionally excluded as it collides with Bitcoin).
patterns.confidence_justification: The "ltc1" bech32 form is a distinctive fixed HRP (85 when domain-gated). The legacy L/M base58 form is a single-letter prefix that collides with other base58 addresses and has no regex-expressible checksum (75). Neither tier is exported bare — precision comes from (distinctive prefix/HRP) times the mandatory cryptocurrency/wallet domain-context gate plus the noise exclusion.
regulations: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)

patterns.name: Monero Address
patterns.description: Detects Monero (XMR) public addresses, encoded in Monero-specific base58 (same 58-character alphabet as standard base58, excluding 0 O I l). Standard addresses (mainnet network byte 18) and subaddresses (network byte 42) are 95 characters and begin with "4" or "8"; integrated addresses (network byte 19, standard address + encrypted 64-bit payment ID) are 106 characters and begin with "4". The fixed 95/106-char length is highly distinctive, gated at 85. Prefixes/lengths verified against the Monero standard-address and integrated-address docs.
patterns.operation: Single tier at confidence 85. Matches a leading "4" or "8" plus 94 base58 chars (95-char standard / subaddress), optionally 11 more (106-char integrated), then AND-gated by cryptocurrency/wallet domain context (crypto-wallet-context dict) within proximity plus a template/sample noise NOT-group (never a bare high tier). Case-sensitive base58 (the Monero checksum is not expressible in a Purview-safe regex).
patterns.confidence_justification: Gated 85: the fixed 95-char (standard/subaddress) or 106-char (integrated) length with a 4/8 leading character is a very distinctive envelope that essentially never occurs by chance, so it earns the high tier — but only when AND-gated by cryptocurrency/wallet domain context plus the noise exclusion. The Monero checksum cannot be validated in a Purview-safe regex, so context gating is retained rather than exporting a bare tier.
regulations: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)

patterns.risk_description: Monero Address detects a public 95- or 106-character base58 destination beginning with 4 or 8, including standard, subaddress, and integrated forms. Sharing a private recipient address can link a person to expected payments or weaken operational privacy, even though Monero hides ledger relationships more strongly than transparent chains. generic.rationale: Low generic treatment reflects a public Monero destination whose disclosure may reduce privacy but does not expose funds or signing authority.

A recipient may connect to the named deployment and read, alter, or delete databases and collections allowed to that account. The expected impact is confined to one MongoDB identity and reachable cluster, though that cluster may hold many records; samples, localhost instances, and revoked credentials can be benign. Risk 8 SENSITIVE captures serious but contained database harm, while PROTECTED requires confirmed administrator access or significant protected holdings.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because the URI contains all elements needed to attempt direct access to one MongoDB deployment. generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls for complete database URIs, including removal from documents and immediate credential rotation. High is reserved for verified privileged access to broad or protected database holdings rather than inferred from one URI.

patterns.name: National Metering Identifier
patterns.description: Detects National Metering Identifier (NMI) patterns used in the Australian energy market. A 10 or 11 digit number identifying electricity and gas connection points. Also covers the gas Meter Installation Registration Number (MIRN), which is allocated in the NMI number space: AEMO reserves the 5 XXX XXX XXX range for the gas industry (NSW/ACT 52, Vic 53, Qld 54, SA 55, WA 56, Tas 57) and MIRNs travel in the same aseXML NMI element with a checksum attribute. Context-dependent: requires energy/meter keywords.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern using universal engine. The top-level regex \b\d{10,11}\b matches 10 or 11 digit numbers. The Purview engine uses three regexes: Pattern_nmi_labeled (labeled format with NMI/MIRN/Meter Installation Registration Number/meter/metering prefix + 10-11 digits), Pattern_nmi_prefix (numbers starting with known NMI prefixes 60/61/70-79, the gas MIRN ranges 52-57, or alphanumeric NGGG/QAAA prefixes), and Pattern_au_nmi (bare 10-11 digit format). No checksum validator is applied: the NMI checksum is documented in the MSATS NMI Procedure, but the Queensland gas Retail Market Procedures do not state the MIRN checksum algorithm, so neither is claimed. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires energy metering + energy provider keywords with template exclusion logic; Medium (75) requires energy metering keywords (using prefix regex); Low (65) requires energy metering + energy provider keywords (using generic regex). Evidence uses 2 keyword groups (13 energy metering terms, 9 energy provider terms) within 500-character proximity. Keyword lists: infrastructure-energy.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence: a bare 10-11 digit number matches phone numbers, ABNs, bank account numbers, and many other numeric sequences. Corroborative evidence keywords such as NMI, meter, energy, or AEMO are essential for reliable detection. MIRN values are shape- and range-checked only; the MIRN checksum algorithm is not verified to equal the NMI algorithm, so no checksum validator is applied to either.
regulations: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)

patterns.name: Nationality and National Origin
patterns.description: Detects references to nationality/citizenship/immigration-status disclosure: nationality fields, national origin, citizenship status, visa status, and naturalization records. Unlike the three sibling Art-9 patterns in this wave (sexual-orientation, religious-beliefs, racial-ethnic-origin), nationality is NOT a GDPR Article 9 special category — it is processed under GDPR's ordinary Article 6 lawful-basis regime. It is grouped with the Art-9 set here because it shares the same detection problem (an attribute value with no fixed format) and was bundled with them in the C3 deprecation/gap analysis, and because national origin carries real discrimination risk. Topic-grade detector, low confidence by design.
patterns.operation: Phrase regex matching indicative nationality/citizenship/immigration-status disclosure terminology (nationality field, national origin, citizenship status, immigration status, visa status, country of citizenship, dual citizenship, naturalization status, non-citizen status). Detects the presence of nationality/immigration subject matter in a disclosure/record context; not a structured-token detector. Pair with corroborative keywords to raise precision.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low by design. Nationality/immigration status has no fixed format, so it is detected purely by topic vocabulary. The bare word "national" appears constantly in unrelated contexts (National Bank, nationally recognized, national holiday); the regex is scoped to full disclosure phrases only, and hits should be paired with corroborative keywords (citizenship, visa, immigration) to raise precision.

false_positives.description: The word "national"/"nationally" appears in unrelated contexts (proper nouns like National Bank, adverbial "nationally recognized", "national holiday") that have nothing to do with a person's nationality or citizenship.
false_positives.mitigation: The regex targets full disclosure phrases ("national origin", "citizenship status", "visa status") rather than the bare word "national"; require corroborative keywords (citizenship, visa, immigration, passport) for confidence.

patterns.risk_description: Nationality and immigration status carry discrimination and safety risk (particularly for refugees, asylum seekers, and undocumented individuals); disclosure can expose individuals to targeted harassment or, in some jurisdictions, legal jeopardy.

classification.rationale: Risk 6 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy and Medium because nationality, citizenship or visa status can expose refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented people to discrimination or legal jeopardy. PROTECTED is not met because this low-confidence topic detector does not establish a bulk or safety-critical immigration record.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling reflects discrimination and safety risk from immigration status, though nationality is not a GDPR Article 9 category. It is not High for a single attribute.

patterns.name: Netlify Access Token
patterns.description: Detects Netlify authentication tokens: the current nf-prefixed family announced by Netlify in November 2023 (nfp_ personal access tokens, nfc_ CLI tokens, nfo_ OAuth tokens, nfu_ app.netlify.com tokens, nfb_ build tokens) and, when labelled with Netlify context, the legacy unprefixed 43-45 character token form that remains valid. A leaked token grants control of the account's sites, deploys and environment variables.
patterns.operation: Two detection branches. Branch 1 (distinctive, value-only capable): the nf-prefixed family -- nfp_ personal access tokens are pinned to a 36-character body by TruffleHog's production detector (40 characters total, matching Netlify's announced maximum), and the other four vendor-announced prefixes (nfc_/nfo_/nfu_/nfb_) use a bounded 20-36 character body consistent with the same 40-character cap. Branch 2 (context-gated only): legacy unprefixed tokens (43-45 character base64url body per TruffleHog's v1 detector; Netlify states existing tokens remain valid), requiring a Netlify label within 40 characters. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the nf-prefix family is documented by Netlify's own format-change announcement (all five prefixes named, 40-character maximum), and the nfp_ body length is pinned by TruffleHog's production v2 detector. Disclosure: TruffleHog's v2 detector wraps even the distinctive nfp_ regex in a blanket "netlify" PrefixRegex gate; this pattern diverges by offering a value-only 65 tier because the nf?-prefix + bounded-body structure is self-distinctive, and TruffleHog's wrapper there is its standard detector convention rather than a response to a documented false-positive problem (unlike Square's EAAA detector, which carries an explicit FP comment). The legacy unprefixed form is deliberately context-gated: it is indistinguishable from other base64url strings, so both TruffleHog v1 and gitleaks gate it on Netlify context and this pattern embeds the same label requirement at the regex level.

Exact 75 probe - vendor-prefixed CLI token with deployment context

classification.rationale: Risk 8 supports QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because a valid Netlify token can directly modify deployments and reveal environment secrets within its account scope. generic.rationale: Medium and Medium InfoTech handling fit Netlify tokens because they grant direct deployment control while token type, team scope, and revocation usually contain the harm.

patterns.name: Neural & Neurotechnology Data
patterns.description: Detects references to neural / neurotechnology data: brain-computer interface signals, EEG/EMG recordings, evoked potentials, neural decoding output and neurofeedback data. Colorado HB24-1058 and California SB 1223 both classify neural data as sensitive personal information. Topic-grade vocabulary detector, not a fixed-format detector.

Template and public-research/guidance framing excluded from 75/85. Converted from keyword_list to regex.

patterns.name: Notion Token
patterns.description: Detects Notion integration tokens in both live formats: the current ntn_ prefix (issued to all new integrations since 25 September 2024) and, when labelled with Notion context, the legacy secret_ prefix (existing tokens remain valid indefinitely). A leaked integration token grants API access to every page and database the integration has been connected to.
patterns.operation: Two detection branches. Branch 1 (distinctive, value-only capable): ntn_ tokens with an 11-digit workspace segment followed by 35 alphanumeric characters -- the exact structure pinned independently by gitleaks and Kingfisher. Branch 2 (context-gated only): legacy secret_ tokens (secret_ + exactly 43 alphanumerics, per TruffleHog's production detector) -- because "secret_" is also a generic identifier fragment in source code (client_secret_..., secret_key_...), this branch requires a preceding Notion label, following Kingfisher's production precedent, and a non-identifier character immediately before secret_ so composites like client_secret_ cannot fire. Notion's own changelog advises against regex-validating its tokens, so both branches lean on corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the ntn_ format is multiply attested -- Notion's own developer changelog announced the prefix change (25 September 2024, explicitly for secret-scanner compatibility), Notion is a GitHub secret-scanning partner with push protection enabled, and gitleaks and Kingfisher independently pin the identical body structure (11 digits + 35 alphanumerics). The legacy secret_ format is pinned at 43 alphanumerics by TruffleHog and confirmed by GitGuardian's v1/v2 detector split; it is deliberately context-gated because its prefix is a generic English word that appears inside longer identifiers. Notion itself warns that token formats may change and recommends treating tokens as opaque -- reflected in the bounded, evidence-pinned regexes and the corroborative keyword requirement at the recommended confidence tier.

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence regex identifies current ntn_ Notion integration tokens and a Notion-labelled legacy secret_ token while excluding generic client_secret fragments. A live integration token can read or modify every page and database explicitly connected to that integration, exposing workspace content and automations. The affected scale is the integration's shared content rather than the entire Notion tenant by default, with granted pages, capabilities, and revocation limiting harm. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE reflect serious contained workspace compromise, while a broadly connected integration holding protected operational content would raise the impact.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because a valid Notion token directly exposes the pages and databases granted to its integration. PROTECTED is not met because access is bounded by explicit sharing and the detector does not establish tenant-wide or protected-operation reach.

generic.rationale: Medium generic classification with Medium InfoTech handling suits Notion tokens because connected workspace data can be seriously compromised while integration grants and revocation contain the scope.

patterns.name: Passport Machine-Readable Zone (MRZ, ICAO 9303)
patterns.description: Detects the Machine-Readable Zone (MRZ) of an ICAO 9303 travel document, the OCR-B text printed at the bottom of passport data pages and scanned at border control. This pattern focuses on the TD3 passport format (two lines of 44 characters): line 1 begins 'P' + document subtype + 3-letter issuing state + the holder's names, and line 2 packs the document number, check digits, nationality, date of birth, sex and expiry. MRZ leakage via scans, photocopies and OCR exports is one of the highest-value passport data exposure vectors because it concentrates every identity field in a single fixed-width block.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine-readable_passport Primary match is the TD3 second line (44 fixed-width [A-Z0-9<] characters: document number + check digit + nationality + DOB + check + sex + expiry + check + optional data + check + composite check). A secondary regex matches the TD3 first line ('P' + subtype + issuing state + name field). The MRZ alphabet is uppercase A-Z, digits 0-9 and the filler '<' only. Checksum: ICAO 9303 weighted (7,3,1) check digits (NOT enforced in this regex-only pattern; the check-digit positions are matched structurally but their arithmetic is not validated).
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the TD3 second line is a 44-character fixed-width structure with field-typed positions (filler characters, sex marker, six-digit dates and trailing check digits) that essentially never occurs by chance in natural text or ordinary identifiers.

patterns.risk_description: A true TD3 passport MRZ match is a two-line fixed-width travel-document block containing holder names, passport number, nationality, date of birth, sex, expiry, and check-digit positions rather than one atomic identifier. Leakage of OCR text or a passport-page scan can support high-quality identity impersonation and document fraud for one traveller even without biometrics. The 44-character layout makes accidental matches uncommon, although this regex does not validate ICAO checksum arithmetic or prove that the text came from an authentic document. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect a single structured OCR block without portrait or demonstrated account use; SENSITIVE requires a passport page, linked itinerary or immigration record, or evidence of consequential identity misuse.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low because one MRZ block is bounded to one traveller and does not include the portrait, visa history, or an authenticated document image. SENSITIVE requires corroboration from a full passport page, travel or immigration record, or a misuse context that turns the identity fields into consequential personal harm.

generic.rationale: Low with Low DLM reflects one structured MRZ block whose identity details are bounded to a single traveller and do not include a portrait, visa history, or authenticated document image. Medium handling requires the MRZ to be part of a complete passport page, linked travel or immigration record, or consequential identity-misuse context.

patterns.name: PayID (New Payments Platform)
patterns.description: Detects Australian PayID payment addresses used on the New Payments Platform (NPP). A PayID is an email address, mobile phone number (+61 / 04xx format), ABN or organisation identifier registered as a real-time payment alias, detected when it appears near an explicit PayID label in a payment context.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine). Pattern_au_payid anchors on the PayID label and uses a bounded proximity lookahead requiring a payment-address value (email, +61/04xx mobile, or 11-digit ABN) within 80 characters. The labelled alias is discovery-only at 65, payment-action context enforces at 75, and independent NPP/Osko/bank context raises it to 85. Enforcing tiers reject explicit templates.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the PayID label plus a co-located payment-address value (email, +61/04xx mobile, or ABN) is a strong signal, but a PayID reuses common identifier shapes, so corroborating NPP/Osko payment keywords are required to separate real payment instructions from generic contact details.

A PayID identifies a payment destination and can support unwanted payment requests, phishing, or correlation of contact and banking relationships, but it does not authenticate a transfer or grant account access. The likely impact is low and reversible for one person or business because the alias is often intentionally shared to receive funds. patterns.name: Payment Card Magnetic Stripe Track 1
patterns.description: Detects ISO/IEC 7813 magnetic-stripe Track 1 (format code B) data for payment cards: a start sentinel %B, the primary account number, the cardholder name, expiry date, service code and discretionary data. Storing full track data after authorization is prohibited by PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 3.3.1.
patterns.operation: Track 1 format-B structure: start sentinel %B, 13-19 digit PAN, field separator ^, cardholder name (NAME/SURNAME), field separator ^, 4-digit expiry (YYMM), 3-digit service code and discretionary data, end sentinel ?. The literal ^ characters are magnetic-stripe field separators, not regex anchors. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the full Track 1 framing (%B start sentinel, two ^ field separators, fixed expiry+service-code structure and ? end sentinel) wrapped around a 13-19 digit PAN is a highly distinctive structure that does not occur in ordinary prose, making false positives extremely unlikely.

patterns.name: PGP Private Key Block
patterns.description: Detects the ASCII-armored header of an OpenPGP (PGP/GnuPG) private key block, as defined in RFC 4880 / RFC 9580. A leaked PGP private key allows an attacker to decrypt the holder's encrypted mail and files and to forge signatures in their name. The registry already covers RSA, EC, OpenSSH and PKCS#8 private keys; this adds the OpenPGP armor format. Header-only hits are discovery-only; armored packet data near the header provides the enforcement tiers.
patterns.operation: Regex_pgp_private_header matches the BEGIN line. The 75 tier requires the armor separator, optional Version/Comment fields, and a 64-character Base64 line whose prefix encodes an old- or new-format secret-key packet. The 85 tier additionally requires three consecutive 64-character body lines near the header. The 65 tier is discovery-only; enforcing tiers reject templates and do not depend on a CRC or END marker at the far end of a normal export.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the armor header string is long, fixed and structurally distinctive, so false positives outside of documentation or training material are extremely unlikely.

patterns.name: Global Phone Number (E.164)
patterns.description: Detects international telephone numbers in ITU-T E.164 form: a leading "+" (the international prefix symbol defined by ITU-T E.123, the companion notation recommendation) followed by a country code and national significant number totalling no more than 15 digits, per E.164's own numbering-space limit (country code 1-3 digits, subscriber number up to 12 digits, 15 digits maximum overall). This pattern covers only the "+"-prefixed international representation — it is the global counterpart to the country-specific domestic-format patterns (us-phone-number, ca-phone-number, uk-phone-number, in-phone-number, and the EU national patterns), which additionally match each country's bare domestic formatting conventions. Real-world renderings commonly use spaces or hyphens between digit groups even though E.123 formally prescribes spaces only; both are accepted here. The "+CC (0)..." letterhead rendering (e.g. "+44 (0)20 7946 0958") is deliberately NOT matched by this pattern: it is not an E.164 representation (E.123 explicitly advises against the parenthesised trunk digit in international notation), and the country-specific patterns whose plans actually use a trunk 0 (uk/de/fr/nl) each cover it themselves — keeping this global pattern strictly E.164-shaped.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (E.164 has no checksum; the regex enforces only the "+" prefix, leading-digit, and 15-digit-maximum structural constraints, not a per-country-code length table). Reference: ITU-T Recommendation E.164, "The international public telecommunication numbering plan", https://www.itu.int/rec/t-rec-e.164/en; ITU-T Recommendation E.123, "Notation for national and international telephone numbers, e-mail addresses and web addresses", https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-E.123. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the mandatory literal "+" prefix is distinctive and rare outside telecom contexts, but the digits that follow it carry no checksum and the regex cannot validate the country-code/national-number split against a real assignment table, so E.164-shaped values remain a high digit-collision format at heart. The bare structure is therefore discovery-only; the 75 tier requires phone context and the 85 tier requires both phone context and an international-phone label, with template/noise exclusion on both enforcing tiers.

should_match.description: Low-tier probe - UK Ofcom-reserved London drama number in bare E.164 form
Medium-tier probe - NANPA-reserved fictional number with generic phone context

India (+91), illustrative synthetic value — no official DoT/TRAI reserved test-number block exists for India (verified absent during research), so a structurally valid but non-allocated-looking descending-digit sequence is used
High-tier probe - 3-digit country code with explicit international-phone context

should_not_match.description: Leading digit after the + is 0 — E.164 country codes never start with 0
Same NANP digit shape as a should_match case but missing the mandatory + prefix — bare domestic-style digit runs are out of scope for this international-only pattern
Only 6 digits after the +, below the practical 8-digit minimum this pattern enforces (ITU specifies only a 15-digit maximum, no minimum)
18 digits after the +, three more than E.164's 15-digit maximum — no valid sub-length cut satisfies the trailing digit boundary

should_not_match.value: Documentation example: international phone number +44 2079460958
should_not_match.description: Structurally valid but explicitly documented example must not enforce

false_positives.description: A syntactically valid "+" followed by 8-15 digits does not confirm the country code is actually assigned or that the subscriber-number length matches that country's real numbering plan — the regex cannot enforce a full per-country-code length table without banned per-alternative length alternation.
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with corroborative phone-context evidence at the 75/85 tiers; deployers needing precise per-country validation should prefer the relevant country-specific pattern (us-phone-number, uk-phone-number, etc.) where one exists.

false_positives.description: Co-fires with any country-specific pattern's international (+CC) sub-regex for the same value (e.g. us-phone-number's Regex_us_phone_intl), since both structurally match a "+"-prefixed digit run. This is expected and by design — the two levels of pattern serve different deployment needs (broad global coverage vs. tight per-country evidence).
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy either this pattern alone for broad international coverage, or the country-specific patterns alone for tighter per-country evidence, or both if RulePack budget allows and de-duplicate at the reporting layer.

patterns.risk_description: The global identifier finds a plus-prefixed E.164-shaped sequence of up to fifteen digits with phone context; it does not validate the country-code assignment, national length, subscriber, or ownership. A genuine number can be used for targeted calls, messaging fraud, harassment, and cross-record correlation when the actor has additional identity or account information. The ordinary exposure is one contact route, and country-specific detectors may co-fire while syntactically plausible but unassigned values also pass the regex. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL capture that bounded misuse value; SENSITIVE would require credentials, protected communications, precise location, or a sensitive identity relationship that makes contact materially dangerous.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with OFFICIAL because an E.164-shaped number enables contact and pretexting but does not authenticate a person or establish a sensitive jurisdiction or relationship. SENSITIVE is not met without linked credentials, communications, location, or vulnerable-person context that creates direct serious harm.

generic.rationale: Generic Low treatment reflects one globally formatted contact identifier whose assignment, owner, and sensitivity cannot be established from syntax alone.

patterns.name: Pinecone API Key
patterns.description: Detects Pinecone API keys in both current live formats: pcsk_ (the dominant format issued by the Pinecone console, CLI, and SDK key-creation flows) and pckey_ (the Enterprise-plan Admin API variant, format pckey_<public-label>_<unique-key>). A leaked key grants unauthorized access to a Pinecone vector database, including any embeddings or vectorised source data it stores.
patterns.operation: Two prefixed token formats. pcsk_ (dominant, console/CLI/SDK-issued): pcsk_<label>_<secret> with a 5-6 character alphanumeric label and a 63-character alphanumeric secret, per TruffleHog's production detector, consistent with Pinecone's own doc placeholders (pcsk_abc123). pckey_ (Enterprise Admin API): pckey_<public-label>_<unique-key> per Pinecone's Admin API reference; segment lengths not formally published, so a generous bounded body range is used for that branch. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: both prefixes are multiply attested. pcsk_ is the dominant live format -- shown in Pinecone's own CLI reference and AGENTS-JAVASCRIPT doc examples, called out in Pinecone's official skills repo contributor guide as the real key shape that security linters flag, and pinned to an exact body structure (5-6 alnum label + 63 alnum secret) by TruffleHog's production detector. pckey_ is explicitly documented on Pinecone's Admin API reference (Enterprise-plan key-creation endpoint). Pinecone is also a confirmed GitHub secret-scanning partner (pinecone_api_key). Older, pre-pcsk_ Pinecone keys (bare UUIDs) are not covered -- documented as a scope limitation rather than invented as an additional format.

Two distinct Pinecone API Key values in one file with context; the 85 tier needs two distinct tokens (one token, or the same token repeated, stays below 85)

patterns.name: PKCS#8 Private Key Header
patterns.description: Detects unencrypted PKCS#8 private-key armor. The generic BEGIN PRIVATE KEY marker is discovery-only; a DER algorithm prelude supports medium confidence, and near-header wrapped body data or an exact compact-key prelude reaches high.
patterns.operation: Regex_pkcs8_private matches the PKCS#8 BEGIN marker. The 75 tier requires an adjacent DER Base64 prelude used by PKCS#8. The 85 tier additionally requires two consecutive 64-character body lines, or the exact PKCS#8 AlgorithmIdentifier prelude used by compact Ed25519, X25519, Ed448, and X448 keys. All enforcing evidence is within 300 characters of the header; 65 inventories header-only candidates.

patterns.risk_description: This pattern finds the generic PKCS#8 BEGIN PRIVATE KEY header, which marks a private-key container but does not validate or capture the cryptographic body. When usable key bytes follow, disclosure may enable signing, decryption, or service impersonation according to the certificate or application that relies on the key. The expected scope is one key pair and its relying identity or system, while header-only documentation, incomplete blocks, encryption, and revocation reduce actual impact. Risk 8 SENSITIVE reflects a strong indication of serious secret material; PROTECTED requires confirmation that the key is usable and controls broad, critical, or protected operations.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because a PKCS#8 private-key header commonly precedes credential material capable of serious compromise. PROTECTED is not met by the marker because the key body, encryption state, validity, purpose, privilege, and system consequence are not established.

generic.rationale: Generic treatment is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls for a PKCS#8 key marker, requiring inspection of the full block and revocation when a usable key is confirmed. High classification depends on evidence that the key has significant operational trust or broad privileged reach.

patterns.name: Plaid Access Token
patterns.description: Detects Plaid API credentials: Item access tokens (access-sandbox-/access-production- followed by an RFC 4122 UUID) and, when labelled with Plaid context, the 30-character hex API secret. A leaked access token exposes a user's linked bank account data; a leaked secret compromises the whole Plaid integration.
patterns.operation: Two detection branches. Branch 1 (distinctive, value-only capable): access tokens in Plaid's documented [type]-[environment]-[uuid] format, matching the access- type with the two current environments (sandbox, production) and an 8-4-4-4-12 hex UUID. Branch 2 (context-gated only): the unprefixed 30-character hex API secret, requiring a Plaid label within 40 characters plus an assignment separator (= or :) directly before the value, mirroring gitleaks' assignment-operator-gated rule (TruffleHog uses a label-only gate, which proved too loose against free-standing hex in prose). Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence for the access-token branch: the [type]-[environment]-[uuid] structure is documented by Plaid's own docs (quickstart glossary) and independently pinned by TruffleHog's production detector and gitleaks. Disclosure: TruffleHog additionally wraps even this distinctive access-token regex in a blanket "plaid" PrefixRegex gate; this pattern diverges by offering a value-only 65 tier because the literal access-sandbox-/access-production- + RFC 4122 UUID structure is self-distinctive, and TruffleHog's wrapper there is its standard detector convention rather than a response to a documented false-positive problem (unlike Square's EAAA detector, which carries an explicit FP comment). The secret branch is deliberately context-gated: a bare 30-character hex string is indistinguishable from other identifiers, so both production scanners gate it on Plaid context; this pattern embeds the label plus an assignment separator (= or :, mirroring gitleaks' assignment-operator requirement) at the regex level, because a label-only gap gate still matched free-standing hex in prose (review regression case).

false_positives.description: A 30-character hex hash or identifier that happens to appear in a labelled assignment near the word "plaid" (a common English word for the fabric pattern).
false_positives.mitigation: The secret branch requires label adjacency plus an assignment separator (already enforced by the regex) and corroborative keywords; the brand-name keyword term is case-sensitive (Plaid) to reduce collisions with the common noun.

false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative Plaid keywords and check for placeholder markers (example, xxxx).

false_positives.description: Plaid public tokens, link tokens, and asset-report tokens (public-/link-/asset-report- prefixes) are short-lived, client-side-by-design tokens and are deliberately out of scope; decommissioned access-development- tokens are dead credentials and also excluded.
false_positives.mitigation: Documented as a scope decision; only durable server-side secrets (access tokens, API secret) are matched.

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence detector finds a Plaid Item access token in the access-sandbox or access-production UUID form and a context-gated Plaid API secret. A live Item token can expose a user's linked bank-account data, while the API secret can compromise the integration more broadly when combined with its client context. The affected scale ranges from one linked Item and account holder to the connected integration, with environment, product grants, client ID, monitoring, and revocation limiting harm. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE reflect serious contained financial-data exposure, while a production integration secret spanning many customers and high-impact transaction capabilities would raise the classification.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because Plaid access tokens and API secrets can reveal material banking data or authorize integration activity. PROTECTED is not met because the ordinary Item token is bounded to one linkage and the detector does not establish severe irreversible financial loss or broad privileged control.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium InfoTech handling fit Plaid credentials because they expose serious financial information while Item, environment, product, and integration scope normally contain the damage.

patterns.name: PLC Program / Project Export File
patterns.description: Machine-format PLC program and project exports: Rockwell Studio 5000 / RSLogix 5000 L5X (RSLogix5000Content XML) and L5K (IE_VER text) files, Siemens TIA Portal Openness block XML (Document / Engineering version / SW.Blocks), and Schneider Control Expert / Unity Pro XEF exchange files (FEFExchangeFile). A populated export carries the controller model, network addresses, I/O modules, tags and control logic of a production control system.
patterns.operation: Per-family tiers, proximity 1000 characters (export headers and the first structures exceed 300 characters). Rockwell L5X - 85: RSLogix5000Content SchemaRevision root + a Controller Use="Target" element with a ProcessorType catalogue number + a hardware or program structure (Ethernet Port Address with an IPv4 address, Module CatalogNumber, Task, Tag or Routine element); 75: root + Controller ProcessorType, or a Routine Type RLL/ST/FBD/SFC element + a Rung element + at least two distinct ladder instruction texts (XIC/XIO/OTE/TON...(tag)). Rockwell L5K - 85: IE_VER := n.n; + CONTROLLER name (ProcessorType := ...) + END_DATATYPE or ladder instruction text; 75: IE_VER + CONTROLLER ProcessorType. Siemens TIA Openness - 85: SW.Blocks.FB/FC/OB/DB ID= element + the Openness Interface namespace + a logic structure (NetworkSource namespace, SW.Blocks.CompileUnit or ProgrammingLanguage LAD/FBD/STL/SCL/GRAPH); 75: the block element + either namespace/logic structure, or Engineering version="Vnn" + a DocumentInfo Created timestamp or the TIA Portal InstalledProducts entry. Schneider XEF - 85: FEFExchangeFile + fileHeader company="Schneider Automation" product=... + two distinct configuration structures (IOConf partItem partNumber, commParameters PLCAddress); 75: FEFExchangeFile + fileHeader. 65 (discovery-only): any export root, the Openness namespace, or the AutomationML AutomationProjectConfigurationRoleClassLib role library (unverified, discovery only). All enforce tiers exclude template/noise text, generator placeholders ({{NAME}} or ${NAME}) and reference-manual, parser-library and blog framing.
patterns.confidence_justification: High: every enforce tier needs vendor-specific export markup (RSLogix5000Content root with a Controller ProcessorType, IE_VER plus CONTROLLER ProcessorType, SW.Blocks plus the Openness namespace, FEFExchangeFile plus the Schneider fileHeader) that does not occur in ordinary prose. Residual false positives are parser-library fixtures, Add-On Instruction library exports and blog posts quoting exports. 85/75 are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; test values are synthetic fragments shaped like published sample exports.

false_positives.mitigation: Mustache / ${} placeholders and template wording are excluded; "blog post", "code snippet" and "Openness XML file" framing are excluded.

false_positives.mitigation: Not detected unless the scanner extracts the XML/L5K text.

patterns.risk_description: A PLC project or program export contains the control logic, controller model, I/O module layout, tags and often the controller IP addresses of a production process. Disclosure lets an attacker understand interlocks and sequences, craft malicious logic or target the controller on the network, with consequences for plant safety and supply; exports are also the operator's engineering intellectual property. Exports for critical infrastructure assets can be SOCI protected information. Manuals, parser code, generator templates and marketing are excluded from enforce tiers. Risk 9 supports PROTECTED InfoTech because one export is enough to craft malicious logic for the process it controls.

classification.rationale: Risk 9 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED InfoTech (PROT_IT) and the High tier because an L5X, TIA Openness or XEF export carries control logic, interlocks, I/O layout and controller addresses, enough to craft malicious logic or defeat safety interlocks. One export enables an attack on the process it controls, the same harm as distributed control system configurations, which are PROTECTED InfoTech at risk 9. Manuals, parser code, generator templates and marketing stay out of enforce tiers.

generic.rationale: High InfoTech handling applies because one controller project is both attack material and engineering IP. Access should be limited to the engineers and integrators responsible for that controller.

patterns.name: Political Opinion & Affiliation
patterns.description: Detects references to political opinions and party affiliation: party membership, voter registration by party, political donations and campaign contributions. GDPR Article 9 lists political opinions as a special category of personal data with no fixed format — it is detectable only by topic vocabulary. Topic-grade detector, low confidence by design.
patterns.operation: The primary regex matches political affiliation/opinion, party membership or affiliation, voted-for and registered-party statements, political donations and campaign contributions. 65 (discovery only): phrase alone - policy, guidance, news and survey-design text naming the category stays here. 75: phrase plus a populated identified-person field (name, DOB, employee/member/customer/patient/participant number or ID, data subject). 85: person field plus a populated political field (party or party code, membership number/status, donation amount, contribution date/amount, electorate, division, voting intention, branch) plus independent record evidence (donor record, constituent, CRM note, membership file, campaign database, electoral roll, doorknock, supporter score). Template framing and guidance/policy/public-aggregate framing are excluded from 75/85. Converted from keyword_list to regex so the tier logic decides matches.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low by design: the attribute has no fixed format. Enforce tiers now require the attribute to be tied to an identified person record (a populated name/DOB/ID field), and 85 also requires a populated political field plus independent record evidence, so policy text, surveys-in-design and news naming the category stay at 65 discovery.

false_positives.description: Phrases like "voted for" or "registered" appear in non-political contexts (board elections, award votes, vendor registration), producing matches with no political-opinion content.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative keywords (election, candidate, donor, constituent, ballot) within the proximity window; treat isolated "voted for"/"registered" hits as low confidence.

patterns.risk_description: The Political Opinion and Affiliation detector recognises party membership, registered-party, political donation and campaign contribution statements and enforces only when they sit with a populated person identifier; policy and news text stays at 65 discovery. Its normal positive cases can contain a person-linked CRM or donor fact rather than only a blank category label, so disclosure may expose an individual's beliefs and enable discrimination, pressure, profiling, or targeted campaigning. Low confidence leaves room for political commentary that is not attributable to a person, but the corroborated true positive concerns one person's sensitive viewpoint or association. Risk 7 and SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy reflect credible direct personal harm, while PROTECTED would require a high-consequence bulk register, coercive targeting context, or severe safety impact.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy DLM, and Medium generic tiers because a true positive can attribute political belief or activity to a person. PROTECTED is not met for the normal single profile fact without bulk exposure, persecution risk, protected operations, or significant damage.

generic.rationale: Person-linked political affiliation is generically Medium with Medium Personal-Privacy DLM because disclosure can directly enable profiling or discriminatory treatment.

patterns.name: Postgresql
patterns.description: Detects Postgresql patterns.
patterns.operation: Corroborative evidence: 8 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: structurally constrained pattern with corroborative keyword support reduces false positive rates significantly. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

should_match.description: Exact 65 probe - complete credential URI without independent config labeling
Exact 75 probe - credential URI in a PostgreSQL-specific config field
Exact 85 probe - provider config label plus required TLS option

should_not_match.description: Wrong scheme (psql instead of postgres/postgresql)

should_not_match.description: Sibling database config label does not corroborate a PostgreSQL URI

should_not_match.description: Malformed connection has an empty password

should_not_match.description: Documentation placeholder with TLS context is excluded

should_not_match.value: template example placeholder record identifier
should_not_match.description: Template/sample context should be excluded even when anchor words are present

false_positives.description: Authentication-related terminology in software documentation, security training materials, or system architecture descriptions without actual credentials.
false_positives.mitigation: Require proximity to credential-specific patterns (API keys, connection strings, tokens) rather than general security terminology.

false_positives.description: Code snippets and configuration examples containing credential-related keywords or placeholder values in developer documentation.
false_positives.mitigation: Check for common placeholder patterns (example.com, localhost, 0000) and documentation file types to reduce false positives from technical writing.

patterns.risk_description: The regex identifies a postgres or postgresql URI containing user, password, host, and database path, making the match a complete login route to a named database. If the endpoint is reachable and credentials remain active, an attacker can use the account's grants to read or alter schema content and disrupt dependent applications. The ordinary affected unit is one PostgreSQL identity and database, though its record volume may be substantial; local examples and revoked accounts can be harmless. Risk 8 SENSITIVE represents serious but contained data and service harm, while PROTECTED needs confirmed privileged access to significant protected or critical holdings.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 is internally consistent with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because the URI contains all normal elements needed to attempt one database login. PROTECTED is not met without proof of validity, network access, administrative grants, database scale, or high-impact data.

generic.rationale: Generic treatment is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls for complete PostgreSQL connection strings, including removal, rotation, and access-log review. High is reserved for validated broad administration or consequential protected holdings, not inferred from URI syntax.

patterns.name: Internal Project Codename Reference
patterns.description: Detects references to internal project or initiative codenames in the "Project <CODENAME>" / "Operation <CODENAME>" labelling style. The public form of this pattern carries fictional example codenames only - it is a customisation skeleton: deployments substitute their organisation's live codename list via the declared customisation, which is what gives the pattern real detection value.
patterns.operation: The regex matches the generic labelling shape (project/operation/codename followed by an upper-case token). Precision comes entirely from the corroborative codename list, which is declared as a required keyword-set customisation - the in-file terms are fictional placeholders and enforcing deployments must replace them. The pattern matches case-sensitively, since the upper-case codename token itself is the signal that distinguishes a labelled codename from ordinary lower-case project-management prose.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence by design: the labelling shape alone matches ordinary project management prose. Real precision requires the organisation-specific codename list supplied through the declared customisation; until then the pattern is a discovery-only skeleton.

customisation.note: Replace the fictional example codenames with your organisation's live project/initiative codenames (deployment overlay). The in-file terms are placeholders; enforcement without substitution is refused by compliant deployment tooling.
