An attacker can try the pair against a nearby application, host, or service and may assume the user's permissions if the credentials remain valid. The normal affected party is one user or service account and its reachable resources, while test accounts, placeholders, login-form documentation, and the missing target system limit certainty. Risk 8 SENSITIVE is retained for serious account compromise; PROTECTED requires evidence that the pair belongs to a broadly privileged or critical identity.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because the match supplies both username and password and can directly compromise one account when the target is identified. PROTECTED is not met because system, validity, privilege, reuse, organisational reach, and criticality are not established.

generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls for complete login pairs, requiring validation, password reset, and access review. High is reserved for confirmed administrator, emergency, or critical-service credentials rather than every unspecified account pair.

patterns.description: Detects completed vendor risk assessments: third-party risk assessment wording with populated vendor/contract fields and inherent/residual risk ratings, supported at high confidence by assurance evidence. Topic wording alone is discovery-only.
patterns.operation: Regex_vendor_risk_primary (third-party/vendor/supplier risk assessment, vendor due diligence, TPRM assessment/questionnaire or Shared Assessments SIG wording) is discovery-only at 65. 75 requires the primary plus one populated structure: a populated vendor field (vendor/supplier, ABN, contract number/value, service, data types, criticality, assessor, owners) or a populated risk rating (inherent/residual/overall/control risk with a level or score). 85 requires a populated vendor field (vendor/supplier, ABN, contract number/value, service, data types, criticality, assessor, owners) (two distinct hits), a populated risk rating (inherent/residual/overall/control risk with a level or score), and independent assurance-evidence (questionnaire response, SOC 2/ISO certificate, pen test, subprocessors, data residency) evidence that does not repeat the primary. Every enforce tier rejects template/noise wording (template-exclusion) and guidance, policy, training and news framing (Keyword_vendor_risk_guidance_exclusion).
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the topic phrase alone is discovery-only; enforcement needs populated structure (a populated vendor field (vendor/supplier, ABN, contract number/value, service, data types, criticality, assessor, owners) or a populated risk rating (inherent/residual/overall/control risk with a level or score)), and 85 needs two distinct structures plus independent assurance-evidence (questionnaire response, SOC 2/ISO certificate, pen test, subprocessors, data residency) evidence, so policies, blank forms and training text stay below 75.

patterns.name: Vercel Access Token
patterns.description: Detects Vercel credentials: the current prefixed token family introduced in February 2026 (vcp_ personal access tokens, vci_ integration tokens, vca_ app access tokens, vcr_ app refresh tokens, vck_ API keys), Vercel Blob read-write tokens (vercel_blob_rw_), and, when labelled with Vercel context in an assignment, the legacy unprefixed 24-character token form. A leaked token grants control of the account's projects, deployments and environment variables; a leaked Blob token grants read/write access to the associated storage.
patterns.operation: Two detection branches. Branch 1 (distinctive, value-only capable): the vc?-prefix family announced by Vercel's changelog (2026-02-09) explicitly for secret-scanning detectability -- Vercel's own Sign in with Vercel docs show literal vca_/vcr_ examples with a 56-character alphanumeric body, so a bounded 40-80 range is used behind the vendor-confirmed prefixes -- plus Vercel Blob read-write tokens in the vendor-documented vercel_blob_rw_<storeId>_<secret> structure (segment lengths not formally published; generous bounded ranges behind the 15-character literal prefix). Branch 2 (context-gated only): legacy unprefixed 24-character alphanumeric tokens (per TruffleHog's label-gated detector, which predates the prefixed family), requiring a Vercel label plus an assignment separator (= or :) before the value; legacy tokens issued before the format change may still be live. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the vc?-prefix family is documented by Vercel's own changelog (all five prefixes named, introduced specifically so scanners can detect them), corroborated by literal vca_/vcr_ token examples in Vercel's own Sign in with Vercel docs (56-character alphanumeric bodies), and Vercel is a GitHub secret-scanning partner with six token types, five push-protection enabled. Exact per-prefix body lengths are not formally published, so an honest bounded 40-80 range is used. The legacy unprefixed form is deliberately context-gated: it is indistinguishable from other 24-character identifiers (GitGuardian lists it as non-prefixed), so it requires a labelled assignment and never fires value-only.

Exact 75 probe - API-key structure with deployment context

Vercel Blob read-write token (vercel_blob_rw_ + store id + secret)
Bare Vercel Blob token (distinctive prefix, no label needed)
Legacy unprefixed Vercel token (24 chars) in a labelled assignment
Legacy context-gated token retained as a discovery candidate

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence detector finds current Vercel personal, integration, app, refresh, API, and Blob read-write tokens plus a context-gated legacy unprefixed form. A live value can control projects and deployments, read or change environment variables, or access the associated Blob store within the token's permissions. The affected scale is one account, team, project portfolio, app, or storage instance, with token type, role, scope, and revocation limiting harm. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE reflect serious contained deployment-platform compromise, while an owner token spanning many critical public services and secret stores would raise the impact.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 supports QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because a valid Vercel token can directly alter deployments or expose environment and Blob data within its scope. PROTECTED is not met because the normal credential is bounded by token type and project or team scope without establishing significant critical-service damage.

generic.rationale: Medium generic classification with Medium InfoTech handling is appropriate for Vercel tokens because they grant direct deployment or storage access while role, project, and token scope contain the outcome.

patterns.name: Vulnerability Assessment, Scan Output and Zero-Day Report
patterns.description: Detects vulnerability assessment reports, vulnerability scanner outputs (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS, Nexpose/InsightVM), and zero-day vulnerability write-ups containing CVE/CVSS details, scanner plugin/QID host-port rows, and unpatched or pre-disclosure status. Report and scanner titles alone are discovery-only; enforcement requires a concrete finding, CVE/CWE/CAPEC ID, CVSS vector or score, scanner output structure, or zero-day status evidence.
patterns.operation: A vulnerability assessment/scan/analysis/report, security vulnerability/posture assessment, threat assessment report, scanner scan/report/results/findings/export (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS, Nexpose, InsightVM), or zero-day/0-day vulnerability report/details/disclosure title is discovery-only at 65. Structural evidence raises it to 75: a CVE-YYYY-NNNN(NNN)/CWE-n/CAPEC-n ID, a CVSS v3.x vector string or labelled CVSS score, or scanner output structure (plugin ID, QID, port/protocol, host:port row, host/port/severity column header). The 85 tier requires one of those plus a second distinct group: another structural type, a concrete finding term, severity-rating terms, or zero-day status phrasing (unpatched, no patch available, no CVE assigned, CVE pending, embargoed, coordinated disclosure). Finding and zero-day wording alone stay at 65. Enforcing tiers reject templates and examples.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: titles are discovery-only; enforcement needs a finding, identifier, CVSS, scanner structure, or zero-day status hit, and 85 needs two distinct evidence groups.

patterns.name: Staff Work Roster or Shift Schedule
patterns.description: Populated staff work rosters and shift schedules (duty rosters, on-call rosters, nursing and custodial post rosters, control room shift patterns), detected from the roster's own structure: repeated shift time ranges, a day or date column header over rows of shift codes (D, N, E, L, AM, PM, RDO, OFF, OT, OC, AL, on call, leave), and site or role context. Staff names are NOT required, because a roster with names removed still shows when a site is staffed or thinly staffed and where a particular line or post will be.
patterns.operation: Primary: a roster phrase (roster, rostering, rota, shift schedule / pattern / plan / allocation, duty list / schedule). 65 is discovery-only (phrase alone) and will surface policies, enterprise agreement clauses and templates. There are two 75 tiers. 75a: the phrase plus at least 8 shift time ranges within 300 characters (06:00-14:30, 0600-1400, 22:00–06:00, 7am-3pm). Repeats count, because real rosters reuse the same few shifts. 75b: the phrase plus a day or date column header (5 or more consecutive day names or dd/mm dates) plus a row of 6 or more consecutive shift codes. 85 requires the phrase, at least 2 distinct shift time ranges, the day/date header, a shift-code row, and a site or role term (station, depot, control room, ward, unit, correctional centre, substation, plant, shift supervisor, officer in charge, on-call contact). Every enforce tier excludes template/fixture text and timetable, TV guide, opening-hours and shift-penalty wording.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium: the roster structures (runs of shift codes under a day/date header, repeated time ranges) are distinctive, and timetable, TV guide and opening-hours text is excluded. Some operational schedules that are not rosters, such as maintenance windows, clinic session lists or rail crew documents that mention a timetable, will be misclassified in both directions. Time-range matching is limited to quarter-hour values in the colon-free form so that year ranges such as 2023-2024 do not count. The 85/75 tiers are heuristic evidence tiers, not measured accuracy; tests are synthetic rosters.

patterns.risk_description: A populated roster shows when a site is staffed, how many people are on each shift, and when coverage is thin: overnight single-officer control rooms, relief gaps in a correctional unit, a ward running on agency staff, or an on-call engineer rota for a substation. For critical infrastructure, prisons, police and hospitals that is operational security information that helps someone time an intrusion, sabotage or escape. It also tells anyone holding it where a particular worker will be and when, which matters for an employee affected by domestic and family violence or stalking, even when names are replaced by line numbers. The classifier does not need names, so these records are caught before they are joined to staff lists. Risk 7 rather than 8 because many rosters (retail, hospitality, back-office) carry low operational risk. OFFICIAL: Sensitive / SENSITIVE fits the combined personal-safety and site-security harm.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy and Medium because a populated roster shows when a site is thinly staffed and where a worker will be, relevant to intrusion, escape or stalking even without names. PROTECTED is not met because many rosters carry low operational risk and one schedule lacks significant-damage consequence.

generic.rationale: Medium Personal-Privacy handling covers staffing patterns and worker whereabouts that aid site intrusion or stalking. It is not High because most rosters are routine operational records.

patterns.name: X.509 Certificate Private Key
patterns.description: Detects X.509 certificate private key PEM headers. This is a broad pattern covering RSA, EC, PKCS#8, and OpenSSH private key formats. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. For more specific detection, see global-rsa-private, global-ec-private, global-pkcs8-private, and global-openssh-private.
patterns.operation: Matches PEM-encoded private key headers including RSA PRIVATE KEY, EC PRIVATE KEY, PRIVATE KEY (PKCS#8), OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY, and DSA PRIVATE KEY formats. Any private key in plaintext represents a critical security exposure. Corroborative evidence: 8 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: PEM private key headers are highly distinctive markers with minimal false positive risk. The BEGIN PRIVATE KEY format is a well-defined standard. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

should_match.description: RSA private key header
PKCS#8 private key header
EC private key header

should_not_match.value: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
should_not_match.description: Public key header, not private

should_not_match.value: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
should_not_match.description: Certificate, not private key

should_not_match.value: template example placeholder record identifier
should_not_match.description: Template/sample context should be excluded even when anchor words are present

false_positives.description: Documentation and tutorials showing private key format examples without actual key material.
false_positives.mitigation: Check if the content following the header contains actual Base64-encoded key data.

false_positives.description: Encrypted private keys (BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY) that require a passphrase.
false_positives.mitigation: Still flag encrypted keys as they reveal the presence of key material and may be decryptable.

patterns.risk_description: This broad pattern recognizes PEM headers for RSA, EC, PKCS#8, OpenSSH, DSA, and encrypted private-key containers, so the match is a private-key marker rather than a validated X.509 key body. If usable material follows, disclosure can enable signing, decryption, host or user impersonation, or certificate misuse according to that key's trust role. The normal affected scale is one key and its relying identity or service, while header-only examples, encrypted containers, missing passphrases, and revoked certificates limit direct harm. Risk 8 SENSITIVE reflects serious potential from a confirmed key exposure; PROTECTED requires evidence that the usable key anchors broad trust, critical services, or otherwise significant damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because the broad PEM marker strongly indicates adjacent private credential material with serious possible consequences. PROTECTED is not met by the header alone because the detector neither verifies the key body nor establishes encryption state, validity, trust role, deployment breadth, or criticality.

generic.rationale: Generic handling is Medium with Medium InfoTech controls for a broad private-key header, requiring inspection of the complete block and replacement of confirmed usable keys. patterns.description: Detects xAI (Grok) API keys, which use a distinctive xai- prefix followed by a long alphanumeric body. A leaked key grants unauthorized, billed access to xAI's Grok models and any prompts or data routed through the API.

patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: the xai- prefix is distinctive (confirmed by xAI's own security FAQ and its own GitHub secret-scanning partner entry with push protection enabled by default), so false positives on the prefix alone are extremely unlikely even though the exact body length is not formally documented.

patterns.risk_description: The high-confidence regex identifies an xAI API credential through the distinctive xai- prefix and bounded alphanumeric body. A live key can authorize billed Grok model use and expose prompts, outputs, or application data transmitted through the associated xAI project. The affected scale is one API account or workload, with quota, project permissions, monitoring, and key rotation limiting harm. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE reflect serious contained service and information exposure, while a shared production key carrying protected data across critical workflows would raise the impact.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with QGISCF SENSITIVE, PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, and SENSITIVE InfoTech because a valid xAI key directly enables unauthorized billed model access within a material project. PROTECTED is not met because the normal credential is bounded to one account or workload and does not establish protected prompt content or broad critical-service compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium InfoTech handling fit xAI keys because they grant direct API use while project scope, quotas, and rotation ordinarily contain the damage.

patterns.name: XRP Ledger Address
patterns.description: Detects XRP Ledger classic addresses: base58-encoded, starting with the character "r", 25-35 characters long, encoding a 21-byte buffer (1-byte prefix value 0 + 160-bit account ID) with a 4-byte checksum. The XRP base58 dictionary excludes 0, capital O, capital I and lowercase l — the same 58-character set as standard base58, so a standard base58 class matches the charset. A single leading letter is weak structure, so detection is context-gated. Length/charset/prefix verified against xrpl.org address docs.
patterns.operation: Single tier at confidence 75. The leading "r" plus 24-34 trailing base58 chars is matched, but a single-letter prefix is weak on its own, so the tier requires cryptocurrency/wallet domain context (crypto-wallet-context dict) within proximity AND a template/sample noise NOT-group. Case-sensitive base58 (the XRP checksum is not expressible in a Purview-safe regex). X-address (X-prefixed) variant not implemented — see false_positives / report.
patterns.confidence_justification: Gated 75, not high: a single leading "r" plus a base58 run is weak structure with no regex-expressible checksum, so it collides with other "r..."-leading base58 tokens. Precision comes from the mandatory cryptocurrency/wallet domain-context gate plus the noise exclusion.
regulations: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth)

should_match.description: Exact 65 discovery probe using a documented bare XRP Ledger address
Genesis account address (documented, 34 chars)
ACCOUNT_ZERO special address (documented, 27 chars — near lower bound)

Exact 85 probe with chain-specific and transfer-destination context

should_not_match.value: zDTXLQ7ZKZVKz33zJbHjgVShjsBnqMBhmN
should_not_match.description: Wrong prefix (does not start with r)
Too short (below the 25-char minimum)
Too long (r + 37 = 38, above the 35-char maximum)

should_not_match.value: rDTXLQ7ZKZVKz33-zJbHjgVShjsBnqMBhmN
should_not_match.description: Hyphen breaks the run so no contiguous 25-35 char body exists — rejected

should_not_match.value: xrp wallet address example placeholder
should_not_match.description: Template/placeholder context should be excluded even when domain anchor words are present

false_positives.description: A single leading "r" followed by a base58 run collides with other "r..."-prefixed base58 tokens and identifiers; the XRP 4-byte checksum cannot be validated in a Purview-safe regex.
false_positives.mitigation: The tier is AND-gated by cryptocurrency/wallet domain context (crypto-wallet-context) within the proximity window plus a template/sample noise NOT-group; held at 75.

patterns.risk_description: XRP Ledger Address detects a public classic account address beginning with r and containing 25 to 35 base58 characters, with wallet context required. A valid address can be queried for public ledger activity and, when attributed, may reveal payment relationships or enable convincing account-targeted scams. It does not disclose the private signing key or provide transaction authority, and the weak single-letter prefix permits collisions with other identifiers. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are suitable; SENSITIVE would require an attributed financial profile, secret key, recovery material, or confidential enforcement record.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, label OFFI, and the Low tier because an XRP classic address is public and non-authorizing. SENSITIVE is not met without reliable attribution, private signing material, or linked non-public financial information.

generic.rationale: Low generic handling is appropriate for a public XRP account identifier whose misuse is limited without wallet secrets or personal attribution.

A formally material weakness identifies control failures capable of materially misstating accounts or enabling major fraud. Disclosure can facilitate exploitation and undermine public financial confidence. The significant-damage threshold is met for the substantive Government Financial Audit - Material Weakness artifact, making risk 9 and PROTECTED Financial appropriate after corroboration.

generic.rationale: A government audit finding of material weakness is High Financial information because it identifies control failure capable of major misstatement, fraud or loss of public confidence. patterns.name: HKSAR Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) passport numbers issued by the Immigration Department under the HKSAR Passports Ordinance (Cap. 539). HKSAR passport numbers are nine characters: the current series is the letter H followed by 8 digits; earlier biometric series used K followed by 8 digits, and KJ (48-page jumbo booklets) followed by 7 digits.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine). Regex_hk_passport_number matches the three documented nine-character series: H + 8 digits, K + 8 digits, or KJ + 7 digits, at word boundaries. The series letters are case-fixed (uppercase H / K / KJ as printed on the document), so the pattern is case-sensitive. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires passport evidence (min 2 unique terms) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires passport evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires passport evidence. Evidence uses one keyword group (English and Chinese passport terms) within 300-character proximity. No public checksum is documented for the digit portion, so detection is structural plus keyword evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the nine-character letter-prefixed structure (H/K + 8 digits, KJ + 7 digits) is distinctive, but a single letter followed by 8 digits also occurs in invoice, serial and booking references, so corroborating passport keywords are required on every tier. No tier fires on the bare value alone (D1 identifier convention).

should_match.value: HKSAR passport number H01234567 was presented at the check-in counter
should_match.description: Current H series with 8 digits, labelled

should_match.value: Passport No.: K12345678 issued by the Immigration Department in 2015
should_match.description: Earlier K series with 8 digits

should_match.value: The applicant's 特區護照 number KJ0123456 expires next March
should_match.description: KJ jumbo series with 7 digits

should_not_match.value: Flight reference H1234567 was rebooked for the delegation
should_not_match.description: H followed by only 7 digits is too short

should_not_match.value: Serial HK123456789 printed on the device label
should_not_match.description: Two-letter HK prefix with 9 digits is not a documented series

should_not_match.value: Container KJ12345678 cleared customs on Tuesday morning
should_not_match.description: KJ followed by 8 digits is too long for the KJ series
Lowercase series letter — passport numbers are printed uppercase (pattern is case-sensitive)
Lowercase KJ series — passport numbers are printed uppercase (pattern is case-sensitive)

false_positives.description: A letter H or K followed by 8 digits also occurs in booking references, invoice numbers and hardware serials.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires corroborating passport keywords within the proximity window; there is no bare value-only tier.

false_positives.description: Malaysian passport numbers (A/H/K + 8 digits, covered by my-passport-number) structurally overlap the H/K series.
false_positives.mitigation: Both patterns share generic terms such as "passport number" and "travel document", so cross-fires on generic-labelled documents are possible; HK-specific terms (HKSAR / 特區護照 / Immigration Department) separate Hong Kong context from Malaysian context only when they are present.

false_positives.description: Sample passport numbers in application guides or templates may match the labelled form.
false_positives.mitigation: The high and medium tiers apply the template-exclusion NOT-group to suppress sample and documentation content.

patterns.risk_description: The HKSAR pattern recognises current H plus eight digits, earlier K plus eight digits, and jumbo-booklet KJ plus seven digits in passport context; it does not capture the data page or Immigration Department record. Disclosure may support a booking, visa, or identity-verification pretext once the traveller's name and document dates are known. A normal match concerns one holder, while booking references, invoices, hardware serials, and some Malaysian passport formats overlap the H or K structure. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect the bounded and partly ambiguous identifier; SENSITIVE would require document imagery, credentials, or a linked identity and travel file.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps consistently to OFFICIAL because the HKSAR number supports correlation but has no public checksum and does not independently prove identity. SENSITIVE is not met without the passport data page, authentication information, or sufficient linked biographical and itinerary content for direct misuse.

generic.rationale: The generic Low classification recognises a context-gated travel identifier whose standalone consequence and jurisdictional certainty are both limited.

patterns.name: India Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects Indian mobile telephone numbers per the Department of Telecommunications' National Numbering Plan 2003 (as amended): 10-digit mobile numbers with a constrained leading digit (6-9, expanded from 7-9 to include 6 when DoT authorized 6-series allocation in 2017), in both the bare domestic form and the +91 international form (leading 0 dropped). Landline/STD (Subscriber Trunk Dialling) numbers are intentionally out of scope: STD codes vary 2-8 digits with no verified structural rule constraining their leading digit, so a regex loose enough to cover them (just "10 digits after a leading 0") would be barely tighter than matching any 11-digit sequence — far too high a digit-collision risk to ship without a genuinely verified constraint. See false_positives.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (Indian mobile numbers have no checksum). Reference: Department of Telecommunications, National Numbering Plan 2003, https://www.dot.gov.in/national-numbering-plan-list; the 2017 6-series mobile allocation to Reliance Jio. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+91) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the mobile leading-digit constraint (6-9) narrows the format, but Indian mobile numbers carry no checksum and a bare 10-digit mobile-shaped sequence is still a high digit-collision format (any 10-digit number starting 6-9 is common). Per the phone-family convention set by au-fixed-line-telephone (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; high digit-collision formats never get a zero-evidence tier), both the domestic and +91 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +91 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating. Unlike NANP (555-01XX) and the UK (Ofcom drama numbers), no DoT/TRAI-published fictional/test number range exists for India — this was confirmed by web research and is documented rather than invented; test_cases below use an illustrative, clearly-non-official descending-digit placeholder instead.

should_match.description: Domestic mobile, leading digit 9, illustrative descending-digit placeholder, common 5+5 spaced grouping
Domestic mobile, leading digit 9, bare digits with no separator
International +91 mobile form, leading 0 dropped, contiguous digits
Domestic mobile, leading digit 6 — the range DoT opened in 2017 for Jio 6-series allocation

should_not_match.description: Leading digit 5 is not in the valid 6-9 mobile range
Only 9 digits — one short of the required 10
Toll-free 1800 number — does not match the mobile leading-digit range
International form but leading digit 5 (after the country code) is not in the valid 6-9 mobile range

false_positives.description: A bare 10-digit mobile-shaped sequence (leading digit 6-9) is a high digit-collision format — it can coincidentally match invoice numbers, order numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +91 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: No official DoT/TRAI fictional or test number range exists for India (confirmed by web research, unlike NANP's 555-01XX or Ofcom's drama numbers), so an illustrative descending-digit test value was used instead of an authoritative reserved range.
false_positives.mitigation: Test values use clearly non-representative digit patterns; deployers should substitute their own tenant's synthetic test data for live validation rather than relying on a non-existent official reserved range.

false_positives.description: Landline/STD numbers are out of scope for this initial release because India's STD codes vary 2-8 digits with no verified leading-digit constraint, so this pattern will not detect landline numbers at all (a false negative, not a false positive, but noted here for completeness).
false_positives.mitigation: A future revision could add STD/landline coverage if a genuinely verifiable structural constraint (beyond "10 digits after a leading 0") is confirmed from a primary DoT/TRAI source.

false_positives.description: The domestic sub-regex also fires inside the +91 international rendering when a separator follows the country code (empirically verified: in "+91 9876543210" it matches the "9876543210" substring — Indian mobiles drop the trunk 0 in international form, so the digits after "+91 " are exactly the domestic form; the contiguous "+919876543210" rendering is protected by the digit-boundary lookbehind).
false_positives.mitigation: Benign co-fire, left in place deliberately: both sub-regexes carry identical evidence gating and confidence levels, so the duplicate match cannot inflate confidence — it can only duplicate a finding at the same level, which reporting layers de-duplicate by offset. A structural fix would need variable-width negative lookbehind, which the universal engine target does not support.

patterns.risk_description: The India pattern detects ten-digit mobile numbers beginning 6-9 in domestic or +91 form with phone evidence; landline and STD formats are intentionally excluded because their structure is insufficiently constrained. A genuine mobile value supports calls, WhatsApp or SMS phishing, harassment, and identity correlation, particularly when the subscriber's name or account relationship is known. One match exposes a contact point rather than a credential, and any ten-digit order or invoice beginning 6-9 can resemble the number. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are appropriate; SENSITIVE would require linkage to authentication, financial access, protected communications, location, or a vulnerable individual's private identity context.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to OFFICIAL because an Indian mobile number enables contact and social engineering but provides no independent identity proof or account authority. SENSITIVE is not met without linked credentials, protected relationships, sensitive communications, or identity and location data supporting serious direct harm.

generic.rationale: Generic Low handling fits a single Indian mobile endpoint whose direct misuse remains bounded and dependent on additional subscriber or account information.

patterns.name: India EPFO Universal Account Number
patterns.description: Detects Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) Universal Account Numbers (UAN). UAN is a 12-digit number assigned to employees to link multiple PF member IDs across employers. Leading digit is non-zero.
patterns.operation: Structural 12-digit UAN with leading 1-9. No public checksum. Corroborative evidence: UAN/EPFO/PF keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: industry-hr, pii-civic-credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: twelve-digit numbers appear in many systems; EPFO/UAN/PF keywords are required for reliable classification.

should_match.description: Typical 12-digit UAN
High-range UAN
Another valid-length UAN

should_not_match.description: Leading zero not allowed
Only 11 digits
13 digits

false_positives.description: Aadhaar is also 12 digits; bare digit matches can overlap.
false_positives.mitigation: Require UAN/EPFO/provident fund keywords; use Aadhaar SIT with Verhoeff for Aadhaar context.

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds a 12-digit nonzero-leading number with nearby UAN, EPFO, provident-fund, payroll, employment, or identity terminology. A genuine UAN persistently links an employee's provident-fund membership across employers, so disclosure can support employment-history correlation, targeted impersonation, and attempts to manipulate retirement-benefit interactions. The normal unit concerns one identifiable worker and can cause serious but contained privacy and financial harm, although the number alone does not authenticate EPFO access and can collide with other 12-digit identifiers. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE are justified, while PROTECTED is not met without authentication factors, a bulk employee register, or significant compromise of provident-fund services.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE Personal-Privacy because a genuine UAN is a persistent worker-linked provident-fund identifier with serious correlation and impersonation consequences. PROTECTED is not met because the standalone number neither grants access nor establishes broad or high-impact compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium generic classification and Medium Personal-Privacy DLM fit a lifelong employment-benefit identifier with serious contained misuse potential but no standalone authentication capability.

patterns.name: India UPI Virtual Payment Address
patterns.description: Detects Unified Payments Interface (UPI) Virtual Payment Addresses (VPA / UPI ID) used in India. Format is a local part and a payment-service provider handle separated by @ (for example name@oksbi or business@ybl). Handles are alphabetic PSP codes; local parts allow letters, digits, dot, underscore and hyphen.
patterns.operation: Structural VPA detection with bounded classes (local 2-64 chars, handle 2-32 chars). Does not validate against the NPCI handle registry. Corroborative evidence: UPI/VPA keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: financial-transaction, banking.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: email-like strings can look similar; UPI-specific keywords and common PSP handles in evidence terms reduce false positives.

should_match.description: SBI YONO-style handle
PhonePe ybl handle
Amazon Pay handle

should_not_match.value: user@domain.com
should_not_match.description: Email with multi-part TLD-like handle containing dot — handle disallows dots

should_not_match.value: @oksbi
should_not_match.description: Missing local part

should_not_match.value: user@
should_not_match.description: Missing handle

false_positives.description: Some short email-like corporate aliases without dots in the domain label.
false_positives.mitigation: Require UPI/VPA/payee keywords; common PSP handles listed in broad evidence.

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds an email-like UPI virtual payment address with nearby UPI, VPA, banking, or transaction terminology, but it does not validate the handle against the NPCI registry. A VPA identifies where payment requests or transfers can be directed and may enable nuisance collect requests, phishing, or correlation to a person or merchant, but it does not authorise payment or grant account access. The normal unit is a deliberately shareable payment alias with low, reversible harm that still needs identity or authentication context for material misuse. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL are appropriate, while a VPA linked to transaction history, a verified holder profile, or usable payment credentials would warrant SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, and the OFFICIAL DLM because a UPI VPA is a payment-routing alias rather than an authentication secret. SENSITIVE is not met without holder, transaction, or authorisation data that turns the alias into a materially harmful financial record.

generic.rationale: Low generic classification and Low DLM fit a shareable UPI endpoint whose standalone disclosure supports only limited correlation and social-engineering harm.

patterns.description: Detects Iceland Physical Addresses patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type that uses machine learning and function-based detection for physical address identification. This keyword list provides address-related terms for supplementary matching.
patterns.operation: Function-based detection in Microsoft Purview. This pattern uses keyword matching for country-specific address terminology to identify physical address data.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence: broad keyword matching on address terms requires additional context and corroborative evidence for accurate physical address detection. Address keywords alone produce high false positive rates without structural validation.

should_match.description: Contains address keyword 'vegur'
Contains address keyword 'gata'
Contains address keyword 'stígur'

should_not_match.value: quarterly financial report for fiscal year 2024

false_positives.mitigation: Require structural address patterns (number + street type + name) rather than isolated keyword matches.

false_positives.mitigation: Use proximity-based corroborative evidence to ensure keywords appear alongside numeric components.

patterns.risk_description: The Icelandic keyword list searches for road-form words including vegur, gata, and stigur near number-like address content. Those terms can identify public roads, walking routes, named sites, and businesses as readily as a person's home, so the detector alone provides weak occupancy evidence. A precise Icelandic address may narrow location in a small community, but harm still depends on attribution to a resident, sensitive service, or repeated activity. Risk 3 supports OFFICIAL; SENSITIVE would require a vulnerable named occupant, confidential shelter or clinic, movement pattern, or aggregated household information.

classification.rationale: Risk 3 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because Icelandic road words do not establish who occupies or visits the location. SENSITIVE is not met without attribution, a protected facility, repeated movement, or meaningful aggregation.

generic.rationale: Icelandic address cues are generically Low with Low DLM because location specificity alone remains low impact until connected to a person or sensitive activity.

patterns.name: Italian Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects Italian mobile telephone numbers per AGCOM's national numbering plan (Delibera n. 8/15/CIR, Allegato A): the mobile/personal-communications block, structurally defined as "3XYZ" plus six further digits (a 10-digit total for numbering assigned under the current plan), in both the domestic and +39 international forms. The delibera permits already-assigned legacy 9-digit mobile numbering to persist, so any surviving legacy 9-digit mobile numbers are a known potential false negative of this 10-digit regex — kept at 10 digits deliberately, since evidence that live 9-digit stock persists today is inconclusive and loosening the length bound would raise digit collision for every match. Geographic (landline) numbers are intentionally out of scope: the AGCOM plan family bounds geographic numbers at a 10-11 digit total (11 maximum), but within that bound the "0" block's second digit is structurally unconstrained and the minimum/per-prefix length variability across the legacy short-number stock is not verified from a primary source — a 0-prefixed regex spanning that length range with no second-digit constraint would be highly collision-prone — and Italian landline numbers are also the one well-known exception where the leading 0 is retained even in the +39 international form, a further formatting axis to model. Mobile numbers carry no such leading-0 quirk (they never had a leading 0 to begin with).
patterns.operation: Validation: none (Italian mobile numbers have no checksum). Reference: AGCOM, Piano di numerazione, https://www.agcom.it/piano-di-numerazione; Delibera n. 8/15/CIR, Allegato A (customer numbering for mobile and personal-communications services: "3XYZ U1U2U3U4U5U6", a 10-digit total for current-plan assignments; legacy 9-digit assignments are permitted to persist — see description), https://www.agcom.it/sites/default/files/migration/attachment/Allegato%2020-2-2015.pdf. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+39) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the leading-digit-3 constraint and the 10-digit length of current-plan assignments (drawn directly from AGCOM's Delibera 8/15/CIR customer-numbering structure; legacy 9-digit assignments the delibera permits to persist are an accepted false-negative trade-off) narrow the format, but Italian mobile numbers carry no checksum and a 10-digit sequence starting with 3 is still a high digit-collision format. Per the phone-family convention (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; a +CC prefix alone is insufficient gating; there is no 65 rung), both the domestic and +39 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +39 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

should_match.description: Domestic mobile, leading 3, illustrative ascending-digit placeholder (no official AGCOM-reserved fictional range exists — verified absent during research), space-separated
Domestic mobile, bare digits with no separator
Domestic mobile, hyphenated grouping
International +39 form of the mobile number, leading 3 unchanged (mobile numbers have no leading 0 to drop)

should_not_match.description: Leading digit 0 is Italy's geographic (landline) block — out of scope for this mobile-only pattern
Leading digit 9 is not the mobile/personal-communications leading digit 3
Only 9 digits — one short of the required 10
Valid-shaped digit run embedded inside a longer reference number, rejected by digit boundaries

false_positives.description: A 10-digit sequence starting with 3 can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, order numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading digit.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +39 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: No official AGCOM-reserved fictional or test number range exists for Italy (confirmed by web research, unlike NANP's 555-01XX or Ofcom's drama numbers), so illustrative synthetic values were used instead of an authoritative reserved range.
false_positives.mitigation: Test values use clearly non-representative sequential digit patterns; deployers should substitute their own tenant's synthetic test data for live validation rather than relying on a non-existent official reserved range.

false_positives.description: Landline/geographic numbers are not detected at all (a false negative, not a false positive, but noted for completeness): the AGCOM plan family bounds geographic numbers at a 10-11 digit total (11 maximum), but within that bound the "0" block's second digit is structurally unconstrained, the minimum/per-prefix length variability across the legacy short-number stock is not verified from a primary source, and Italian landlines additionally keep the leading 0 in the +39 international form (unlike almost every other country) — so a landline regex at that length range would be highly collision-prone without a verified narrowing constraint.
false_positives.mitigation: A future revision could add landline coverage if a genuinely verifiable per-prefix length/structure constraint is confirmed from a primary AGCOM source, following the same verification bar applied here.

false_positives.description: Legacy 9-digit mobile numbering already assigned before the current plan is permitted to persist under Delibera 8/15/CIR, and any surviving live 9-digit numbers will not be detected by this 10-digit regex (a false negative, noted for completeness).
false_positives.mitigation: Deliberate trade-off: evidence that live 9-digit stock persists today is inconclusive, and loosening the length bound to 9-10 digits would measurably raise digit collision for every match; revisit if a primary source confirms surviving 9-digit assignments.

false_positives.description: The mobile sub-regex also fires inside the +39 international rendering when the number is written with separators (empirically verified: in "+39 345 678 9012" it matches the "345 678 9012" substring — Italian mobiles have no trunk 0, so the digits after "+39 " are exactly the domestic form; the contiguous "+393456789012" rendering is protected by the digit-boundary lookbehind).
false_positives.mitigation: Benign co-fire, left in place deliberately: both sub-regexes carry identical evidence gating and confidence levels, so the duplicate match cannot inflate confidence — it can only duplicate a finding at the same level, which reporting layers de-duplicate by offset. A structural fix would need variable-width negative lookbehind, which the universal engine target does not support.

patterns.risk_description: The Italian identifier targets current ten-digit mobile numbers beginning 3 in domestic or +39 form with phone context; geographic landlines and possible legacy nine-digit mobiles remain outside scope. Disclosure can enable calls, messaging scams, harassment, and subscriber correlation when combined with a person's name, service, or account information. The normal unit is one contact route, not an account credential, and ten-digit invoices or orders beginning 3 can collide with the pattern. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit the limited standalone harm; SENSITIVE would require credentials, intimate communications, protected-service context, precise location, or identity data that makes targeted abuse materially more serious.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with OFFICIAL because an Italian mobile number enables contact and correlation but does not authenticate the subscriber or reveal a protected relationship. SENSITIVE is not met without linked credentials, sensitive communications, location, or vulnerable-person context capable of serious direct harm.

generic.rationale: The generic Low classification treats one Italian mobile endpoint as bounded contact information rather than a credential or complete subscriber record.

references.title: AGCOM: Piano di numerazione (national numbering plan — service classification by leading digit)

AGCOM: Allegato A alla Delibera n. 8/15/CIR (mobile customer numbering structure "3XYZ U1..U6", 10-digit total for current-plan assignments; pre-existing legacy 9-digit mobile assignments permitted to persist)

patterns.name: Lawful Interception Warrant and Intercept Product
patterns.description: Detects telecommunications interception warrants, stored communications warrants and the intercept product they produce (call transcripts, line / session logs, intercepted communications) under the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 (Cth). Disclosure of the existence of an interception warrant or of interception product is a criminal offence under the TIA Act and alerts targets to switch to unmonitored channels. Absorbs the former lawful-intercept-transcripts classifier.
patterns.operation: Primary: interception phrases (telecommunications interception, TI / interception / stored communications / B-party warrant, TIA Act, lawful interception, interception product, intercepted call transcript, intercepted communications, telephone / line intercept, preservation notice). 65 = phrase only (discovery). 75 = phrase plus one populated intercept record field (warrant number, target service / line / number, intercepted line, line / session / call / product number, A- or B-party, IMSI, MSISDN) or an IMEI. 85 = phrase plus two distinct record fields; or a labelled warrant number plus warrant-process evidence (eligible judge, AAT member, issuing authority, interception agency, carrier, warrant period, secrecy provision); or a record field / IMEI plus process evidence or a s.63 secrecy marker. Parliamentary, academic and media framing excluded.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: interception terminology with populated target / warrant fields is highly distinctive; warrant numbers are unpublished, so the warrant reference is a documented label-anchored fallback that only counts with warrant-process evidence.

customisation.note: Replace the documented labelled-reference fallback with the customer's real format (see docs/identifiers.md#surveillance-warrant-reference). Earlier versions used the TIA/YYYY/AGENCY/NNNNN and SCW-YYYY-NNNN warrant format, which does not appear in any published source.

false_positives.mitigation: Negative keyword exclusion: 'parliamentary', 'annual review', 'reporting period', 'tabled', 'committee'. Require proximity to specific target identifiers.

patterns.risk_description: This detector recognises telecommunications interception, stored-communications, or B-party warrants together with warrant references and target services such as phone numbers, IMEI values, or email accounts. Disclosure alerts a target that communications are monitored, prompting migration to unobserved channels and compromising evidence, associates, collection methods, and an active investigation. Parliamentary statistics, textbooks, legal commentary, and news about completed matters are excluded from the normal true positive. Risk 10 requires PROTECTED Law-Enforcement because the warrant's existence and targeting data are operationally decisive and statutorily restricted; no higher QGISCF tier exists.

classification.rationale: Risk 10 aligns with PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, PROTECTED Law-Enforcement, and High because revealing a live interception warrant can immediately defeat covert collection and prejudice serious proceedings. No higher QGISCF classification exists above this maximum tier.

generic.rationale: High and High Law-Enforcement DLM protect covert interception authority, target services, and collection scope whose exposure can terminate effective surveillance.

changelog.description: Purview upload fix, matching unchanged: Regex_lawful_interception_warrant_intercept_record_fields character class [A-Za-z0-9/.+-] reordered to [A-Za-z0-9/+.-]. Quality pass (2026-09-24): removed the invented TIA/YYYY/AGENCY/NNNNN warrant-reference detector family (it was a primary with its own 65/75/85 tiers) and the invented SCW-YYYY-NNNN regex; a labelled warrant number now uses the surveillance-warrant-reference fallback (identifier-format slot) and counts at 85 only together with warrant-process evidence (eligible judge, issuing authority, carrier, warrant period ...); 75 = interception phrase + a populated intercept record field or an IMEI; 85 = two distinct record fields, or labelled warrant number + warrant-process evidence, or a record field/IMEI + process evidence or s.63 secrecy marker; tests converted to labelled warrant numbers with a blank-register decoy; references added.

Interception-phrase regex gains lawful interception, interception product, intercept(ed) (call) transcript, intercepted communications / calls and telephone / line intercept, and becomes a second primary family (65 phrase / 75 plus one populated intercept record field, TIA / SCW reference or IMEI / 85 plus two record fields or two independent evidence types). Corroborative terms that duplicate record fields or primary phrases (IMEI, target service, mobile number, interception product) removed from that list to avoid same-span double counting. Not imported: phone tap, wiretap, wire intercept, electronic surveillance, surveillance transcript and intercept order (US / news vocabulary, and surveillance-device material is a different regime) and the absorbed self-corroborating label/domain tiers. Added intercept transcript and line-log positives (85), a 75 cover note, and vendor-copy and procedure decoys. Risk unchanged at 10.

patterns.risk_description: This low-confidence keyword-proximity detector looks for internal assessments of legal-professional-privilege claims, privilege logs, waiver risk, and vulnerability analysis in government context. A genuine assessment maps which documents have strong or weak privilege claims, enabling an opponent or requester to target vulnerable communications and increasing the risk of waiver or compelled disclosure. Academic articles, judgments, templates, and public RTI decisions can use the same language, so internal matter and analysis context is essential. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require broad compromise of a major privileged portfolio or significant institutional damage beyond one review.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to SENSITIVE and Medium tiers because an internal LPP assessment exposes claim weaknesses and waiver risks in a defined document set. PROTECTED is not met without broad privileged compromise or significant institution-wide damage.

generic.rationale: An LPP claim assessment is generically Medium with Medium Legal DLM because it reveals where privilege protection is vulnerable within a specific matter or review set.

changelog.description: Add the classification block (tier, rationale, generic classification/DLM/rationale). Text copied verbatim from the reviewed SIT-Reference master, which until now held it only in PurviewDeploy.

Wired the shared template-exclusion dictionary (Keyword_noise_exclusion) into every tier alongside the existing exclusion group and citation filter; dropped the marking and matter-context keyword groups; "vulnerable" narrowed to "vulnerable to challenge/waiver"; recommended_confidence 85 -> 75; confidence low -> medium to match the gated design. Added populated 85/75 positives and a blank privilege-log decoy; one-line/prose positives re-described as 65. Added Evidence Act and RTI Act references.

Targeted blocker remediation: split matter facts, legal conclusions, and privilege/marking evidence into canonical keyword references; make RTI case-sensitive; author 65 discovery, 75 populated-matter, and 85 matter-plus-conclusion-plus-marking tiers with exact probes while preserving public-decision and template exclusions.

TP-01482 approved reduced scope: add a policy-capable 75 tier wiring the existing primary keyword group to the existing corroborative group, NOT-gated by the existing exclusion group (all references pre-existing in this YAML; no new detection structure). The 65 tier remains discovery-only. Deferred per QA/independent review: the proposed 85 tier, pending a split of the flat corroborative group into independently referenceable marking/matter-detail/waiver-conclusion groups. patterns.risk_description: The Lithuanian driving-licence detector matches any eight-digit value and uses five nearby licence terms to infer document context. A verified number can connect a driver to entitlement, insurance, vehicle, or infringement records and support impersonation with additional personal details. Dates, customer IDs, invoices, and administrative references share the same short numeric shape, and the hit contains no holder, class, status, or validity period. Risk 5 OFFICIAL recognises bounded harm after confirmation; SENSITIVE would require an attributable driver record or licence copy.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low because a bare eight-digit candidate has broad overlap and limited direct misuse value. SENSITIVE is not met without verified driver and licensing context.

generic.rationale: Low generic treatment suits one Lithuanian licence candidate with no validator or holder information. Medium controls should apply to licence documents, driver histories, insurance files, or attributable number collections.

patterns.name: Mexico Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects Mexican passport numbers issued by the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE). Older passports use a single letter followed by 7-8 digits; newer books carry an 8-9 character alphanumeric serial. Mixed alphanumeric serials are broad candidates that also match order IDs, booking codes, and product serials — they are not treated as Mexican passport numbers without issuer or passport-document evidence. Because the format is short and loosely structured, corroborative keyword proximity is strongly recommended to reduce false positives.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_passport Matches a single letter followed by 7-8 digits, or an 8-9 character alphanumeric serial containing at least one letter and one digit. patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the alphanumeric body is only 8-9 characters and lacks a fixed prefix, so the pattern can match unrelated reference codes and serial numbers. Corroborative passport keywords within 300 characters are essential for reliable detection.

patterns.name: Malaysia Tax Identification Number (TIN)
patterns.description: Detects Malaysian individual Tax Identification Numbers (TIN / Nombor Pengenalan Cukai) issued by the Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia (LHDN / HASiL). Since 2 January 2023 individual TINs use the prefix IG followed by 9-11 digits (11-13 characters total); the legacy individual prefixes SG (employment income) and OG (business income) with the same digit range remain in circulation in older records. Entity TINs (C, D, F, PT, TA and similar prefixes) are deliberately out of scope: single-letter prefixes over a digit run are too collision-prone and entity TINs are not personal data.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine). Regex_my_tax_number matches the IG / OG / SG prefix (optionally separated by a single space) followed by 9-11 digits at word boundaries. The prefix is case-fixed (uppercase IG / OG / SG as issued by LHDN), so the pattern is case-sensitive. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires tax evidence (min 2 unique terms) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires tax evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires tax evidence. Evidence uses one keyword group (English and Malay tax terms) within 300-character proximity. LHDN publishes no checksum for the digit portion, so detection is structural plus keyword evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the two-letter prefix over a 9-11 digit run is distinctive but not unique (e.g. SG also prefixes Singapore-related reference codes), so corroborating LHDN / tax keywords are required on every tier. No tier fires on the bare value alone (D1 identifier convention).

false_positives.description: SG- and OG-prefixed codes appear in non-tax contexts (Singapore-related references, order codes, part numbers).
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires corroborating LHDN / tax keywords within the proximity window; there is no bare value-only tier.

false_positives.description: Sample TINs in LHDN guidance, e-Invois documentation, or tax-agent templates may match the labelled form.

false_positives.mitigation: Rely on prefix structure, length bounds, and keyword evidence; the digit run is variable length so a repeated-digit filter is not applicable.

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds Malaysian individual TINs using current IG or legacy OG and SG prefixes followed by nine to eleven digits, with LHDN or tax context and no checksum validation. Disclosure can support taxpayer impersonation, targeted tax scams, or correlation of a person across filings, but the identifier alone does not expose income, assessment, refund, or account access. The normal unit is one personal tax number with bounded harm that requires additional identity and tax-record information for material misuse. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are appropriate, while a populated return, assessment, or identity bundle containing the TIN would warrant SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, and the OFFICIAL DLM because the Malaysian TIN is an atomic taxpayer identifier without financial facts or authentication capability. SENSITIVE is not met without an attributable tax record, income data, or access context.

generic.rationale: Low generic classification and Low DLM fit a Malaysian individual TIN whose material tax and identity harm depends on correlation with richer records.

patterns.name: NATO Marking - RESTRICTED / CONFIDENTIAL / SECRET / COSMIC TOP SECRET
patterns.description: Detects NATO security classification markings under the NATO security policy (C-M(2002)49): the spelled-out national-security levels NATO RESTRICTED (NR), NATO CONFIDENTIAL (NC) and NATO SECRET (NS), and the highest level COSMIC TOP SECRET (CTS) — where the codeword COSMIC attaches only to TOP SECRET. ATOMAL caveat markings (NATO CONFIDENTIAL ATOMAL, NATO SECRET ATOMAL, COSMIC TOP SECRET ATOMAL) are covered as suffixes of their parent level marking. Marking syntax verified directly against the International Programs Security Handbook (US-government primary source reproducing NATO security-directive marking rules) and corroborating NATO security briefings; matched case-sensitively so ordinary lowercase prose ("a nato secret") does not trigger it.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the distinctive spelled-out form "NATO <LEVEL>" (RESTRICTED, CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET) where the NATO prefix is itself strong context. A second tier 85 matches the distinctive codeword banner COSMIC TOP SECRET, tolerant of a hyphen or PDF-line-wrap-inserted whitespace between the words. ATOMAL caveats ride on these forms (e.g. NATO SECRET ATOMAL matches via NATO SECRET; COSMIC TOP SECRET ATOMAL via COSMIC TOP SECRET). Both tiers carry only a template/noise NOT-exclusion — the case-sensitive ALL-CAPS marking token is the high-confidence evidence.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on both forms. "NATO RESTRICTED / CONFIDENTIAL / SECRET" is a case-sensitive two-word phrase whose NATO prefix is itself a strong, low-collision context marker verified against primary sources; "COSMIC TOP SECRET" is a case-sensitive three-word codeword banner unique to NATO's highest classification. The bare two/three-letter abbreviations (NR, NC, NS, CTS, and the ATOMAL abbreviations CTSA/NSA/NCA) are attested marking forms but are deliberately NOT shipped: even hard-gated on NATO context they collide catastrophically with everyday tokens (NSA = National Security Agency, NC/NR = US state/business shorthand, NS = Nova Scotia, CTS = many uses), with no reliable disambiguation — documented as a skip rather than shipped as noise.

should_match.value: This report is marked NATO SECRET and must be handled per NATO security policy.
should_match.description: Spelled-out NATO SECRET (NS) national-security level — the NATO prefix is strong context

should_match.value: Cover sheet: COSMIC TOP SECRET — access restricted to briefed personnel only.
should_match.description: COSMIC TOP SECRET (CTS) codeword banner, NATO's highest level

should_match.value: The annex is classified NATO CONFIDENTIAL ATOMAL and covers released atomic information.
should_match.description: ATOMAL caveat form — matched via its parent level marking NATO CONFIDENTIAL (NC)

should_match.value: Distribution list for the NATO RESTRICTED briefing pack is attached.
should_match.description: NATO RESTRICTED (NR), the lowest NATO classified level

should_match.value:
Header reads COSMIC
TOP SECRET ATOMAL for the working-group papers.
should_match.description: PDF line-wrap between COSMIC and TOP SECRET (the [\s-]+ separator tolerates a wrap-inserted newline); ATOMAL suffix rides on the COSMIC TOP SECRET match

should_not_match.value: the nato secret was leaked to a journalist last spring, allegedly
should_not_match.description: lowercase prose (case-sensitive exclusion — the marking regex only matches ALL-CAPS tokens)

should_not_match.value: THE NSA REGULARLY MONITORS NATO COMMUNICATIONS ACROSS THE ALLIANCE
should_not_match.description: ALL-CAPS prose naming NSA (the agency) and NATO but with no marking — fails at the regex level (NATO is followed by COMMUNICATIONS, not a level word; the NSA abbreviation is deliberately not a shipped marking form)

should_not_match.value: THE SUMMIT WILL COVER COSMIC BACKGROUND RADIATION AND OTHER TOP RESEARCH TOPICS
should_not_match.description: ALL-CAPS prose containing COSMIC and TOP but not the contiguous COSMIC TOP SECRET banner — fails at the regex level

false_positives.description: ALL-CAPS prose (headings, legal boilerplate, or documents rendered entirely in capitals) defeats the case-sensitivity signal; an all-caps rendering of "NATO SECRET" or "COSMIC TOP SECRET" with no marking intent (e.g. a headline or book title) can fire.
false_positives.mitigation: Treat hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps. The NATO/COSMIC prefixes keep collision low relative to bare classification words, and the corroborative NATO/COSMIC/ATOMAL keywords within 300 characters reinforce genuine marking context.

false_positives.description: The bare NATO classification abbreviations (NR, NC, NS, CTS) and the ATOMAL abbreviations (CTSA, NSA, NCA) are real, verified marking forms but are not implemented: they are two/three-letter tokens that collide with extremely common non-marking uses (NSA = National Security Agency, NS = Nova Scotia, NC/NR = US-state and business shorthand, CTS = numerous), and no jurisdiction gate can reliably separate a genuine NATO marking abbreviation from these.
false_positives.mitigation: Documented as a deliberate coverage gap rather than shipped as ungovernable noise. The spelled-out NATO <LEVEL> and COSMIC TOP SECRET forms capture the same marking vocabulary at high confidence.

false_positives.description: NATO UNCLASSIFIED (NU) is a NATO marking but is a releasability/handling designation, NOT one of the four NATO classification levels (RESTRICTED and above) per C-M(2002)49; it is deliberately excluded from the level regex because it denotes releasable/unclassified content, carries little data-loss value, and would only broaden matches.
false_positives.mitigation: Out of scope by design; this SIT targets protectively-marked (RESTRICTED and above) NATO content.

false_positives.description: This SIT's SECRET / TOP SECRET / CONFIDENTIAL vocabulary overlaps with the US/UK/NZ/AU marking families, but the mandatory NATO or COSMIC prefix means a genuine NATO marking will not, on the prefix alone, co-fire those nations' bare-word tiers; conversely a document carrying both a NATO marking and a national marking is expected to fire both SITs as corroborating signals.
false_positives.mitigation: No mitigation needed — the prefix makes the NATO forms structurally distinct from the national bare-word markings.

patterns.risk_description: The NATO marking detector is an umbrella for NATO RESTRICTED, NATO CONFIDENTIAL, NATO SECRET, COSMIC TOP SECRET, and ATOMAL forms, so the normal true-positive unit is a marking event spanning materially different damage levels. NATO RESTRICTED does not imply the consequence of COSMIC TOP SECRET, while the highest branches can expose strategic defence or atomic information and damage alliance operations. The current deployment cannot pass the exact matched branch into policy, so a fixed SENSITIVE outcome would under-handle NATO SECRET, COSMIC TOP SECRET, or ATOMAL matches. Until branch-aware routing is implemented and tested, risk 10 and PROTECTED retain the necessary fixed protection; the future event model must enforce the actual NATO level and caveat.

sensitivity_labels.nato: NATO RESTRICTED / NATO CONFIDENTIAL / NATO SECRET / COSMIC TOP SECRET
sensitivity_labels.ca_gov: Protected B / Confidential / Secret / Top Secret

classification.rationale: Risk 10 maps to PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, Marking Protected, and High because the detector includes NATO SECRET, COSMIC TOP SECRET, and ATOMAL branches associated with grave alliance, defence, intelligence, or atomic-security damage. NATO RESTRICTED and NATO CONFIDENTIAL can carry lower consequences, but a positive umbrella match does not identify the branch and can therefore represent the highest-consequence marked content covered by the detector. PROTECTED is the highest accepted classification tier, and branch-aware routing remains an owner-review requirement before lower NATO markings can receive a reduced treatment.

generic.rationale: High with High Government DLM is appropriate because a positive NATO marking match can represent COSMIC TOP SECRET or ATOMAL information whose disclosure could gravely harm alliance operations, defence capabilities, intelligence relationships, or atomic security.

patterns.name: Netherlands Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects Dutch national telephone numbers per the ACM-administered numbering plan: 10-digit numbers (leading trunk 0 included) covering geographic numbers (area code first significant digit 1-5 or 7, e.g. 020 Amsterdam, 010 Rotterdam, 070 Den Haag) and mobile numbers (06 prefix), plus the +31 international form (leading 0 dropped), including the widespread "+31 (0)6 12345678" letterhead rendering (a common-but-nonstandard practice — ITU-T E.123 advises against the parenthesised trunk digit in international notation, but it is ubiquitous on Dutch letterheads, so it is matched for detection purposes). Numbers beginning 08 (0800 free-of-charge service numbers, 088 non-geographic business lines) and 09 (0900/0906/0909 premium-rate information numbers) are intentionally out of scope — these are organizational/service numbers rather than personal PII, mirroring how uk-phone-number and fr-phone-number scope out their own non-geographic service ranges. Note this also excludes the 085 and 091 location-independent subscriber ranges (VoIP numbers ACM makes available to individuals as well as businesses): a personal 085/091 VoIP line is therefore a known false negative, accepted because the 085/088/091 block is predominantly organizational in practice and cannot be split from it structurally.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (Dutch numbers have no checksum). Reference: ACM (Autoriteit Consument & Markt), Telefoonnummers, https://www.acm.nl/nl/telefoonnummers; ACM ConsuWijzer, De verdeling van telefoonnummers in Nederland, https://consument.acm.nl/telefoon-internet-en-televisie/telefoonnummers/verdeling-telefoonnummers-nederland (geographic area-code-to-region mapping; "een mobiel nummer begint altijd met 06"; 0800/0900/0906/0909/18 service-number prefixes); ACM factsheet on 06 numbers (10-digit total), https://www.acm.nl/sites/default/files/old_publication/publicaties/16001_097-en-06-nummers-informatie-voor-telecomaanbieders-20160701.pdf. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+31) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the leading-digit constraint (01-07 domestic, restricting to geographic area codes and the 06 mobile block) and the fixed 10-digit total length narrow the format, but Dutch numbers carry no checksum and a 10-digit sequence with those leading digits is still a high digit-collision format. Per the phone-family convention (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; a +CC prefix alone is insufficient gating; there is no 65 rung), both the domestic and +31 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +31 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

should_match.description: Domestic mobile, 06 prefix, illustrative synthetic value (no official ACM-reserved fictional range was found — verified absent during research), space-separated
Domestic geographic, Amsterdam area code (020), illustrative synthetic value
Domestic geographic, Den Haag area code (070), hyphenated
International +31 form of the mobile number, leading 0 dropped
Widespread "+CC (0)" letterhead rendering — nonstandard per E.123 but ubiquitous on Dutch letterheads

should_not_match.description: Leading digit 8 is a free-of-charge service number (0800), out of scope for this personal-communications pattern
085 location-independent VoIP range — out of scope with the rest of the 08 block (documented known false negative for personal 085 lines)
Leading digit 9 is a premium-rate information number (0900), out of scope
Only 7 digits after the 06 mobile prefix, one short of the required 8
Valid-shaped digit run embedded inside a longer reference number, rejected by digit boundaries

Australian mobile in 4-3-3 grouping (signature block, 2026-10-16 boilerplate run). 0412 is a real Dutch area code (Oss), but Dutch notation writes a 6-digit subscriber number unsplit or in pairs, never 3-3.
Australian landline in 2-4-4 grouping; no Dutch geographic area code is two digits long

false_positives.description: Australian numbers share the 10-digit trunk-0 shape (04 mobiles, 02/03/07/08 landlines), and 01-07 are Dutch geographic prefixes, so an Australian signature-block number next to "Mobile:" reached 75.
false_positives.mitigation: Two lookaheads on the domestic sub-regex reject groupings that Dutch notation does not use: a separator straight after a two-digit 01-05/07 prefix (Dutch geographic area codes are three or four digits; only 06 is two), and 4-3-3 grouping (a four-digit area code is followed by a six-digit subscriber number written unsplit or in pairs). Residual risk: an Australian number written without separators still matches and relies on the phone-context gating; a Dutch four-digit-area-code number written 4-3-3 is now a false negative.

false_positives.description: A 10-digit sequence with a 01-07 leading digit can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, order numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +31 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: No official ACM-reserved fictional or test number range was found for the Netherlands (confirmed by web research, unlike NANP's 555-01XX or Ofcom's drama numbers), so illustrative synthetic values were used instead of an authoritative reserved range.
false_positives.mitigation: Test values use clearly non-representative sequential digit patterns; deployers should substitute their own tenant's synthetic test data for live validation rather than relying on a non-existent official reserved range.

patterns.risk_description: The detector recognizes Netherlands ten-digit domestic numbers beginning 01 through 07 and +31 international forms, including optional trunk-code notation, rather than identifying the subscriber. A genuine number can support spam, voice phishing, messaging discovery, or correlation with a person's address or service account. The ordinary unit is one individual or business contact and meaningful harm generally needs identity, vulnerability, or account context; invoices and other ten-digit references can share the same shape. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect bounded standalone exposure, while a protected contact, sensitive-service link, or aggregated directory would move the information toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because one Netherlands phone number is a contact route rather than an authentication factor or personal dossier. SENSITIVE is not met without vulnerable-person, sensitive-service, persistent-harassment, or bulk-directory context causing moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM are appropriate for one Dutch contact number with limited independent confidentiality impact. Sensitive linkage or aggregation would warrant stronger treatment.
