patterns.name: Norway Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects Norwegian passport numbers issued by the police (politiet). The 2020 series uses a nine-character document number: ordinary (C) and emergency (K) passports are one prefix letter plus two characters that may be letters or digits plus six digits (specimen CCC002251); diplomatic (FG), service (FH), special (FJ), travel-document (FK) and foreigner (FL) passports are a two-letter prefix plus one letter-or-digit plus six digits. Pre-2020 series passports (in circulation until October 2030) carry an eight-digit document number.
patterns.operation: Regex patterns (boost_regex engine, case-sensitive). Pattern_no_passport_2020 matches the prefix-anchored nine-character 2020-series forms ([CK] plus 2 alphanumerics plus 6 digits, or F[GHJKL] plus 1 alphanumeric plus 6 digits). Pattern_no_passport_legacy matches the eight-digit pre-2020 form and is only exported with stronger evidence requirements because a bare 8-digit run is ambiguous (dates, order numbers). Tiers: High (85) 2020-series with passport evidence (min 2 unique) and template exclusion; Medium (75) 2020-series with evidence and exclusion, or legacy with min-2 evidence and exclusion; Low (65) 2020-series with evidence. No public checksum exists for the printed number (the MRZ check digit is not part of the printed field), so detection relies on structure plus keyword evidence; AllDigitsSameFilter guards the all-numeric legacy form.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the 2020-series prefix-anchored nine-character shape is structurally distinctive, but the legacy eight-digit form is a plain digit run, so corroborating passport keywords are required on every tier and the legacy form is additionally held to a min-2-unique-terms evidence bar. recommended_confidence is the evidence-gated 75 workhorse tier per registry convention.

should_match.value: Passport number CCC002251 was checked against the register by politiet
should_match.description: 2020-series ordinary passport number (national control-guide specimen) with label context
2020-series ordinary passport with digit in the second position
2020-series diplomatic passport number (FG prefix)

should_match.value: Emergency travel: pass K2B654321 utstedt i dag
should_match.description: 2020-series emergency passport number (K prefix)
Legacy eight-digit passport number

should_not_match.description: Eight characters in the 2020-series form — one digit short
Nine characters but the prefix letter A is not an issued Norwegian passport series
Lowercase — passport numbers are printed uppercase (pattern is case-sensitive)
FM is not an issued two-letter prefix (only FG, FH, FJ, FK, FL)
Nine digits — too long for the legacy eight-digit form and not a valid 2020-series shape

false_positives.description: Eight-digit runs such as dates written as DDMMYYYY, invoice or order numbers can match the legacy form.
false_positives.mitigation: The legacy regex is only exported in a 75 tier requiring two unique passport-evidence terms plus the template-exclusion NOT-group; AllDigitsSameFilter suppresses repeated-digit placeholders.

false_positives.description: Nine-character product or serial codes beginning with C, K or F could match the 2020-series form.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires passport keywords within the 300-character proximity window; the prefix letters and trailing six-digit block keep the collision surface small.

patterns.risk_description: Norway's detector covers prefix-constrained nine-character 2020 passport numbers and the older eight-digit series still circulating, not a passport image or police travel record. A genuine number may help populate a form or strengthen a targeted travel pretext after the holder's identity and document dates are obtained elsewhere. One ordinary match affects one traveller, while the legacy branch overlaps dates, invoices, and orders and the newer branch can resemble C-, K-, or F-prefixed serial codes. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit that context-dependent atomic value; SENSITIVE would require document contents, credentials, or a substantive combined identity and movement record.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 with PSPF and QGISCF OFFICIAL reflects one Norwegian passport reference whose legacy branch is especially ambiguous and whose printed number has no public checksum. SENSITIVE is not met without verified document data, authentication factors, or rich personal context enabling consequential misuse.

generic.rationale: Generic Low handling is appropriate for a context-gated travel identifier that cannot authenticate the holder and includes a broad legacy numeric branch.

patterns.name: New Zealand Inland Revenue number
patterns.description: Detects New Zealand Inland Revenue number patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Due to the numeric format, corroborative evidence keywords are essential for reliable detection.
patterns.operation: Corroborative evidence: 5 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: tax-id, nz-financial.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: eight to nine digit numbers are very common. Keywords like 'IRD' or 'inland revenue' are essential for reliable New Zealand tax number detection.

should_match.description: Eight-digit NZ IRD number
Nine-digit NZ IRD number
NZ Inland Revenue format

should_not_match.description: Seven digits, too short for NZ IRD number
Ten digits, exceeds NZ IRD number format

false_positives.description: Generic numeric sequences in non-tax contexts such as reference numbers or account identifiers
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords within the proximity window to distinguish tax identifiers from general numeric data.

false_positives.description: Numbers from other identification schemes with similar digit patterns
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with jurisdiction-specific detection to prioritise matches in tax-related documents and cross-reference with other identifier types.

patterns.risk_description: The medium-confidence rule identifies an eight- or nine-digit New Zealand Inland Revenue number near tax context. A valid number can support taxpayer correlation or social engineering, but it does not reveal income, filing status, account balance, or authentication credentials. The normal match concerns one taxpayer identifier and practical fraud requires identity and account information from elsewhere. Risk 4 OFFICIAL reflects low standalone harm; SENSITIVE requires a linked tax record or usable service-access context.

classification.rationale: An atomic Inland Revenue identifier with no tax facts or access capability aligns with risk 4 OFFICIAL. SENSITIVE is not met because credible direct harm requires material personal and account data beyond this detector.

generic.rationale: Low generic classification reflects a tax-record locator whose confidentiality impact depends on linkage to identity, filing, or account information.

patterns.name: New Zealand Marking - CONFIDENTIAL
patterns.description: Detects the New Zealand Government CONFIDENTIAL national-security classification under the Protective Security Requirements (PSR) classification system: the verified control/dissemination marking separator (CONFIDENTIAL//..., e.g. CONFIDENTIAL//NZEO) and a gated bracket form ([CONFIDENTIAL]). Deliberately narrow v1: no bare-word tier (CONFIDENTIAL is overwhelmingly common as generic business/legal boilerplate — NDAs, email footers, "STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL", "PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL" — and would swamp any bare-word detector), and the bracket tier is hard-gated by New Zealand government context because, unlike its sibling markings, [CONFIDENTIAL] is not a verified SEEMail trigger word. Regex logic verified directly against official PSR marking-format guidance (protectivesecurity.govt.nz); matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the verified national-security marking format: CONFIDENTIAL followed immediately by the double-forward-slash control/dissemination-marking separator. Tier 75 matches the bracket form [CONFIDENTIAL], but only when gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative context, since this bracket form (unlike [RESTRICTED]/[SENSITIVE]/[IN-CONFIDENCE]) is not an attested official convention on its own. There is no bare CONFIDENTIAL tier.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the `//` national-security-marking form: a structurally distinctive, case-sensitive token with low natural-English collision risk, directly verified against the official PSR marking-format guidance (not inferred); the regex requires an uppercase letter immediately after the separator (//[A-Z]) so URL/path double-slash artifacts cannot fire it. The gated bracket tier (75) is lower evidence — no primary source attests [CONFIDENTIAL] as a real marking convention the way [RESTRICTED]/[SENSITIVE]/[IN-CONFIDENCE] are attested as SEEMail trigger words — so it requires positive New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence rather than firing on the bracket alone. There is deliberately no bare-word tier: "CONFIDENTIAL" alone is one of the most common words in generic business/legal boilerplate and would produce overwhelming noise.

should_match.value: New Zealand Government agencies must handle this [CONFIDENTIAL] briefing under PSR requirements.

should_not_match.value: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL — do not distribute beyond this list
should_not_match.description: no bare-word tier — bare/title-case "CONFIDENTIAL" boilerplate never matches (locked design decision)

should_not_match.description: no bare-word tier — common legal/NDA boilerplate never matches

should_not_match.description: bracket form present but excluded by the missing New Zealand government/PSR AND-gate (no corroborative context nearby)

should_not_match.value: please keep this confidential between us until the announcement
should_not_match.description: lowercase English word (case-sensitive exclusion)

false_positives.description: ALL-CAPS prose (legal boilerplate, headers, or documents rendered entirely in capitals) defeats the case-sensitivity signal the CONFIDENTIAL tokens rely on.
false_positives.mitigation: Treat hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps; the `//` tier (85) remains the most reliable signal since it additionally requires the structural separator.

false_positives.description: CONFIDENTIAL is one of the most common words in generic business and legal boilerplate: NDAs, email footers/disclaimers, and stock phrases like "STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL" or "PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL" vastly outnumber genuine PSR classification use.
false_positives.mitigation: A bare CONFIDENTIAL tier is deliberately omitted (locked design decision) rather than attempting to gate it — none of "CONFIDENTIAL" alone, "STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL", or "PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL" will fire this SIT under any tier.

false_positives.description: Unlike [RESTRICTED], [SENSITIVE], and [IN-CONFIDENCE] — confirmed as the complete SEEMail bracket trigger-word set ([SEEMAIL], [TRUSTED], [RESTRICTED], [SENSITIVE], [IN-CONFIDENCE], verified directly against the PSR marking-guidance page) — [CONFIDENTIAL] is NOT a SEEMail trigger word, and structurally cannot be: SEEMail's classification ceiling is RESTRICTED/ SENSITIVE (the "Restricted group" service tier), so it never carries CONFIDENTIAL-classified content in the first place. Any "[CONFIDENTIAL]" bracket found in the wild is far more likely to be informal business bracket-tag notation than a genuine PSR marking.
false_positives.mitigation: The bracket tier is hard-gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence specifically because no attested official convention exists for it, unlike its sibling markings' bracket tiers (which carry real, if legacy, SEEMail provenance).

false_positives.description: New Zealand's CONFIDENTIAL//... marking format is interoperable with the Five-Eyes REL TO convention, so genuine hits (e.g. CONFIDENTIAL//REL TO NZL, AUS) also fire the existing us-classification-banner pattern, whose alternation includes CONFIDENTIAL with the same separator syntax. This co-fire is expected and correct - both SITs are identifying the same interoperable classification banner.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy policies should expect the double-hit and treat the SITs as corroborating, not conflicting, signals.

false_positives.description: This is a deliberately narrow v1 for CONFIDENTIAL. Structured detection beyond the verified `//` form awaits clarity on the Secure Government Email (SGE) Framework's own marking-rendering conventions (SEEMail's replacement, rolling out during 2026), which had no published marking syntax at the time of writing.
false_positives.mitigation: Revisit this SIT once SGE marking conventions (if any) are published; the `//` tier is expected to remain valid regardless of the SEEMail-to-SGE transition.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies New Zealand CONFIDENTIAL national-security markings through the verified CONFIDENTIAL// control syntax or a government-gated bracket form, while excluding the ordinary business use of confidential. A genuine marked asset requires restricted government handling and can cause serious legal, diplomatic, or operational harm if released, but the marking alone does not establish the significant-damage content required for PROTECTED. The bracket form and quoted examples are weaker still. Risk 7 with SENSITIVE and Marking Sensitive is proportionate; SECRET or TOP SECRET markings, or independently corroborated significant-damage material, require a higher classification route.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, Marking Sensitive, MARK_SENS, Medium, and Medium Government because New Zealand CONFIDENTIAL denotes serious restricted government information without itself proving the significant-damage threshold. The verified double-slash banner supports confident handling, while the bracket branch still requires contextual validation. Higher New Zealand markings and substantive protected content remain separately classified.

generic.rationale: A genuine New Zealand CONFIDENTIAL marking requires Medium Government handling because it establishes restricted national-security or official information below the PROTECTED damage threshold. Quoted examples and the weaker bracket form require corroboration, while SECRET, TOP SECRET, or independently significant-damage content follows a higher route.

patterns.name: New Zealand Marking - IN-CONFIDENCE
patterns.description: Detects the New Zealand Government IN-CONFIDENCE protective marking under the Protective Security Requirements (PSR) classification system: endorsed forms (e.g. MEDICAL IN-CONFIDENCE, BUDGET: IN-CONFIDENCE), the legacy SEEMail bracket trigger-word convention ([IN-CONFIDENCE]), and the bare ALL-CAPS document-banner form. Regex logic verified against the official PSR Classification Handbook (protectivesecurity.govt.nz) and Cabinet Office Circular CO(08)1; matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches an endorsed form (an endorsement word directly followed by IN-CONFIDENCE, space- or colon-separated). Tier 85 also matches the legacy SEEMail bracket form [IN-CONFIDENCE]. Tier 75 matches the bare IN-CONFIDENCE document/email banner, gated by a template/noise NOT-exclusion to suppress documentation-sample hits.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the endorsed and legacy-bracket forms: both are case-sensitive, structured markings with low natural-English collision risk. The bare IN-CONFIDENCE banner (75) is a distinctive hyphenated compound absent from ordinary prose, but is one tier lower and gated by a template/noise NOT-exclusion since it lacks the endorsement/bracket's structural signal.

should_match.description: Endorsed form, space-separated — matches the PSR Classification Handbook's own worked example (MEDICAL IN-CONFIDENCE)

should_match.value: Cabinet paper: BUDGET:IN-CONFIDENCE — do not distribute before the Budget announcement.

should_match.value:
The attached briefing is classified BUDGET
IN-CONFIDENCE pending Cabinet sign-off.
should_match.description: PDF-wrapped endorsed form — line wrap inserts a newline between the endorsement and the classification word

should_match.value: Subject: [IN-CONFIDENCE] Draft policy paper for review
should_match.description: Legacy SEEMail bracket trigger-word form

should_match.value:
IN-CONFIDENCE
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment — briefing for the Minister
should_match.description: Bare document-banner form (PSR Classification Handbook document-marking convention — centred, bold, ALL CAPS)

should_not_match.value: Please keep this in confidence between us until the announcement.
should_not_match.description: lowercase English idiom (case-sensitive exclusion)

should_not_match.value: IN-CONFIDENCE (template only) — replace this sample paragraph with your own content
should_not_match.description: bare banner tier excluded by the template/noise NOT-group (documentation/sample content)

should_not_match.value: STAFF IN CONFIDENCE handling applies to this personnel file
should_not_match.description: non-hyphenated "IN CONFIDENCE" (two words) is a known coverage gap — canonical PSR guidance renders the classification as the single hyphenated token IN-CONFIDENCE

false_positives.description: ALL-CAPS prose (legal boilerplate, headers, or documents rendered entirely in capitals) defeats the case-sensitivity signal the bare IN-CONFIDENCE banner tier relies on.
false_positives.mitigation: Treat banner-tier-only (75) hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps; the endorsed and legacy-bracket tiers (85) remain the reliable signal.

false_positives.description: The SEEMail square-bracket trigger-word convention ([IN-CONFIDENCE]) is being decommissioned during 2026 as the Secure Government Email (SGE) Framework replaces SEEMail. It retains legacy detection value for circulated documents and email archives but is not the durable long-term signal.
false_positives.mitigation: Weight the bracket tier (85) as a transitional/legacy indicator; the endorsed and bare-banner tiers reflect the current PSR Classification Handbook convention and are expected to remain valid after SEEMail's decommissioning.

false_positives.description: The non-hyphenated form "IN CONFIDENCE" (two words, no hyphen) is not matched — canonical PSR guidance renders it as the single hyphenated token "IN-CONFIDENCE", but some agency drafting may omit the hyphen.
false_positives.mitigation: No mitigation implemented; documented as a known coverage gap for a future revision.

patterns.risk_description: This detector recognises New Zealand IN-CONFIDENCE banners, endorsed forms such as MEDICAL IN-CONFIDENCE or BUDGET IN-CONFIDENCE, and the legacy SEEMail bracket convention. A genuine marking can cover pre-announcement policy, personnel, medical, budget, or ministerial information whose disclosure causes material privacy, fiscal, or government-process harm. Archived messages, marking guidance, and quoted legacy examples can also match, so the banner alone does not establish strategic or system-scale compromise. Risk 8 and SENSITIVE Marking treatment fit consequential but context-dependent protected information; PROTECTED requires an explicit higher marking or content capable of Cabinet-scale, life-safety, protected-operation, or other significant damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to OFFICIAL: Sensitive, SENSITIVE, Marking Sensitive DLM, and Medium tiers because IN-CONFIDENCE content can cause material but bounded government or personal harm. PROTECTED is not met without a higher marking or credible Cabinet, safety, protected-operation, or significant-damage consequence.

generic.rationale: A New Zealand IN-CONFIDENCE marking is generically Medium with Medium Government DLM because it denotes controlled non-public information with context-dependent harm.

patterns.name: New Zealand Marking - RESTRICTED
patterns.description: Detects the New Zealand Government RESTRICTED national-security classification under the Protective Security Requirements (PSR) classification system: the verified control/dissemination marking separator (RESTRICTED//..., e.g. RESTRICTED//REL TO NZL, GBR), the legacy SEEMail bracket trigger-word convention ([RESTRICTED]), and the bare ALL-CAPS document-banner form gated by New Zealand government context and a collocation-noise exclusion. Regex logic verified directly against official PSR marking-format guidance (protectivesecurity.govt.nz); matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the verified national-security marking format: RESTRICTED followed immediately by the double-forward-slash control/dissemination-marking separator. Tier 75 matches the legacy SEEMail bracket form [RESTRICTED] (attested but business-reused, so it sits below the // tier). Tier 65 matches the bare RESTRICTED banner, gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative context and a NOT-exclusion for common non-government "RESTRICTED" collocations (RESTRICTED AREA, AGE RESTRICTED, etc).
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the `//` national-security-marking form and the legacy-bracket form: both are structurally distinctive, case-sensitive tokens with low natural-English collision risk, and the `//` separator convention is directly verified against the official PSR marking-format guidance (not inferred). The bare RESTRICTED banner (65) is a common English word used constantly outside government context (RESTRICTED AREA, AGE RESTRICTED, RESTRICTED ACCESS, etc.), so it is the widest tier and is gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence plus a dedicated NOT-exclusion for the most common non-government collocations.

false_positives.description: ALL-CAPS prose (legal boilerplate, headers, or documents rendered entirely in capitals) defeats the case-sensitivity signal the bare RESTRICTED banner tier relies on.
false_positives.mitigation: Treat banner-tier-only (65) hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps; the `//` tier (85) and legacy-bracket tier (75) remain the reliable signal.

false_positives.description: RESTRICTED is an extremely common English word in everyday non-government usage (RESTRICTED AREA, RESTRICTED ACCESS, ACCESS RESTRICTED, AGE RESTRICTED, RESTRICTED STOCK, RESTRICTED USE, USE RESTRICTED), all of which are more common in general text than the PSR classification marking.
false_positives.mitigation: The bare tier (65) requires New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence and excludes this collocation set via a dedicated NOT-group. The `//` (85) and bracket (75) tiers are unaffected — they are structurally distinctive and do not require the gate.

false_positives.description: The SEEMail square-bracket trigger-word convention ([RESTRICTED]) is being decommissioned during 2026 as the Secure Government Email (SGE) Framework replaces SEEMail. RESTRICTED is confirmed as one of SEEMail's five bracket trigger words (the complete list is [SEEMAIL], [TRUSTED], [RESTRICTED], [SENSITIVE], [IN-CONFIDENCE] — verified directly against the PSR marking-guidance page), so this tier reflects a real, current, if soon-to-be-legacy convention.
false_positives.mitigation: Weight the bracket tier (75) as a transitional/legacy indicator; the `//` and gated bare-banner tiers reflect the durable PSR marking convention and are expected to remain valid after SEEMail's decommissioning.

false_positives.description: The `\bRESTRICTED//` trigger requires the double-forward-slash to immediately follow the classification word with no space. No verified source shows a spaced variant (e.g. "RESTRICTED //"); if one exists in the wild it would not be matched by this tier. The regex additionally requires an uppercase letter immediately after the separator (//[A-Z]) so that accidental double-slashes in URLs or file paths (e.g. /RESTRICTED//shared/) cannot fire it.
false_positives.mitigation: No mitigation implemented; documented as a known coverage gap rather than broadening the regex on unverified syntax.

patterns.risk_description: The pattern detects New Zealand RESTRICTED markings in double-slash control form, the legacy bracket convention, or a government-gated banner while excluding common phrases such as restricted area or restricted access. An authentic hit denotes national-security or government information whose release can expose distribution, partner, operational, or policy material and cause serious contained harm. The lower banner tier and archived email examples still require context, and the marking is below SECRET or TOP SECRET. Risk 8 supports SENSITIVE marking treatment; PROTECTED would require a higher classification or specific evidence of significant strategic, safety, or protected-operation damage.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 aligns with OFFICIAL: Sensitive, SENSITIVE, Marking Sensitive DLM, and Medium because RESTRICTED denotes serious controlled information below the high-damage tier. PROTECTED is not met without a higher marking or credible significant strategic, safety, or operational consequences.

generic.rationale: A New Zealand RESTRICTED marking is generically Medium with Medium Government DLM because it imposes national-security controls without establishing SECRET-level damage.

patterns.name: New Zealand Marking - SECRET / TOP SECRET
patterns.description: Detects the New Zealand Government SECRET and TOP SECRET national-security classifications under the Protective Security Requirements (PSR) classification system: the verified control/dissemination marking separator ((TOP )SECRET//..., e.g. SECRET//NZEO, TOP SECRET//REL TO NZL, FVEY), the TOP SECRET banner-words phrase (tolerant of a hyphen or PDF-line-wrap-inserted whitespace between TOP and SECRET), and a New Zealand government/PSR-context-gated bare SECRET banner. Deliberately omits a SEEMail square-bracket trigger-word tier: the complete SEEMail bracket trigger-word set is [SEEMAIL]/[TRUSTED]/[RESTRICTED]/[SENSITIVE]/[IN-CONFIDENCE], all at or below SEEMail's own RESTRICTED-tier service ceiling, so [SECRET]/[TOP SECRET] bracket forms are structurally implausible and unattested. Regex logic verified directly against official PSR marking-format guidance (protectivesecurity.govt.nz); matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the verified national-security marking format: (TOP )SECRET immediately followed by the double-forward-slash control/dissemination-marking separator, requiring an uppercase letter immediately after the separator so URL/path double-slash artifacts cannot fire it. A second tier 85 matches the TOP SECRET banner-words phrase, tolerant of a hyphen or PDF-line-wrap-inserted whitespace between TOP and SECRET. Tier 75 matches the bare SECRET banner, gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative context and a NOT-exclusion for common non-government SECRET collocations (TRADE SECRET(S), CLIENT SECRET, API SECRET, SECRET MANAGER).
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the `//` national-security-marking form and the TOP SECRET banner-words phrase: both are structurally distinctive, case-sensitive tokens with low natural-English collision risk, and the `//` separator convention is directly verified against the official PSR marking-format guidance (not inferred). The bare SECRET banner (75) is a common English word used constantly outside government context (TRADE SECRET, API SECRET, SECRET MANAGER, etc.), so it is the widest tier and is gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence plus a dedicated NOT-exclusion for the most common non-government collocations.

false_positives.description: A [SECRET] or [TOP SECRET] SEEMail-style square-bracket trigger word is not shipped. SEEMail's confirmed bracket trigger-word set — [SEEMAIL], [TRUSTED], [RESTRICTED], [SENSITIVE], [IN-CONFIDENCE] (verified directly against the PSR marking-guidance page) — tops out at RESTRICTED/SENSITIVE (the "Restricted group" service tier), so SEEMail structurally cannot carry SECRET or TOP SECRET-classified content in the first place. This is a stronger case than nz-marking-confidential's unattested-bracket omission: there, no source attested [CONFIDENTIAL] as a real convention; here, the service's own classification ceiling rules it out entirely.
false_positives.mitigation: No mitigation needed — this is a documented coverage decision, not a gap. Any "[SECRET]"/"[TOP SECRET]" bracket found in the wild would not be a genuine SEEMail marking.

false_positives.description: This SIT's gated bare-SECRET tier (75) shares vocabulary with two Australian SITs: au-marking-secret-topsecret's own SECRET/TOP SECRET banner tier (85, ungated apart from the noise-exclusion NOT-group) and au-marking-protected's SECRET roll-up tier (85, also ungated apart from noise/collocation NOT-groups — neither AU tier requires positive AU government context). A genuine New Zealand SECRET or TOP SECRET document will therefore typically co-fire both AU SITs as well, since their bare-SECRET tiers have no jurisdiction gate of their own.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy policies should expect this cross-jurisdiction triple-hit and treat the SITs as corroborating, not conflicting, signals; do not add an NZ-context exclusion to the AU SITs, as that would break their own intended (broader) coverage.

false_positives.description: New Zealand's SECRET//... and TOP SECRET//... marking format is interoperable with the Five-Eyes REL TO convention, so genuine hits with a US-recognized control token (e.g. SECRET//REL TO NZL, FVEY) also fire the existing us-classification-banner pattern, whose alternation includes SECRET and TOP SECRET with the same separator syntax. This co-fire is expected and correct — both SITs are identifying the same interoperable classification banner. (A dissemination marking not in us-classification-banner's control-token alternation, e.g. the NZEO-only example above, will not co-fire it.)
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy policies should expect the double-hit and treat the SITs as corroborating, not conflicting, signals.

patterns.risk_description: This detector finds New Zealand SECRET and TOP SECRET national-security markings in verified control syntax, the distinctive TOP SECRET banner, or a government-gated SECRET banner. A confirmed hit can expose defence, intelligence, international-partner, protected-operation, or human-source information and create strategic, diplomatic, or life-safety consequences. The pattern omits implausible legacy bracket forms and guards common secret collocations, making the normal marked unit high consequence despite residual title or all-caps collisions. Risk 10 requires PROTECTED as the maximum Australian crosswalk; no higher QGISCF tier exists, and the original New Zealand SECRET or TOP SECRET controls still govern remediation.

classification.rationale: Risk 10 maps to the highest accepted PSPF/QGISCF PROTECTED tier, Marking Protected DLM, and High because compromise can cause strategic or life-safety damage. No higher QGISCF classification exists, while native SECRET/TOP SECRET controls remain mandatory.

generic.rationale: New Zealand SECRET or TOP SECRET markings are generically High with High DLM because they identify national-security information capable of major strategic harm.

patterns.name: New Zealand Marking - SENSITIVE
patterns.description: Detects the New Zealand Government SENSITIVE protective marking under the Protective Security Requirements (PSR) classification system: the legacy SEEMail bracket trigger-word convention ([SENSITIVE]), endorsed forms (e.g. BUDGET SENSITIVE, COMMERCIAL: SENSITIVE, CABINET SENSITIVE), and the bare ALL-CAPS document-banner form gated by New Zealand government context. Regex logic verified against the official PSR Classification Handbook (protectivesecurity.govt.nz) and Cabinet Office Circular CO(08)1; matched case-sensitively.
patterns.operation: Tier 85 matches the legacy SEEMail bracket form [SENSITIVE]. Tier 85 also matches an endorsed form (an endorsement word directly followed by SENSITIVE, space- or colon-separated). Tier 65 matches the bare SENSITIVE banner, gated by New Zealand government/PSR corroborative context and a NOT-exclusion for generic commercial-sensitivity idioms (e.g. COMMERCIALLY SENSITIVE).
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence on the legacy-bracket and endorsed forms: both are case-sensitive, structured markings with low natural-English collision risk. The bare SENSITIVE banner (65) is a common English word and is the widest tier, so it requires positive New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence plus a NOT-exclusion for generic commercial-sensitivity idioms.

false_positives.mitigation: Treat banner-tier-only (65) hits as lower confidence when the surrounding text is itself all-caps; the legacy-bracket and endorsed tiers (85) remain the reliable signal.

false_positives.description: Uppercase SENSITIVE in generic commercial-sensitivity idioms (e.g. "COMMERCIALLY SENSITIVE", "MARKET SENSITIVE") is common in non-government business writing and is unrelated to PSR classification.
false_positives.mitigation: The bare tier (65) requires New Zealand government/PSR corroborative evidence and excludes the commercial-sensitivity idiom set via a dedicated NOT-group.

false_positives.description: The Australian PSPF SIT (au-marking-sensitive) also detects a bare ALL-CAPS SENSITIVE banner gated by Australian government context. Text that is ambiguously or jointly Australian/New Zealand government context (e.g. trans-Tasman agency correspondence) can legitimately fire both SITs on the same SENSITIVE occurrence.
false_positives.mitigation: This is expected, acceptable co-firing rather than a defect — downstream consumers should treat concurrent AU/NZ SENSITIVE hits as a signal to check which jurisdiction's corroborative evidence actually matched, not as a false positive to suppress.

false_positives.description: The SEEMail square-bracket trigger-word convention ([SENSITIVE]) is being decommissioned during 2026 as the Secure Government Email (SGE) Framework replaces SEEMail. It retains legacy detection value for circulated documents and email archives but is not the durable long-term signal.
false_positives.mitigation: Weight the bracket tier (85) as a transitional/legacy indicator; the endorsed and bare-banner tiers reflect the current PSR Classification Handbook convention and are expected to remain valid after SEEMail's decommissioning.

patterns.risk_description: The regex identifies New Zealand SENSITIVE markings through endorsed BUDGET, COMMERCIAL, or CABINET forms, the legacy bracket convention, and a government-gated uppercase banner. A genuine asset may contain pre-release fiscal decisions, Cabinet working material, commercial negotiations, personal information, or ministerial advice whose disclosure causes serious but contained harm. Generic commercially sensitive phrases and archived SEEMail examples can collide, so the marking alone does not prove high national-security impact. Risk 8 supports SENSITIVE marking treatment; PROTECTED would require a higher classification or clear significant damage to Cabinet, safety, strategic operations, or critical services.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to OFFICIAL: Sensitive, SENSITIVE, Marking Sensitive DLM, and Medium because the marking denotes material government, fiscal, or commercial harm. PROTECTED is not met without a higher level or credible significant Cabinet, safety, strategic, or critical-service damage.

generic.rationale: A New Zealand SENSITIVE marking is generically Medium with Medium Government DLM because it signals elevated handling without automatically establishing significant damage.

patterns.name: New Zealand Business Number (NZBN)
patterns.description: Detects New Zealand Business Numbers (NZBNs) — the 13-digit universal business identifier administered by MBIE. Every NZBN is a GS1 Global Location Number (GLN): the first two digits are 94 (the GS1 prefix identifying New Zealand entities), the next ten digits are the business entity identifier, and the final digit is a GS1 mod-10 check digit. A bare 13-digit run has a phone-number-sized collision surface (NZ mobile/landline numbers, card fragments, timestamps), so every tier requires the number to be directly attached to an NZBN label — label-embedded-in-regex counts as label gating per the D1 decision record. There is deliberately no bare unlabelled tier.
patterns.operation: Validation: the GS1 mod-10 check digit (alternating 1/3 weights over the first 12 digits) is not expressible as a regex and no Purview validator function exists for GLN/NZBN, so the check digit is enforced only as a structural digit. Reference: NZBN registry (nzbn.govt.nz, "About the NZBN") and GS1 New Zealand GLN documentation. Detection is a label-embedded regex requiring an NZBN / New Zealand Business Number label directly attached to a 94-prefixed 13-digit number, with optional space/hyphen grouping. AllDigitsSameFilter guards repeated-digit sentinels. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the 94 GS1 prefix plus fixed 13-digit length is a solid structural signal, but 13-digit runs collide with phone numbers and other identifiers, and the GS1 mod-10 check digit cannot be enforced in the exported SIT. The label-embedded regex is the evidence gate for every tier (75 workhorse per the D1 convention); the 85 tier additionally requires NZ business-registry keywords in proximity.

should_match.description: NZBN label with colon and solid 13-digit 94-prefixed number (GS1 mod-10 check digit valid)
NZBN label with space-grouped number (4-4-4-1, GS1 mod-10 check digit valid)
Full label form with solid 13-digit number (GS1 mod-10 check digit valid)

should_match.value: The NZBN is 9429041234563 for invoicing purposes
should_match.description: Prose form with "is" between label and number

should_not_match.description: Bare 13-digit 94-prefixed number with no NZBN label — bare digit runs are never matched
13 digits not starting with the GS1 New Zealand prefix 94
Only 12 digits, one short of the GLN length
16-digit card-like number — the trailing digit guard rejects NZBN-prefixed longer runs

should_not_match.value: Call us on +64 21 123 4567 about your NZBN application
should_not_match.description: NZ phone number near the NZBN keyword but not label-attached and not 94-prefixed

false_positives.description: 13-digit runs are common — NZ phone numbers written with country code, EAN-13 barcodes (which share the GS1 GLN format and 94-prefix space), card-number fragments and timestamps all collide with an unlabelled NZBN.
false_positives.mitigation: The regex only matches when the number is directly attached to an NZBN label; there is no bare tier. EAN-13 product barcodes beginning 94 are the closest collision but rarely appear label-attached to "NZBN".

false_positives.description: The GS1 mod-10 check digit is not enforced in the exported SIT, so a label-attached 13-digit 94-prefixed number with an invalid check digit still matches, and repeated-digit sentinels pass any weighted-mod checksum.
false_positives.mitigation: AllDigitsSameFilter drops repeated-digit values; downstream consumers can verify candidates against the NZBN register API for authoritative validation.

patterns.risk_description: The NZBN rule requires an NZBN or New Zealand Business Number label directly attached to a 94-prefixed thirteen-digit business identifier. NZBNs are public entity references used for registry, invoicing, and trading-party verification and do not identify a private individual merely because a business may be closely held. A copied number can support company-document linkage or supplier impersonation, but meaningful loss requires representative details, payment instructions, or access to a business workflow. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL reflect the low standalone harm; confidential ownership, banking, tax, or transaction records would raise the context toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low for a public New Zealand business identifier. SENSITIVE is not met because the NZBN alone contains no personal dossier, credential, financial result, or authority to act for the entity.

generic.rationale: Low classification and Low DLM fit a public registry number with modest linkage and spoofing utility. Any sensitive handling must arise from the private business, banking, ownership, or transaction information accompanying it.

patterns.name: Payroll Master File with Tax File Numbers

patterns.operation: Regex for canonical nine-digit TFN format within 300 characters of payroll keywords (payroll, TFN, tax file, salary). High confidence when multiple validated TFNs appear in the same document indicating a bulk file.
patterns.confidence_justification: High confidence: checksum-valid TFN-format numbers co-occurring with payroll context keywords and BSB patterns in a document strongly indicates a payroll master file. The TFN validator plus sentinel/test filters reduce generic digit-run, phone-number, and placeholder false positives.

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a bulk payroll master file through validated Australian TFNs near payroll terms, salary information, and bank-account or BSB context, with multiple TFNs increasing confidence. Disclosure can enable coordinated identity theft, fraudulent tax filings, payroll diversion, and highly targeted social engineering against employees. The intended unit is a composite employee dataset rather than one TFN, although a single onboarding form and aggregate payroll summary are documented false positives. Risk 8 SENSITIVE preserves the accepted serious bulk-record outcome; PROTECTED would require evidence that the matched file's scale or privilege creates significant damage beyond the normal payroll extract.

classification.rationale: Risk 8 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Financial, SENS_Fin, and Medium because validated TFNs, payroll values, and banking context expose a composite employee dataset that can support coordinated fraud. PROTECTED is not met unless record scale, privileged scope, or foreseeable consequence establishes significant damage beyond a normal payroll extract.

generic.rationale: Generic Medium and Medium Financial handling fit a payroll master extract with serious multi-person fraud and privacy consequences. Generic High would require demonstrated large-scale or high-consequence coverage rather than the classifier label alone.

patterns.name: Philippine Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN)
patterns.description: Detects Philippine Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN) issued by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) under Section 236(j) of the National Internal Revenue Code. The base TIN is a 9-digit number (the 9th digit is a check digit), usually written XXX-XXX-XXX. Registered businesses append a branch code — historically 3 digits (000 for the head office, 12 digits total) and, since eBIRForms v7.9.6.0 (RMC No. 36-2026, April 2026), up to 5 digits (14 digits total).
patterns.operation: Regex pattern. Matches a 9-digit TIN with optional dash or space group separators (XXX-XXX-XXX) and an optional 3-digit or 5-digit branch-code suffix (XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX or XXX-XXX-XXX-XXXXX). The 9th-digit checksum algorithm is not publicly documented and is NOT enforced in this regex-only pattern; detection is structural. Because bare 9-14 digit runs are ambiguous, every confidence tier requires positive TIN/BIR evidence: High (85) requires a TIN/BIR label-context match plus specific keywords with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires specific TIN/BIR keywords with template exclusion; Low (65) requires domain-context tax keywords with template exclusion. AllDigitsSameFilter suppresses all-zeros and other repeated-digit values.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the 9/12/14-digit structure with optional dash grouping is common enough in unrelated numeric data (order numbers, phone fragments, other countries' IDs) that corroborating TIN/BIR keywords are required on every tier. The dash-separated XXX-XXX-XXX form plus label evidence raises precision substantially; no bare value-only tier is exposed.

should_not_match.description: 16-digit payment-card run — no 9/12/14-digit boundary match inside a longer digit run

All-zeros TIN — matches structurally but is suppressed by AllDigitsSameFilter

false_positives.description: Bare 9-digit or 12-digit runs (US SSNs written without dashes, order numbers, PhilSys numbers in 4-4-4 grouping collapse to the same 12-digit run when unseparated) can match the structural regex.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires TIN/BIR keyword or label evidence within the 300-character proximity window; no value-only tier is exposed.

false_positives.description: The 9th digit is a BIR check digit whose algorithm is not publicly documented and cannot be expressed in regex, so structurally valid but non-issued numbers will match.
false_positives.mitigation: Rely on structure, AllDigitsSameFilter (suppresses all-zeros/repeated-digit values, which defeat checksum-free matching) and mandatory keyword evidence.

false_positives.description: A longer dashed number such as 123-456-789-0001 partially matches on its 9-digit core.
false_positives.mitigation: Keyword gating limits this to documents already discussing Philippine tax identifiers.

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds Philippine nine-digit base TINs with optional three- or five-digit branch codes, requires BIR or tax context, and suppresses repeated-digit placeholders without validating the unpublished check digit. A genuine individual TIN can support taxpayer impersonation, fraudulent registration or filing, and correlation across employment and tax records. The normal unit is one taxpayer identifier with credible moderate financial and identity harm, although entity and branch forms as well as unrelated digit runs can also match. Risk 7 and SENSITIVE are justified, while PROTECTED is not met without authentication data, a complete tax file, bulk taxpayer records, or significant fiscal-system compromise.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, and SENSITIVE Financial because a genuine Philippine TIN can directly facilitate tax and identity fraud against a taxpayer. PROTECTED is not met because the number alone does not grant account access or establish broad, high-impact compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium generic classification and Medium Financial DLM fit a taxpayer identifier with moderate fraud value but no standalone authentication or tax-record content.

patterns.name: PESEL
patterns.description: Detects PESEL patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Validation: Weighted sum mod 10. Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PESEL Corroborative evidence: 3 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: pattern has structural constraints but corroborative keywords are recommended to reduce false positive rates.

should_match.description: Standard PESEL number
Alternate PESEL
PESEL for 2000s-born person

should_not_match.description: Only 10 digits instead of 11
12 digits instead of 11
Contains a letter instead of all digits

false_positives.description: Long numeric sequences in unrelated contexts (tracking numbers, serial codes) matching the PESEL format
false_positives.mitigation: Use corroborative keywords and, where available, checksum validation to filter false matches.

patterns.risk_description: A PESEL match is an eleven-digit Polish population identifier checked with a weighted Mod-10 rule and supported by civic terminology, not a resident register extract. With the holder's name and other identity details it could facilitate impersonation, but the number alone does not authenticate a service. One person is normally affected, while unrelated tracking or serial numbers can still resemble the structure. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL preserve bounded atomic harm; linkage to health, financial, benefits, or full identity records would raise the sensitivity.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because a PESEL is one validated reference without the underlying citizen record or credentials. SENSITIVE is not met without a confirmed person and substantive government, financial, or authentication information.

generic.rationale: The PESEL is generically Low with Low DLM because consequential identity harm depends on corroborating personal data and an access or transaction context.

patterns.name: Poland Physical Addresses
patterns.description: Detects Poland Physical Addresses patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type that uses machine learning and function-based detection for physical address identification. This keyword list provides address-related terms for supplementary matching.
patterns.operation: Function-based detection in Microsoft Purview. This pattern uses keyword matching for country-specific address terminology to identify physical address data.
patterns.confidence_justification: Low confidence: broad keyword matching on address terms requires additional context and corroborative evidence for accurate physical address detection. Address keywords alone produce high false positive rates without structural validation.

should_match.description: Contains address keyword 'ulica'
Contains address keyword 'aleja'
Contains address keyword 'plac'

should_not_match.value: quarterly financial report for fiscal year 2024
should_not_match.description: Business text with no address keywords

should_not_match.value: the meeting is scheduled for next Tuesday morning
should_not_match.description: Scheduling text with no address terminology

false_positives.description: References to street names in non-address contexts such as business names or landmarks
false_positives.mitigation: Require structural address patterns (number + street type + name) rather than isolated keyword matches.

false_positives.description: Navigation or mapping references that mention road types without containing actual addresses
false_positives.mitigation: Use proximity-based corroborative evidence to ensure keywords appear alongside numeric components.

patterns.risk_description: The Polish address list searches for ulica, aleja, and plac around numbers or location wording. Those terms can identify public streets, avenues, squares, transport points, companies, and landmarks without establishing that a person lives there. A normal Polish address has limited standalone sensitivity and needs a named occupant, private relationship, or sensitive purpose to support harassment or discrimination. Risk 3 supports OFFICIAL; SENSITIVE would require a confidential residence, vulnerable individual, protected institution, repeated visit pattern, or aggregated personal address records.

classification.rationale: Risk 3 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because Polish street and square cues predominantly describe public geography. SENSITIVE is not met without private attribution, safety implications, sensitive activity, or aggregation.

generic.rationale: Polish physical-address indicators are generically Low with Low DLM because public-place names require additional identity and occupancy context for material harm.

patterns.name: REGON
patterns.description: Detects REGON patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/sit-defn-poland-regon-number Corroborative evidence: 3 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: pattern has structural constraints but corroborative keywords are recommended to reduce false positive rates.

should_match.description: Nine-digit REGON (small entity)
Fourteen-digit REGON (local unit)
Another nine-digit REGON

should_not_match.description: Too few digits (8)
Invalid length (10 digits)

false_positives.description: Nine-digit or fourteen-digit numeric sequences may match phone numbers or other administrative references.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords such as "REGON" within the proximity window.

false_positives.description: In multiple languages, similar terminology used in formal or administrative contexts (education, professional documentation) that does not constitute sensitive data collection.
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with additional contextual signals such as structured identifiers, form fields, or database column headers to distinguish sensitive records from general references.

patterns.risk_description: A REGON match is a nine- or fourteen-digit Polish statistical registration number for a business or organisation, not a personal identity credential. It could be copied into sham company paperwork, but the value is organisation-level registration data and does not establish authority over the entity or its funds. The normal impact concerns one enterprise, with fraud requiring names, contacts, banking details, or transaction instructions, while generic numeric references can collide. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL retain bounded business risk; confidential company records or payment authority would raise the classification.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 reconciles to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because REGON is an organisation registration identifier rather than personal-privacy data. SENSITIVE is not met without confidential corporate information, transaction authority, or linked data about identifiable individuals.

generic.rationale: The REGON is generically Low with Low DLM because organisation registration data has limited standalone confidentiality value and misuse needs broader corporate or payment context.

patterns.name: Poland Tax Identification Number
patterns.description: Detects Poland Tax Identification Number patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Due to the numeric format, corroborative evidence keywords are essential for reliable detection.
patterns.operation: Corroborative evidence: 5 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: tax-id, pl-financial.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the 3-3-2-2 digit grouping pattern with optional hyphens is somewhat distinctive but can match other formatted numbers. Keywords like 'NIP' improve accuracy.

should_match.description: Polish NIP with hyphens
Polish NIP continuous digits
Polish tax ID with separators

should_not_match.description: Only 9 digits, too short for Polish NIP
Wrong grouping for Polish NIP format

false_positives.description: Generic numeric sequences in non-tax contexts such as reference numbers or account identifiers
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords within the proximity window to distinguish tax identifiers from general numeric data.

false_positives.description: Numbers from other identification schemes with similar digit patterns
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with jurisdiction-specific detection to prioritise matches in tax-related documents and cross-reference with other identifier types.

patterns.risk_description: The Polish detector matches a ten-digit NIP, optionally in its 3-3-2-2 grouping, when Polish tax terminology is nearby. NIP is chiefly used for businesses and taxable economic activity, so it is often present on invoices and public or shared registration material rather than representing a private personal dossier. Reuse may help fabricate supplier paperwork or link business records, but meaningful fraud requires entity details, bank instructions, and access to a filing or payment process. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL capture that bounded business risk; private tax filings, sensitive sole-trader records, or live payment changes would raise the context toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low for one contextual Polish NIP. SENSITIVE is not met by the identifier alone because it neither establishes a confidential taxpayer record nor authorizes tax or banking action.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM reflect a commonly exchanged business tax reference with limited independent confidentiality. The filing, invoice, banking, or sole-trader information around it determines any stronger protection.

patterns.name: Police Body Worn Camera Metadata
patterns.description: Detects metadata records from police body-worn camera (BWC) systems including activation timestamps, officer identification, incident cross-references, and footage catalogue entries. This pattern targets the metadata and logs, NOT the footage itself. BWC metadata reveals which officers attended which incidents, activation patterns, and evidence chain-of-custody details.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary keywords (body worn camera, BWC, activation log, footage reference, officer ID, incident link) within 300 characters of metadata fields such as timestamps, officer identifiers, and incident reference numbers. Negative keyword exclusion for BWC policy documents and procurement tenders.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: requires co-occurrence of BWC-specific metadata terminology with officer identification and incident reference numbers. Policy documents and tenders discuss BWC in general terms without activation logs or specific officer-incident linkages.

patterns.risk_description: This detector targets body-worn-camera metadata and catalogue records, not footage, including officer identity, device ID, activation time, GPS location, incident link, evidence reference, and activation patterns. Disclosure can reveal which officers attended an event, when recording started or stopped, and how evidence maps to an operation, supporting witness coordination, officer targeting, or challenges to custody and completeness. Public policy, procurement, effectiveness research, and deployment announcements are excluded, while a normal match remains metadata for a bounded incident or reporting period. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require covert-team movements, protected locations, or system-wide evidence-catalogue compromise.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium because attributed activation and incident metadata can prejudice evidence handling and expose officer movements. PROTECTED is not met without covert, protected-location, or system-scale compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium Legal DLM protect officer-linked evidentiary metadata while distinguishing it from the footage itself or a complete covert evidence platform.

patterns.name: Police Use-of-Force Investigation (Internal)
patterns.description: Detects internal investigation documents of police use of lethal or serious force, including compelled officer statements under s.7.2 PPRA and Ethical Standards Command evidence before investigation completion.
patterns.operation: Primary: use-of-force investigation phrases (critical incident investigation/report/review, police shooting investigation, use of force investigation, Ethical Standards Command, ESC investigation, discharge of firearm report, lethal force review). 65 = phrase only (discovery). 75 = phrase plus a populated person/file field (officer, witness, subject, name, date of birth, file/case number) or a labelled file reference. 85 = phrase plus two distinct populated fields plus independent evidence (self-incrimination notice, s.7.2 PPRA, compelled statement, body-worn camera, tactical assessment, CCC oversight). Media, annual report and training framing excluded.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: enforcement requires populated internal-investigation fields; ESC file numbers are unpublished, so the reference is a documented label-anchored fallback.

customisation.note: Replace the documented labelled-reference fallback with the customer's real format (see docs/identifiers.md#case-reference-number). Earlier versions used the ESC-YYYY-NNNN format, which does not appear in any published source.

patterns.risk_description: This detector identifies an incomplete internal investigation into police lethal or serious force, including subject officers, compelled statements, body-worn evidence, tactical assessments, and Ethical Standards Command findings. Disclosure can prejudice parallel criminal or coronial processes, expose witnesses and officers, undermine procedural fairness, and allow evidence or testimony to be coordinated before investigators finish. Published oversight findings, media reporting, and training are excluded, leaving one bounded internal matter rather than a force-wide integrity system. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require protected witnesses, immediate retaliation risk, or compromise of multiple major investigations.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium because compelled evidence and preliminary findings can materially prejudice a serious internal inquiry. PROTECTED is not met without protected-person danger or significant multi-investigation compromise.

generic.rationale: Medium and Medium Legal DLM protect compelled statements, officer details, and unresolved findings while reserving High treatment for broader integrity or life-safety compromise.

patterns.risk_description: The proximity detector targets pre-award tender evaluation matrices that combine procurement terms, bidder scoring, comparative pricing, value-for-money analysis, recommendations, and probity or confidentiality context. Disclosure can reveal each bidder's commercial position and the evaluation committee's reasoning, enabling bid manipulation, collusion, challenge strategy, or unfair negotiating advantage before award. The normal unit is a multi-bidder composite evaluation for one procurement and creates serious financial and integrity harm, while published notices and blank scoring templates are excluded where possible. Risk 8 SENSITIVE Financial is justified; PROTECTED is not met without a strategically critical procurement, protected operation, or credible significant government-wide damage.

classification.rationale: Nonpublic bidder pricing and comparative tender evaluations. Existing classification level retained.

generic.rationale: Generic Medium Commercial-in-Confidence handling protects confidential bidder pricing, weighted scores, evaluation reasoning, and recommendations within a defined competitive procurement.

patterns.risk_description: A Portuguese Citizen Card match is a structured alphanumeric card number with Portuguese civic context, not an image of the Cartao de Cidadao or its chip data. It can help an attacker make an identity claim more convincing when paired with a name and other attributes, but the number alone does not authenticate the holder. The ordinary exposure affects one person, and the mixed format is distinctive enough to limit unrelated matches. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect bounded atomic harm; a card copy, digital certificate, or full identity profile would be more sensitive.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because the detector returns one Portuguese card number without the document, certificate, or credentials. SENSITIVE is not met without correlated biographical, financial, or authentication data.

generic.rationale: The Portuguese Citizen Card number is generically Low with Low DLM because material identity misuse needs a verified holder and additional document or account context.

patterns.risk_description: Portugal's licence detector looks for one or two uppercase letters, a separator, and a six- or seven-digit tail in driving-licence context, rather than a card image or driver history. A disclosed number could make a vehicle-hire enquiry or identity-verification pretext more credible when combined with the driver's name, date of birth, and issuing details. One ordinary match concerns a single licence holder, and similarly shaped administrative codes can be caught despite the contextual controls. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL cover that limited facilitation risk; a copied licence, credentials, or a linked infringement record would move the information into SENSITIVE territory.

patterns.description: Detects Portugal Tax Identification Number patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Due to the numeric format, corroborative evidence keywords are essential for reliable detection.
patterns.operation: Corroborative evidence: 5 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: tax-id, pt-financial.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: nine-digit numbers are common. Portuguese NIF keywords like 'NIF' or 'contribuinte' are required for reliable detection.

should_match.description: Nine-digit Portuguese NIF
Portuguese tax identification number
Portuguese NIF format

should_not_match.description: Eight digits, too short for Portuguese NIF
Ten digits, exceeds Portuguese NIF format

false_positives.description: Generic numeric sequences in non-tax contexts such as reference numbers or account identifiers
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords within the proximity window to distinguish tax identifiers from general numeric data.

false_positives.description: Numbers from other identification schemes with similar digit patterns
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with jurisdiction-specific detection to prioritise matches in tax-related documents and cross-reference with other identifier types.

patterns.risk_description: The Portugal pattern detects a nine-digit NIF when contribuinte, NIF, or other Portuguese tax language is present. The number is routinely requested in purchases and administration and may identify a person or organization, so exposure can support record linkage, false documentation, or a tailored tax-themed approach. It does not disclose a return, income, debt, payment method, or authenticated tax-service access, and nine-digit references are otherwise common. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit that bounded correlation value; connection to private fiscal records, refund instructions, or a complete identity file would raise the context toward SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, DLM OFFICIAL, and Low for one Portuguese NIF. SENSITIVE is not met because the number is commonly exchanged and harmful use still requires holder identity, confidential tax facts, credentials, or transactional context.

generic.rationale: Low classification and Low DLM reflect the NIF's bounded standalone linkage and impersonation value. Returns, assessments, payment records, and taxpayer-account credentials are separate, more sensitive units.

patterns.name: بطاقة الهوية القطرية
patterns.description: Detects بطاقة الهوية القطرية patterns. This pattern is based on a Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information type. Users already running Purview may prefer to enable the built-in SIT directly, or use this version as a starting point for customisation.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/sit-defn-qatari-id-card-number Corroborative evidence: 4 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials. Uses additional domain-context evidence and explicit exclusion logic for template/sample/test text.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: pattern has structural constraints but corroborative keywords are recommended to reduce false positive rates. Added context gating and exclusion rules improve precision and reduce incidental matches.

should_match.description: Qatari ID card number
Another Qatari ID
Valid format Qatari ID

should_not_match.description: Too few digits (10)
Too many digits (12)

should_not_match.value: template example placeholder record identifier
should_not_match.description: Template/sample context should be excluded even when anchor words are present

false_positives.description: Eleven-digit numeric sequences may match phone numbers or other administrative identifiers.
false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords such as "QID" or "Qatar ID" within the proximity window.

false_positives.description: In multiple languages, similar terminology used in formal or administrative contexts (education, professional documentation) that does not constitute sensitive data collection.
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with additional contextual signals such as structured identifiers, form fields, or database column headers to distinguish sensitive records from general references.

patterns.risk_description: A Qatari identity-card match is an eleven-digit personal number found with Arabic or local civic terminology, not a scan of the card or a resident file. It could support identity impersonation when paired with the holder's name and other attributes, but the number alone does not authorise a service. The normal exposure concerns one person, and phone or administrative identifiers can share the same length. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL reflect bounded atomic harm; a card copy or linked immigration, financial, or identity record would raise the sensitivity.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low tiers because one Qatari card number contains no complete identity document or credentials. SENSITIVE is not met without a confirmed holder and substantive biographical, financial, immigration, or access data.

generic.rationale: The Qatari identity number is generically Low with Low DLM because consequential misuse requires additional personal attributes and an account or transaction context.

patterns.name: QLD Treasury Pre-Release Budget Allocation
patterns.description: Detects unreleased Queensland state budget allocation figures, forward estimates, and expenditure projections. These are market-moving documents that enable insider trading on government-linked securities if disclosed prematurely.
patterns.operation: Keyword proximity: primary financial keywords (budget, forward estimates, appropriation) within 300 characters of Treasury context keywords (Queensland Treasury, QTC, CBRC) and dollar amounts or allocation terms. Requires pre-release markers (draft, pre-release, not for distribution, PROTECTED).
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: co-occurrence of Treasury-specific terms with pre-release markers and dollar amounts in a document context makes false positives unlikely. Published budget documents are excluded by negative keywords.

should_match.value: PROTECTED - Queensland Treasury - CBRC Budget Submission Draft FY26-27. Total new appropriation request: $2,450M across capital program and recurrent expenditure. Forward estimates show growth of 3.2% over the forward estimates period. NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION.
should_match.description: Pre-release CBRC budget submission with dollar amounts and Treasury context

should_match.value: Draft budget allocation — Queensland Treasury Corporation. Capital program allocation $890M for transport infrastructure. This document is pre-release and must not be distributed outside authorised Treasury personnel.
should_match.description: QTC draft budget with capital allocation figures

should_match.value: PROTECTED. Forward Estimates Update - QLD Treasury. Revised appropriation: Health $18.2B, Education $14.7B, Transport $6.3B. Draft — not for publication until Treasurer's budget speech.
should_match.description: Forward estimates update with department allocations

should_not_match.value: Queensland Budget 2025-26 — Budget Paper No. 2: Capital Statement. Published by Queensland Treasury. Total capital program: $55.6 billion over four years.
should_not_match.description: Published budget paper — public document, not pre-release

should_not_match.value: The department's annual report shows expenditure of $1.2B against a budget allocation of $1.3B, representing an underspend of $100M.
should_not_match.description: Annual report referencing past budget — routine operational document

should_not_match.value: Budget template for FY2026 submissions. Departments should use this template to prepare their forward estimates. Example: allocation $XXX,XXX.
should_not_match.description: Template document with placeholder values, not real budget data

should_not_match.value: PROTECTED — Draft. Internal budget summary: departmental expenditure of $3.8M against an allocation of $4.1M for the period. Not for distribution — working figures only.
should_not_match.description: shared financial substrate without distinctive signature must not fire

false_positives.description: Published budget papers and budget-related media releases that reference Treasury and dollar amounts
false_positives.mitigation: Exclude documents containing 'published', 'media release', 'budget paper no', 'annual report', 'publicly available' using negative keyword list

false_positives.description: Budget submission templates with placeholder amounts
false_positives.mitigation: Exclude documents containing 'template', 'example', 'placeholder', '$XXX' patterns

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a pre-release Queensland budget allocation or forward-estimate record by combining fiscal terms, Treasury or QTC context, monetary values, and explicit draft or restricted markers. Premature disclosure can enable market positioning, insider dealing, lobbying advantage, and disruption of Cabinet or fiscal announcement processes before the figures are public. The normal true positive is a substantive government financial record rather than an atomic amount, and its impact can extend across agencies, counterparties, and markets. Risk 10 PROTECTED is justified because authentic unreleased allocation material can create broad market and government consequence; no higher confidentiality tier exists in this schema.

classification.rationale: Risk 10 aligns with PSPF PROTECTED, QGISCF PROTECTED, the PROTECTED Financial DLM, PROT_Fin, and the High tier because the classifier requires a pre-release, market-sensitive composite budget record with potential for significant government and market damage. This is the top accepted tier; the key deployment control is distinguishing unreleased material from published budget papers.

generic.rationale: Generic High and High Financial handling are warranted for an unreleased sovereign budget decision record capable of broad market and public-administration impact. Published allocations lose that confidentiality, but the detector's intended pre-release unit remains high consequence.

patterns.name: QPS Incident Report
patterns.description: Detects Queensland Police Service (QPS) incident reports containing operational details about reported offences, informant information, and occurrence records. These are non-covert operational documents that are sensitive due to informant and victim details but do not involve covert methodology or life-safety risks.
patterns.operation: Primary: incident report phrases (QPS incident report, occurrence number/report, reporting officer, offence code, QPRIME entry/reference/record). 65 = phrase only (discovery). 75 = phrase plus a populated incident field (occurrence number, QPRIME reference, reporting/attending officer, informant, complainant, victim, witness, suspect, offence code, date of occurrence, location, badge ...) or a QPRIME occurrence number (QP + 10 digits). 85 = phrase plus two distinct populated fields plus independent evidence (witness statement, CCTV, forensic examination, statutory declaration, patrol group, badge number ...). Media releases, statistics, fiction and training framing excluded.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: enforcement requires a populated incident record or a QPRIME occurrence number; phrase-only mentions stay at discovery.

Date of Occurrence: 14 February 2026. Offence Code: 0711 — Assault Occasioning Bodily Harm. Informant: Ms J. Williams attended Fortitude Valley station at 2245hrs. QPRIME entry created.
should_match.description: QPS incident report with occurrence number, reporting officer details, and QPRIME reference (reaches 85)

should_not_match.value: Policy guidance: the reporting officer must record the occurrence number and offence code for every incident before the end of shift.

false_positives.description: Published QPS annual statistical reviews and crime reports
false_positives.mitigation: Negative keyword exclusion: 'annual report', 'statistical review', 'published'. Require proximity to specific occurrence numbers.

false_positives.description: QPS media releases about charged persons and completed investigations
false_positives.mitigation: Negative keyword exclusion: 'media release', 'charged', 'will appear in court', 'sentenced'

false_positives.description: Crime fiction and television scripts referencing police terminology
false_positives.mitigation: Negative keyword exclusion: 'novel', 'fiction', 'screenplay', 'episode'

false_positives.description: Police training manuals and academy materials
false_positives.mitigation: Negative keyword exclusion: 'training manual', 'academy', 'exercise', 'scenario'

patterns.risk_description: The detector identifies a Queensland Police incident or QPRIME occurrence report containing an offence, location, reporting officer, victim, informant, witness, person of interest, forensic request, and operational reference. Disclosure can expose affected people, alert suspects, enable witness coordination, or reveal preliminary facts and evidence before a routine investigation is complete. Published statistics, media releases, fiction, and academy training are excluded, and the pattern expressly targets non-covert reports rather than protected methodology or source identities. Risk 7 supports SENSITIVE Legal; PROTECTED would require covert sources, protected witnesses, immediate safety danger, or compromise across a major operation.

classification.rationale: Risk 7 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL: Sensitive, QGISCF SENSITIVE, SENSITIVE Legal, and Medium because an occurrence report exposes attributed allegations, locations, witnesses, and preliminary evidence. PROTECTED is not met without covert-source, protected-person, acute safety, or major-operation consequences.

generic.rationale: Medium with Medium Legal DLM protects person-linked incident and evidentiary details while distinguishing routine occurrence reporting from covert or life-critical intelligence.
