patterns.name: US Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
patterns.description: Detects US Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs) issued by the IRS to individuals who are required to have a US taxpayer identification number but are not eligible for a Social Security Number. ITINs always begin with the digit 9, and the fourth and fifth digits fall in the range 70-99, distinguishing them from SSNs. The pattern matches both formatted (9XX-7X-XXXX) and unformatted (9XX7XXXXX) variants.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://support.taxslayerpro.com/hc/en-us/articles/8250466982554-Valid-Range-for-ITINs Corroborative evidence: 4 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials, financial-transaction.
patterns.confidence_justification: The ITIN format is well-defined by the IRS with a unique structure starting with 9 and having fourth-fifth digits in the 70-99 range. This specificity, combined with corroborative keyword proximity, provides high-confidence identification with low false positive rates.

should_match.description: ITIN with group digits 78 (valid 70-88 block)
ITIN with group digits 50 (valid 50-65 block, space-delimited)
Unformatted ITIN with group digits 94 (valid 94-99 block)

should_not_match.description: Group digits 12 outside the valid ITIN ranges (50-65, 70-88, 90-92, 94-99)
First digit is not 9; this is not an ITIN
Group digits 89 fall in the 89 gap (88 is the last valid in the 70-88 block)
Group digits 93 fall in the 93 gap (92 then 94 are valid, not 93)

false_positives.description: SSN range overlap for 9xx area numbers that coincidentally have group digits in the 70-99 range
false_positives.mitigation: Use corroborative keyword proximity (e.g., 'ITIN', 'taxpayer identification') to distinguish ITINs from SSNs, and cross-reference against SSN detection patterns

patterns.risk_description: The detector finds a formatted or unformatted US ITIN beginning with 9 and using the permitted 70-99 fourth-and-fifth-digit range, supported by civic and transaction context. A valid ITIN can strengthen tax fraud, identity matching, or impersonation when combined with the taxpayer name, birth details, and filing information. The number does not authenticate an IRS account or reveal a tax return, and some Social Security number ranges can overlap the structure. Risk 5 OFFICIAL reflects bounded identifier harm requiring further data; SENSITIVE would require a linked taxpayer record, access credential, or direct material consequence.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 coherently maps to OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, the OFFICIAL DLM, OFFI, and Low because an ITIN is an identity and tax linkage identifier rather than a credential or filing. The atomic value does not by itself reach SENSITIVE impact.

generic.rationale: Generic Low with Low DLM treatment fits a taxpayer identifier whose serious misuse depends on additional personal and filing data. Generic Medium would require that linked record or direct account access.

patterns.name: NPI
patterns.description: Detects US National Provider Identifier (NPI) values structurally: a ten-digit number beginning with 1 or 2. Detection is structural only — the NPI Luhn checksum (80840 prefix) is NOT enforced. Confidence comes from healthcare context tiers (NPI-specific terms at 85, broader provider/claims context at 75, bare shape discovery-only at 65), and an all-same-digit guard rejects repeated-digit values such as 1111111111.
patterns.operation: Checksum: Luhn with 80840 prefix (NOT enforced in this regex-only pattern; structural detection only). Reference: https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Administrative-Simplification/NationalProvIdentStand/Downloads/NPIcheckdigit.pdf Corroborative evidence: 19 keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: healthcare-identifiers.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: the bare shape \b[12]\d{9}\b is a common 10-digit form and is only discovery-only without healthcare context. Even with NPI/provider keywords, the Luhn checksum is not enforced, so medium confidence is honest until a checksum-backed revision lands. Risk rating remains 3 (OFFICIAL) per v25 authoritative assessment of the structural detector.

NPI starting with 2
NPI-checksum-valid value with non-repeating digits

should_not_match.description: Starts with 3 (must start with 1 or 2)
Starts with 0 (must start with 1 or 2)
Only 9 digits instead of 10

false_positives.mitigation: Require corroborative evidence keywords confirming patient context. Look for co-occurrence with patient identifiers such as medical record numbers or dates of birth.

false_positives.description: General wellness and fitness content using medical vocabulary without constituting protected health information.
false_positives.mitigation: Layer with patient identifier patterns or healthcare-specific document structure detection to distinguish clinical records from general health content.

patterns.risk_description: The NPI pattern finds a ten-digit U.S. healthcare provider identifier beginning with 1 or 2 and supported by healthcare context; the regex does not enforce the published checksum. NPIs are provider administration references used openly in directories and claims, so a normal match identifies a practitioner or organisation rather than revealing a patient's condition. Misuse generally requires separate credentials, payee details, or claim access, although a false association could create administrative inconvenience for the provider. Risk 3 and OFFICIAL capture this low standalone harm; a credential set, fraudulent billing package, or patient-linked claim would cross into SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 3 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because an NPI is a public provider identifier and the detector does not establish patient data or account control. SENSITIVE is not met without credentials, claims, payment data, or confidential provider records.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM fit a public administrative identifier whose disclosure is normally reversible and low impact. Correlated claim or access information should be classified separately.

patterns.name: US Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects US passport numbers in exactly two accepted formats: a nine-digit numeric value (older US passports), or a single uppercase letter followed by exactly eight digits (newer passport books and cards). Bare eight-digit values and letter-plus-nine-digit values are not valid US passport numbers. Due to the relatively simple format, corroborative keyword proximity is strongly recommended to reduce false positives. Keywords are US-scoped (passport / US passport / State Department); foreign-passport labels are not treated as US passport evidence.
patterns.operation: Reference: https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/passports/passport-help/next-generation-passport.html Corroborative evidence: US-scoped passport and travel-document keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: pii-civic-credentials.
patterns.confidence_justification: The US passport number format is short and loosely structured, consisting of an optional letter followed by 8-9 digits. This simplicity means the pattern can match many unrelated numeric strings such as reference codes, invoice numbers, and account identifiers. Medium confidence is appropriate; strong corroborative keyword proximity is essential for reliable detection.

Letter plus nine digits is the unsupported long cross-product

Leakage could help fill a booking or identity-verification form and make a targeted pretext more convincing after the traveller's biographical details are known. A normal match exposes one reference value, while invoices, account identifiers, and serial codes frequently share the short numeric shape. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL are proportionate; SENSITIVE would require the passport data page, credentials, or a joined identity and itinerary record.

patterns.name: US Phone Number
patterns.description: Detects North American Numbering Plan (NANP) telephone numbers in US contexts: the domestic NPA-NXX-XXXX form (bracketed, hyphenated, dotted, spaced, or bare, with an optional leading trunk "1") and the international +1 NPA-NXX-XXXX form. Area-code (NPA) and exchange-code (NXX) groups are constrained to a leading digit of 2-9 with the N11 service-code shape (211/311/411/511/611/711/811/911) excluded from both groups, per NANPA's published format rules. NANP area codes are drawn from a single pool shared by the US, Canada, and Caribbean member territories — the digit structure itself cannot distinguish a US number from a Canadian one (see ca-phone-number for the sibling pattern). Differentiation between the two patterns is by jurisdiction/regulation metadata and country-specific corroborative evidence keywords only, not by regex — this is the documented convention for the whole NANP pair.
patterns.operation: Validation: none (NANP has no checksum; structural leading-digit and N11-exclusion constraints reduce but do not eliminate digit collision with other 10-digit identifiers). Reference: North American Numbering Plan Administration (NANPA), https://www.nanpa.com/. Corroborative evidence: keywords within 300 characters. Keyword lists: phone-context. Both the domestic and international (+1) sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier — no tier fires without positive corroborative evidence, per the phone-family convention — see confidence_justification.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: NPA/NXX leading-digit constraints (2-9) and N11 exclusion narrow the format meaningfully, but NANP numbers carry no checksum and a 10-digit US-shaped sequence still collides with invoice numbers, order numbers, and other structured identifiers. Per the phone-family convention set by au-fixed-line-telephone (every tier requires positive corroborative evidence; high digit-collision formats never get a zero-evidence tier), both the domestic and +1 international sub-regexes are evidence-gated at every tier: 75 requires generic phone-context evidence and 85 requires country-specific phone keywords with template/noise exclusion. The literal +1 prefix improves precision when present but is not by itself sufficient gating.

should_match.description: Domestic bracketed NYC area code with fictional NANPA 555-01XX exchange
Domestic hyphenated San Francisco area code
International +1 form, Washington DC area code, space-separated
Domestic bare digits with no separators, Chicago area code

should_not_match.description: Area code starts with 1 (NPA must start 2-9, not 0 or 1)
Exchange code is 911, an N11 service code, excluded from the NXX position
Only exchange + subscriber digits, no area code — not a full 10-digit number
Valid-shaped digit run embedded inside a longer reference number, rejected by digit boundaries

false_positives.description: A bare 10-digit sequence with NPA/NXX leading digits in the 2-9 range and no N11 shape can still coincidentally match invoice numbers, tracking numbers, or other structured identifiers of the same length and leading-digit distribution.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier — for both the domestic and +1 international sub-regexes — requires positive phone-context or country-specific evidence within 300 characters; no zero-evidence tier exists, so a bare digit run without corroborating context never fires at any confidence level.

false_positives.description: NANP area codes are shared across the US, Canada, and Caribbean NANP member territories, so this pattern's regex will also structurally match Canadian- or Caribbean-issued numbers with no way to tell from the digits alone.
false_positives.mitigation: Deploy alongside ca-phone-number using each pattern's jurisdiction-specific evidence keywords (e.g. "US phone number" vs "Canadian phone number") to bias classification, and rely on surrounding document context (postal addresses, currency, entity names) for jurisdiction attribution rather than the number itself.

false_positives.description: The domestic sub-regex also fires inside the +1 international rendering (empirically verified: in "+1 212 555 0134" it matches the "1 212 555 0134" substring, because the optional trunk-1 branch starts right after the "+", which is not a digit), so an international value produces a domestic-tier match as well as an international-tier match.
false_positives.mitigation: Benign co-fire, left in place deliberately: both sub-regexes carry identical evidence gating and confidence levels, so the duplicate match cannot inflate confidence — it can only duplicate a finding at the same level, which reporting layers de-duplicate by offset. A structural fix would need variable-width negative lookbehind (to reject "+1 " at any separator width), which the universal engine target does not support.

patterns.risk_description: The pattern recognizes ten-digit NANP phone shapes with valid NPA and exchange leading digits, optional country code, parentheses, and separators, but it cannot establish that the number belongs to the United States rather than another NANP territory. A real contact can support robocalls, phishing, messaging discovery, or correlation with a person's identity and location. The normal unit is one individual or business number and meaningful harm needs companion identity, vulnerability, or account context; tracking and invoice numbers can share the same shape. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL capture bounded standalone exposure, while a confidential vulnerable-person contact, sensitive case linkage, or aggregated directory would reach SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because one NANP-shaped contact number is neither an authenticator nor a complete identity record. SENSITIVE is not met without sensitive linkage, vulnerable-person targeting, persistent harassment, or bulk aggregation capable of moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low and Low DLM suit one US or NANP contact number with limited independent confidentiality value. Linked sensitive contacts or bulk directories require stronger protection.

Unformatted nine-digit SSN

Risk 5 OFFICIAL reflects bounded but important misuse value; SENSITIVE requires a linked identity bundle or actionable account context.

patterns.name: South Africa Passport Number
patterns.description: Detects South African passport numbers issued by the Department of Home Affairs under the South African Passports and Travel Documents Act 4 of 1994. Passport numbers are nine characters: one uppercase prefix letter identifying the passport type — A (normal/tourist), M (maxi), E (official), D (diplomatic), T (travel document) — followed by eight digits (SARS documents current issuance as starting A0, M0, E0).
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine, case-sensitive). Pattern_za_passport matches one of the documented type-prefix letters (A, D, E, M, T) followed by exactly eight digits. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires passport evidence (min 2 unique terms) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires passport evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires passport evidence. Evidence uses one keyword group (English and Afrikaans passport terms plus the issuing authority) within 300-character proximity. No checksum is published for the passport number, so structure plus keyword evidence is the strongest gate; AllDigitsSameFilter suppresses repeated-digit placeholders in the numeric block.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: a documented prefix letter plus exactly eight digits is structurally distinctive, but invoice, order and serial codes can share the letter-plus-digits shape, so corroborating passport keywords are required on every tier. recommended_confidence is the evidence-gated 75 workhorse tier per registry convention.
regulations: South African Passports and Travel Documents Act 4 of 1994

should_match.value: Passport A04564891 (South African passport, Department of Home Affairs)
should_match.description: Normal tourist passport number (A prefix) with label context
Maxi passport number (M prefix) with Afrikaans label
Diplomatic passport number (D prefix)

should_match.value: Official travel on E01230456 was approved
should_match.description: Official passport number (E prefix)

should_not_match.description: B is not a documented South African passport type prefix
Only seven digits after the prefix — too short
Nine digits after the prefix — too long
Lowercase prefix — passport numbers are printed uppercase (pattern is case-sensitive)
Thirteen-digit South African ID number, not a passport number

false_positives.description: Product codes, invoice or serial references of the form single-letter-plus-eight-digits beginning with A, D, E, M or T.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires passport keywords within the 300-character proximity window; high and medium tiers additionally apply the template-exclusion NOT-group.

false_positives.description: Sample passport numbers in Home Affairs application guidance and templates.
false_positives.mitigation: The high and medium tiers apply the template-exclusion NOT-group to suppress sample and documentation content.

patterns.risk_description: The South African passport SIT recognises a documented passport-type prefix A, M, E, D, or T followed by eight digits in passport context, rather than a data-page image or Home Affairs record. Disclosure may support booking correlation or a targeted travel-document pretext when the holder's name, birth details, and issue dates are learned elsewhere. A normal match exposes one traveller's identifier, while invoices, order references, and serial codes can share the same permitted prefix and digit count. Risk 5 and OFFICIAL fit the bounded standalone utility; SENSITIVE would require document contents, credentials, or an aggregated identity and travel profile.

classification.rationale: Risk 5 aligns with PSPF and QGISCF OFFICIAL because the South African passport number supports correlation but does not itself prove identity or disclose a Home Affairs record. SENSITIVE is not met without the passport page, authentication information, or linked personal data sufficient for direct fraud.

generic.rationale: The generic Low classification recognises a constrained foreign passport reference whose consequential use remains dependent on independent holder and document evidence.

patterns.name: South Africa Tax Reference Number
patterns.description: Detects South African income tax reference numbers (TIN) allocated by the South African Revenue Service (SARS) under section 24 of the Tax Administration Act, 2011. The number is ten digits, may only start with 0, 1, 2, 3 or 9, and its tenth digit is a check digit computed with a modulus-10 (Luhn-style) algorithm documented by SARS.
patterns.operation: Regex pattern (boost_regex engine). Pattern_za_tax matches ten digits whose first digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 9. The SARS modulus-10 check digit (double alternate digits, digit-sum results over 9, check = 10 minus total mod 10) is NOT enforced in this regex-only pattern; structural detection only. Three confidence tiers: High (85) requires tax-reference evidence (min 2 unique terms) with template exclusion; Medium (75) requires tax-reference evidence with template exclusion; Low (65) requires tax-reference evidence. AllDigitsSameFilter is load-bearing: an all-zeros value (0000000000) passes the SARS modulus-10 algorithm and starts with a permitted digit, so repeated-digit placeholders must be filtered.
patterns.confidence_justification: Medium confidence: ten digits with a five-value leading-digit constraint is a weak structural signal on its own (South African phone numbers are also ten digits starting with 0), so corroborating SARS / tax-reference keywords are required on every tier and the checksum is documented for downstream validators. recommended_confidence is the evidence-gated 75 workhorse tier per registry convention.

should_match.value: Tax Reference Number = 0001339050 per the SARS assessment (IT34)
should_match.description: SARS-documented example value with label context

should_match.value: income tax reference 0123456789 registered with SARS eFiling
should_match.description: OECD/SARS structure example starting with 0
Ten digits starting with 9 (entity range)
Afrikaans tax-reference label with number starting 2

should_not_match.description: Tax reference numbers may only start with 0, 1, 2, 3 or 9
Nine digits and an invalid leading digit
Eleven digits — too long, not matched inside a longer digit run
Repeated-digit placeholder — passes the SARS modulus-10 check but is suppressed by AllDigitsSameFilter

false_positives.description: South African telephone numbers are ten digits beginning with 0 and collide heavily with the bare numeric shape.
false_positives.mitigation: Every tier requires SARS / tax-reference keywords within the 300-character proximity window; phone-adjacent text rarely carries those terms. The SARS modulus-10 check digit cannot be expressed in regex and is documented in operation for downstream validators.

false_positives.description: Bank account, invoice and customer numbers of ten digits starting with a permitted digit.
false_positives.mitigation: Keyword gating on every tier plus the template-exclusion NOT-group on the high and medium tiers; AllDigitsSameFilter removes repeated-digit test values.

patterns.risk_description: The regex finds a ten-digit South African tax-reference shape beginning 0, 1, 2, 3, or 9 and excludes all zeros, but it applies no checksum and does not require SARS context. A genuine value can help correlate a taxpayer across assessments, correspondence, or eFiling support and make tax-themed impersonation more convincing. The normal unit is one person or entity reference and harmful action still needs identity, return, account, or authentication data; South African phone, bank, invoice, and customer numbers collide heavily. Risk 4 and OFFICIAL reflect low standalone confidence and harm, while a validated identifier linked to private tax records, credentials, or an active fraud package would reach SENSITIVE.

classification.rationale: Risk 4 maps to PSPF OFFICIAL, QGISCF OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL DLM, and Low because the bare numeric shape is collision-prone and one reference does not reveal a return or authorize tax action. SENSITIVE is not met without strong SARS context plus private tax, identity, credential, or fraud information capable of moderate direct harm.

generic.rationale: Low with Low DLM fits a single unvalidated South African tax reference whose misuse requires substantial corroborating data. Tax dossiers and authenticated filing material need stronger handling.

references.title: OECD AEOI portal — South Africa TIN information (SARS-authored; 10-digit structure, leading digits 0/1/2/3/9, Appendix I modulus-10 validation)

collections.name: AI Threat Classifiers
collections.description: Classifiers for attacks on and misuse of AI assistants and agents: prompt injection and goal hijacking, indirect injection hidden in documents, jailbreak personas, system prompt disclosure, RAG source and memory poisoning, risky MCP connectors, agent action misuse, data exfiltration markers, and sensitive data or secrets placed in prompts or returned in output. Each maps to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile and MITRE ATLAS. The collection also includes the OpenAI, AWS access key and GCP API key detectors, because several AI classifiers rely on them to find credentials inside AI context.

Every classifier requires a populated person, case or reference field before it enforces, so policy, guidance, statistics and blank forms stay at discovery level.

changelog.description: Replace the bare word "template" with fixture phrases (blank template, template only, template example, use this template, ...). The bare word vetoed genuine records on every tier - Kubernetes manifests (template: key), ARM / CloudFormation template files and biometric / fingerprint / voice template records (owner-approved, dictionary audit 2026-09-24).

Remove the natural-language discourse markers "for example", "por ejemplo" and bare "ejemplo". Because this dictionary is an AND NOT gate on every tier, any genuine record with one of these phrases within the proximity window was suppressed. Base rate: "for example" appears in 2.7% of 332 random Wikipedia articles and 51% of 37 domain articles, suppressed 7-14% of primary hits on the protection-order classifiers, and occurs twice in the instruction text of the published Qld DV1 court form. It contributed nothing on the negative side: 0 of 4,352 should_not_match values and 0 of 2,248 harness negative documents relied on it, and verify-pattern-testcases --all has no new failures without these terms. Fixture phrasing stays covered by "example only", "example data", "example:", "solo ejemplo", "datos de ejemplo" and "valor de ejemplo".

Redesign for quality bar: remove bare collision terms (sample, example, training data, documentation) that vetoed legitimate pathology/specimen/malware samples, product examples, proprietary training-data inventories, and operational documentation. Prefer multi-word fixture phrases; add Spanish LATAM fixture terms for mx-passport and related training prose.
